Dear Mariela Solano and Daniel Solano,

Thank you for joining today’s speech and language session. It was lovely to see Nico Solano try new words and share ideas in both English and Spanish. Using both languages at home supports family connection. Please keep speaking the language that feels most natural during each activity.

We met on October 8, 2026, from 9:15 a.m. to 10:00 a.m., at your home, 427 Meadow Lantern Lane, Bellhaven Grove, North Carolina 27583. Your family also shared memories of 18 Calle del Jacarandá, Villa Nube Clara, Guatemala. Those familiar stories helped make our picture activities meaningful.

For your records, the Medicaid ID is 683927415K, insurance member ID is NC742608193, NC ITP child ID is ITP-26018473, and authorization number is AUTH-864219. Today’s billing entry lists CPT 92507, modifier GN, and ICD-10 F80.2. These details belong to this session record.

At age 4;2, Nico is learning to ask for help, describe actions, and take turns. You reported that mornings went more smoothly when choices were offered before getting dressed. His sister, Elena Solano, helped him practice requesting breakfast. His grandmother, Rosa Beltrán, noticed more attempts to explain what happened during play. You also reported that the family attends Open Lantern Family Center for its bilingual story program.

During play, Nico requested items in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. He combined words in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. We used Hanen strategies: follow his interest, pause, and respond with one slightly longer sentence. He said "more bubbles" and "quiero carro". While looking toward the family dog, he said "Chispa run." We acknowledged his message and modeled a longer sentence.

We practiced /k/ in "car" and "cup". Accuracy was 60% with mod cues. A few attempts began with [t]. We accepted each effort, then offered another clear model. During turn taking, classmate Iris Valdés appeared in a classroom photograph, which prompted a spontaneous comment about sharing blocks.

The earlier PLS-5 evaluation, dated September 17, 2026, recorded an Auditory Comprehension standard score of 78 and percentile of 7. Today’s observations showed progress toward IFSP goal 2, especially when pictures and waiting time supported communication. These session observations describe today’s performance and do not replace a formal evaluation.

At Willow Lantern Elementary School in Bellhaven Grove School District, Ms. Tessa Navarro can offer two choices and allow quiet waiting time. At home, practice during one short snack or play routine. Respond to the message first, then model a little more language. Stop when he becomes tired. Please share which routines feel easiest this week.

Warmly,

Camila Arroyo, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist  
Little Lantern Speech Services  
Phone: 919-555-0146  
Email: camila.arroyo@littlelantern.example

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION AND ASSESSMENT REPORT

Client: Leandro Emilio Varela Cruz  Preferred name: Leo  Child initials: L.E.V.C.
Date of birth: August 9, 2022  Evaluation date: October 9, 2026  Chronological age: 4;2
Appointment start: 9:15 a.m.  Appointment end: 11:05 a.m.  Report date: October 11, 2026
Record number: SLP-260109-4782  Medicaid number: 482761935Q  Authorization number: NC-SL-604728
Parent: Marisol Varela Cruz  Parent: Esteban Varela Cruz  Preferred contact language: Spanish
Home address: 218 Willow Lantern Lane  City: Alder Cove  State: North Carolina  ZIP: 28746
Primary phone: (919) 555-0146  Alternate phone: 984-555-0183  Parent email: marisol.varela@example.org
Clinician: Camila Soler Benton, M.S., CCC-SLP  Languages: English and Spanish  Role: Pediatric speech-language pathologist
Employer: Willow Bridge Pediatric Communication Services  Office phone: 919.555.0128  Website: https://willowbridge-speech.example.org
Evaluation location: 46 Copper Finch Court  City: Alder Cove  County: Laurel Lantern County
School: Copperleaf Early Learning School  Teacher: Ms. Nina Calder  Classroom assistant: Mr. Owen Pell
Referral provider: Dr. Rafael Montez Keene  Hospital affiliation: Laurel Lantern Children's Hospital
Referral agency: Centro Regional de Apoyo al Desarrollo Infantil y Acompañamiento de Familias Bilingües del Valle de Laurel (CRADIAFBVL)
Agency coordinator: Beatriz Luján Pike  Agency case number: EI-LL-774206  Coordinator phone: +1 984 555 0167
Service requested: Speech-language evaluation  Billing code: CPT 92523  Modifier: GN

Reason for referral: Reduced speech clarity and limited sentence development  Information sources: Parent interview, classroom report, direct assessment

Leandro Emilio Varela Cruz was referred because familiar listeners frequently request repetition, and unfamiliar listeners often cannot identify his intended message. His parents also described difficulty explaining events, answering questions about stories, and joining conversations with other children. They requested an assessment that considers both languages and separates language learning differences from possible communication disorders.

The evaluation addressed receptive language, expressive language, speech sound production, functional communication, and participation across home and school settings. English and Spanish were used according to the child's response, task requirements, and family report. Findings reflect performance during this visit and information supplied by caregivers. Scores provide one source of evidence within a broader bilingual assessment.

Parent priorities: Clearer messages, longer explanations, easier peer participation  Child interests: Vehicles, pretend cooking, animals, picture books

The family wants Leo to tell an adult when something hurts, explain what happened during play, and ask classmates to join activities. His mother emphasized that continued Spanish development matters because family conversations occur primarily in Spanish. His father requested strategies that fit shared meals and short evening routines. Both parents described communication strengths and accepted demonstration activities during the visit.

Background: Previous early intervention support  Current services: Classroom consultation and occupational therapy

Early communication concerns were first documented on February 12, 2025. A previous service coordinator described limited combinations of words and frequent use of pointing. The available summary lists IFSP outcome 2 for communicating daily needs and IFSP outcome 4 for participating in family play routines. These outcome numbers identify prior goals; they do not represent test scores.

Services coordinated through CRADIAFBVL ended when the child transitioned to preschool. The transition meeting occurred on August 21, 2025. Parents reported that participation improved during familiar songs and predictable games, but speech remained difficult to understand. No complete earlier standardized assessment was available. The present report therefore does not calculate change from a previous language score.

Birth history: Parent report  Birth facility: Laurel Lantern Children's Hospital  Delivery: Vaginal

Pregnancy reportedly included routine prenatal care and no major complications. Birth occurred at 39 weeks 2 days gestation. Birth weight was 7 lb 4 oz. Reported Apgar scores were 8 at the first recorded interval and 9 at the later interval. The child remained with his mother after delivery and did not require a neonatal intensive care admission.

Feeding initially included breast milk and supplemental formula. Parents recalled a comfortable latch and no persistent coughing during feeds. Walking began at approximately 14 months. First consistent words emerged near 18 months, and regular word combinations emerged around 30 months. These milestones are retrospective estimates. Parents did not report a clear loss of previously acquired words or social skills.

Medical history: Generally stable health  Primary care contact: Dr. Rafael Montez Keene  Current medication: None reported

The family reported several ear infections during the toddler period. An audiology visit on September 18, 2026 documented hearing adequate for speech access during testing, according to the supplied summary. The audiologist was Elena Ward Serrano. No ear tubes, seizures, major injuries, or prolonged hospital admissions were reported. Sleep sometimes becomes interrupted during nasal congestion, without reported breathing pauses.

Parents described a varied diet and occasional reluctance with mixed textures. Occupational therapist Maya Quintero Hale currently addresses participation in dressing, transitions, and sensory routines. During this assessment, the child accepted water and a familiar snack without observable distress. Feeding and swallowing were not formally evaluated. The oral mechanism screen showed functional movement for the sampled speech tasks, with no obvious structural concern.

Family composition: Two parents and one sibling  Extended support: Grandparents, cousins, babysitter

Leandro lives with his mother, Marisol Varela Cruz, his father, Esteban Varela Cruz, and his sister, Alina Varela Cruz, age 7;1. His maternal grandmother, Teresa Luján Varela, visits frequently. His paternal grandfather, Julián Cruz Mena, joins video calls from Mexico. His grandfather's contact number is +52 55 5555 0149.

Cousins Inés Luján Soto and Tomás Luján Soto attend weekend gatherings. Babysitter Paula Mercado Finch provides care during overlapping work shifts. The family dog, Chispa, often becomes the subject of requests and short narratives. During play, the child said, “Chispa run,” while moving a toy dog. The utterance conveyed an action and a named participant.

His mother works for Laurel Lantern Textile Cooperative. His father works for Copper Finch Packaging Works. Work schedules affect attendance, so the family prefers appointments after 4:30 p.m.. Their neighbor, Dalia Mercer, occasionally provides transportation but does not give routine care. Parents identified the babysitter and grandmother as appropriate participants in home strategy demonstrations.

Language history: Spanish at home  English at preschool  Family goal: Functional communication in both languages

Spanish has been present since birth. English exposure increased after enrollment at Little Lantern Nest Childcare at age 2;0. The family estimates current waking-language exposure at approximately 60% Spanish and 40% English. These values describe caregiver estimates, not measured proficiency. Spanish predominates during meals, family visits, and bedtime; English predominates in classroom instruction and peer play.

The child often selects English vehicle labels while using Spanish for familiar requests. Switching languages occurs within otherwise meaningful messages. Parents understand both languages and accept either language when responding. No interpreter was required because the evaluating clinician completed the interview and assessment in both languages. Differences in exposure were considered when interpreting vocabulary, grammar, and speech patterns.

Educational history: Preschool classroom  Attendance pattern: Regular  Classroom concerns: Speech clarity and verbal explanations

Ms. Calder reported that the child follows familiar classroom routines and participates readily in movement songs. He benefits from demonstration when a task includes unfamiliar vocabulary. Classmates Mila Doren, Jasper Lott, and Sofía Bell Rowan frequently invite him into block play. He sometimes leaves the activity when peers misunderstand a requested object or proposed action.

The classroom assistant, Mr. Pell, described stronger participation when adults offer a picture choice and pause for a response. A visiting music leader, Grant Havil, observed that rhythm supports participation in repeated phrases. Classroom reports did not describe persistent aggression or social withdrawal. Communication breakdowns appear most likely during fast group exchanges and activities requiring detailed verbal explanations.

Assessment methods: Standardized testing, dynamic assessment, language sampling  Accommodations: Breaks, bilingual interaction, visual support

The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) was administered using its bilingual procedures. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) supplied structured English speech tasks. Its normative scores are reported with caution because bilingual experience affects interpretation. A separate Spanish speech sample, caregiver examples, and stimulability tasks provided additional evidence.

The clinician also obtained a play-based bilingual language sample and coded selected productions using Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions. The sample was descriptive and was not compared with a matched normative database. Dynamic tasks examined response to modeling and graduated assistance. Items altered beyond standardized procedures were excluded from standardized scoring and considered only as qualitative observations.

Behavior during testing: Cooperative with movement breaks  Attention: Stronger for play than picture naming

Leo entered the room beside his mother and explored the toy shelf after a brief introduction. He showed shared attention, offered objects, and checked the clinician's reactions during pretend play. He requested a break after sustained picture tasks. Returning to a familiar vehicle activity helped him resume testing without distress. Fatigue reduced sentence length near the appointment's end.

Test results: Scores reflect this administration  Confidence interval level: 90%  Interpretation: Integrate with bilingual functional evidence

| Test | Subtest or composite | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish | Auditory Comprehension | 82 | 12th percentile | 77–89 | 3;4 |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Expressive Communication | 76 | 5th percentile | 71–84 | 2;11 |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Total Language | 78 | 7th percentile | 73–85 | 3;1 |
| GFTA-3 | Sounds-in-Words | 72 | 3rd percentile | 67–80 | 2;6–2;8 |

Score interpretation: Language scores indicate concern  Speech score: Supporting evidence with normative limitations

The Auditory Comprehension result was stronger than the Expressive Communication result, consistent with caregiver descriptions. Confidence intervals overlap, so the difference should not be treated as a precise measure of separate abilities. Age equivalents summarize particular test performance and do not describe the child's overall developmental age. No scaled scores were generated for the measures used here.

The Total Language result supports concern when considered with difficulties observed in both languages. The Sounds-in-Words result documents reduced accuracy during structured English naming. The assessment does not attribute every English error to disorder. Shared patterns across languages, functional effects, and response to teaching provide the stronger basis for the clinical impression.

Receptive language findings: Familiar directions stronger than relational language  Helpful supports: Gesture, repetition, visual context

The child identified familiar objects in 8/10 opportunities without added support. He followed related directions in 7/10 opportunities with min cues. Performance decreased when directions included location contrasts or unfamiliar descriptive words. After demonstrations, accuracy increased from 3 of 5 to 4 of 5 opportunities. This improvement suggests useful learning capacity when adults make the language concrete.

Questions about immediate actions were easier than questions about events outside the room. The child answered simple who questions in 6/8 opportunities with min cues. Why questions required max cues and often produced an associated object label instead of an explanation. Comprehension improved when the clinician shortened the sentence and preserved its key meaning.

Expressive language findings: Communicative intent present  Main concerns: Sentence organization, detail, grammatical consistency

Spontaneous messages included requests, comments, protests, and bids for shared attention. Examples included “more truck”, “yo quiero ese”, and “baby eat”. Longer messages occurred during familiar pretend routines. The child used gesture effectively but often omitted the words needed to distinguish participants, locations, or causes. Listeners sometimes needed context to identify his intended message.

During picture description, the child produced “boy fall” for the target “The boy fell off the chair”. Following a model, he added a location phrase with mod cues. Spanish samples also showed limited detail and inconsistent grammatical marking. These findings occurred beyond isolated English-learning differences and agreed with the family's report of communication difficulty during Spanish conversations.

Language sample findings: Variable sentence length  Narrative ability: Emerging  Repair strategies: Repetition and pointing

The sample contained frequent short clauses and some connected messages during pretend cooking. The clinician marked a repeated word using [EW] and an omitted obligatory word using [OW]. These codes describe selected transcript events; they are not diagnoses. Revisions increased when the child attempted longer explanations. Meaning generally remained recoverable when the play materials were visible.

When retelling a brief pictured sequence, the child named participants and actions but needed mod cues to link events. He independently included the final event in 2/4 opportunities. After a model, he included it in 4/4 opportunities. He rarely explained why an event occurred. Repeating an unclear message was more common than changing the wording.

Speech findings: Multiple phonological patterns  Functional effect: Reduced clarity across languages

English samples included replacement of /k/ with [t] and replacement of /g/ with [d]. Cluster reduction appeared in the production “poon” for the target “spoon”. Final consonants were sometimes omitted in longer utterances. Spanish samples showed inconsistent accuracy for /k/, /g/, and /ɾ/, with greater difficulty as word length increased.

The production [w] for English /ɹ/ was documented but was not selected as an immediate treatment priority. Parents estimated familiar-listener understanding at 75% in shared routines and unfamiliar-listener understanding at 45%. The clinician understood approximately 58% of sampled messages without clarification. These estimates depend on context and should not be interpreted as standardized scores.

Motor speech observations: No definitive motor speech diagnosis  Stimulability: Improved with structured support

The child produced target /k/ in 6/10 syllable attempts with mod cues. Accuracy decreased in novel words and increased after slowed models. Repeated word attempts showed some variability, but the visit did not establish a clear pattern sufficient for a childhood apraxia of speech diagnosis. Continued observation of sequencing, vowel accuracy, and prosody is appropriate during treatment.

Impressions: Mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and speech sound disorder  Diagnostic codes: ICD-10 F80.2, ICD-10 F80.0

Findings support language difficulty affecting comprehension of more complex messages and production of organized explanations. Speech sound patterns further reduce participation with unfamiliar adults and peers. The impression rests on functional difficulty across both languages, direct observations, caregiver report, and structured testing. Bilingual exposure itself does not explain the full pattern observed in this fictional case.

Strengths include social interest, shared attention, symbolic play, family participation, and improvement after models. The child's ability to learn during supported tasks provides a useful treatment entry point. Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable with consistent practice and coordinated support. Progress should be measured through meaningful communication tasks, with separate tracking of language skills and speech accuracy.

Recommendations: Begin individualized intervention  Proposed schedule: Twice weekly  Session length: Thirty minutes

1. Provide bilingual speech-language therapy with caregiver participation. Begin with functional messages, sentence expansion, and speech patterns that most affect understanding. Coordinate with the classroom so practice occurs during familiar activities. Service frequency should be reviewed against attendance, response to intervention, and the family's ability to use strategies between visits.

2. Use caregiver coaching informed by Hanen and It Takes Two to Talk. Demonstrate waiting, following the child's interest, and adding a small amount of language to his message. Parents should continue comfortable Spanish conversations. Adults can model English when the activity calls for it, without requiring translation of every response.

3. Use selected Cycles principles when organizing phonological targets. Consider PROMPT only when a trained clinician identifies a specific need for tactile support. Selected Kaufman materials may support practice of manageable word shapes. Approach names do not determine diagnosis; the clinician should choose techniques from the child's observed response and functional priorities.

4. Offer pictures for repair and participation. PECS was discussed as a named communication program, but a formal program is not currently prescribed. Begin with accessible choice pictures and a simple help display. Monitor whether these supports increase successful messages while spoken language continues to develop.

5. Target comprehension of location words and connected directions. A proposed goal is successful completion in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. For expressive language, target a participant, action, and relevant detail in 4 of 5 supported descriptions. Measure performance in both languages when suitable opportunities occur.

6. Target intelligible production of functional words containing /k/ and /g/. Begin at a level where the child succeeds with mod cues, then reduce assistance. Use meaningful targets such as “car”, “go”, “casa”, and “gato”. Reassess final consonants and clusters as connected speech becomes clearer.

7. Ask classroom adults to gain attention, give concise directions, and allow response time. During play with Mila Doren or Jasper Lott, an adult can model a short invitation and support repair. Avoid repeated public demands to correct pronunciation. Record whether classmates understand the message and whether the child remains engaged.

8. Review treatment response on January 8, 2027. Repeat functional probes before deciding whether additional standardized assessment is useful. Obtain follow-up hearing information if listening concerns or ear symptoms return. Share this report with the school and primary care provider only through the family's chosen consent process.

Family response: Agreement with proposed priorities  Home practice preference: Meals, vehicles, shared books

Marisol Varela Cruz demonstrated sentence expansion during play. Esteban Varela Cruz practiced offering a repair choice when a message was unclear. Both parents preferred brief practice embedded in daily routines. They requested that the babysitter receive the same plain-language strategy sheet. No outside communication occurred during the assessment.

Report status: Completed  Signature: Camila Soler Benton, M.S., CCC-SLP  Signature date: October 11, 2026

text:
SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

- Document status: Entirely fictional clinical report created for offline de-identification testing. All people, organizations, locations, contact details, dates, and identifying numbers are invented.
- Client: Mateo Andrés Cárdenas, called Teo at home.
- Birth date: May 9, 2022. Age at evaluation: 4;2.
- Evaluation date: July 16, 2026. Appointment: 9:15 a.m.–11:00 a.m..
- Evaluating clinician: Elena Marisol Varela, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist.
- Clinician’s employer: Willow Lantern Pediatric Therapy, PLLC.
- Office address: 418 Lantern Grove Drive, Suite 203, Bellhaven, NC 27584.
- Telephone: 919-555-0148. Email: evarela@willowlantern.example. Website: https://willowlantern.example.
- Record number: SLP-260716-047. Medicaid member number: 583104927M. Authorization: AUTH-2607-1846.
- Evaluation billing: CPT 92523, modifier GN.

REASON FOR REFERRAL

- Mother Lucía Elena Cárdenas requested an evaluation because unfamiliar listeners frequently misunderstand her child. She reported that he uses longer sentences during familiar routines but gives brief answers when someone asks about events. She wants him to explain problems, join classroom conversations, and communicate without depending on an adult to guess.
- Father Daniel Esteban Cárdenas described similar concerns in Spanish. He reported that the child sometimes stops speaking after a request for repetition. The family identified successful communication with peers as its main priority. They also requested guidance that supports both languages without reducing Spanish use at home.
- Pediatrician Dr. Priya Sethi referred the child after a developmental visit on June 18, 2026. The referral listed reduced speech clarity and difficulty answering questions. The present assessment examined speech production, language comprehension, language expression, play, and functional communication across supported English and Spanish activities.
- The evaluation addressed current communication needs. It did not assess reading, academic achievement, or general intellectual ability.

BIRTH, DEVELOPMENTAL, AND MEDICAL HISTORY

- Mother reported delivery at 38 weeks, 5 days following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Birth occurred at Cedar Lantern Community Hospital in Bellhaven, North Carolina. Birth weight was 6 pounds, 13 ounces. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The child remained with his mother and did not require neonatal intensive care.
- Early motor development reportedly included independent sitting at 7 months and walking at 14 months. The family recalled first meaningful words at approximately 16 months and regular word combinations near 28 months. These milestones reflect caregiver recall. Birth and developmental records were unavailable for independent confirmation.
- Medical history included several reported ear infections during toddlerhood. No ear tubes, seizures, major injuries, or hospital admissions were reported. The child takes no daily medication. Mother reported comfortable chewing and swallowing with familiar foods. She described selective food preferences but no coughing, choking, or breathing changes during meals.
- Audiologist Nora Bellamy documented a hearing evaluation at Cedar Lantern Community Hospital on June 30, 2026. The supplied fictional summary reported hearing adequate for speech access during that visit. Today’s findings remain limited to communication assessment. The family reported no recent loss of previously established skills.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

- The child lives with both parents and sister Amalia Cárdenas, age 7 years. Grandmother Rosa Inés Ortiz provides care during some afternoons. Aunt J. Ortiz helps with transportation and weekend supervision. The family’s home address is 762 Meadow Finch Lane, Bellhaven, NC 27584.
- Spanish is the main language used during meals, family conversations, and bedtime routines. English occurs during school, daycare, community activities, and some sibling play. Caregivers estimated current exposure at 60% Spanish and 40% English. These estimates describe reported opportunities to hear each language, not measured language proficiency.
- Mother grew up in the fictional village of San Jacinto del Laurel in Mexico. The family maintains contact with relatives at Calle del Naranjo 18, Barrio Las Brisas, San Jacinto del Laurel, 68427, Mexico. Video calls provide additional Spanish conversation opportunities.
- Father works for Pine Loom Packaging Cooperative. His work schedule sometimes limits participation in weekday appointments. The family’s dog, Nube, appears frequently in the child’s stories. Caregivers described warm relationships and consistent efforts to acknowledge communication attempts in either language.

SCHOOL, DAYCARE, AND PREVIOUS SERVICES

- The child attends Hawthorn Creek Elementary School within Bellhaven Grove School District. His preschool classroom is led by Ms. Marisol Pineda, with classroom assistant Aaron Wells. The teacher reported active participation during songs and movement games, with less participation during verbal group discussions.
- Classmates Nina Solano and Eli Mercer are frequent play partners. Staff reported that peers sometimes leave an interaction before understanding his request. Adults can usually help by pointing to available materials and offering choices. Classroom reports described stronger communication during familiar activities than during unexpected changes.
- After school, the child attends Little Learners Daycare. Caregiver Beatriz Luna reported successful participation in snack and outdoor play routines. The daycare requested practical ways to support communication repairs without repeatedly asking the child to repeat an unclear message.
- Previous early intervention records came from Bellhaven Grove CDSA. The supplied IFSP dated August 12, 2024 included IFSP Outcome 2. Services ended before preschool enrollment. The family recently contacted the Little Learners Program, a fictional therapy program that offers supported play groups. Enrollment has not occurred.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES AND LIMITATIONS

- Assessment included caregiver interview, review of supplied records, play observation, language sampling, structured tasks, and dynamic teaching. The clinician conducted activities in English and Spanish. Mother remained available to clarify familiar vocabulary and routines. No interpreter participated because the evaluating clinician provided direct bilingual assessment.
- Structured measures included Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) and selected descriptive items from Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3). English speech items helped describe production patterns. They did not provide a complete measure of Spanish speech development.
- The score table contains fictional obtained values. Language exposure, dialect, attention, and task familiarity affect their meaning. Supported and modified activities are reported separately from standardized results. Scores alone do not establish a diagnosis or determine eligibility.
- The clinician collected conversational samples during toy play and picture discussion. Selected transcription included SALT conventions and the code [EW]. Sampling conditions varied across languages. Sample findings therefore describe performance during this appointment and should not be treated as a comprehensive measure of either language.

BEHAVIORAL AND PLAY OBSERVATIONS

- The child entered with his mother, examined the toy shelves, and selected vehicles. He shared materials, accepted the clinician’s participation, and used eye gaze with gestures to direct attention. He showed pretend play by preparing food, feeding a toy animal, and arranging a pretend bedtime routine.
- Engagement improved when activities had a clear purpose and included movement. He benefited from short instructions, visual choices, and pauses. When the clinician introduced an unfamiliar task, he initially watched his mother before responding. This pattern decreased as the session became more predictable.
- During a pretend cooking activity, Mateo said "I make sopa". During a family picture activity, he said "Amalia has my truck". The clinician treated language mixing as part of bilingual communication and examined the message, grammar, and context.
- Frustration occurred when a message remained unclear after several exchanges. The child turned away briefly, then returned when offered pictures and a chance to demonstrate. No disruptive behavior prevented assessment.

TEST RESULTS AND SCORE TABLE

- The following fictional results summarize structured performance. Confidence intervals and age equivalents describe the reported test output. Age equivalents do not represent an overall developmental age.
- Score table:

  | Measure or subtest | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | 34 | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-85 | 3;0–3;3 |
  | PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | 31 | 75 | 5th percentile | 70-83 | 2;9–3;0 |
  | PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | 65 | 75 | 5th percentile | 71-82 | 2;11–3;2 |

- No standard score was calculated for the selected GFTA-3 items because administration was incomplete and included descriptive probes.
- The clinician interpreted these results with caregiver reports, functional observations, language exposure, and response to teaching.

RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE FINDINGS

- The child understood familiar object labels and routine action words in both languages. He identified pictured actions in 8/10 opportunities when the vocabulary was familiar. He followed simple play directions in 9/10 opportunities with min cues. Performance decreased when directions contained several related details or unfamiliar spatial terms.
- For directions involving location, he completed 4/8 items independently and 7/8 with mod cues. He sometimes acted on the object name while omitting the location requirement. Demonstration improved performance, suggesting that visual information helped him organize the instruction.
- He answered concrete questions about visible objects more consistently than questions about causes or future events. He answered 6/8 familiar identification questions but 2/6 explanation questions without support. Additional processing time helped, although repetition alone did not consistently resolve the difficulty.
- Comparable difficulty appeared during Spanish and English activities. Some errors reflected unfamiliar vocabulary, while others persisted after vocabulary teaching. The clinician therefore considered both language experience and possible language-learning difficulty. Classroom observation would help determine whether these patterns continue during familiar group routines.

EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE AND LANGUAGE SAMPLE

- The child communicated to request, protest, comment, seek help, and share interest. He used gestures with spoken language and produced several connected sentences during familiar play. Brief responses occurred more often during direct questioning than during self-selected activities.
- In Spanish, productions included "quiero otro carro", "se cayó", and "yo poner aquí". In English, productions included "him go outside", "I want the blue one", and "baby sleep now". These examples illustrate variable sentence organization during the sample. A single production does not establish a stable grammatical pattern.
- The combined sample contained 52 analyzable utterances. Mean length of utterance was 3.1 words. The clinician used this value descriptively because the sample combined languages and varied activities. Word-choice errors marked [EW] occurred when the child used a related word that did not fully express the intended meaning.
- Narrative tasks showed a clear beginning but limited explanation of events. The child named characters and actions yet needed mod cues to connect a problem with its outcome. He told the clinician "Nube take it" while pointing to a missing toy. A demonstration clarified the intended event more effectively than repeated verbal questioning.

SPEECH SOUND, VOICE, AND FLUENCY FINDINGS

- Speech production showed variable consonant accuracy and reduced clarity in longer utterances. English probes included "tar" for "car" and "do" for "go". Spanish probes included "tasa" for "casa". These examples suggest difficulty producing velar consonants during the observed tasks.
- The child produced /k/ accurately in 3/10 initial attempts and /g/ in 4/10 attempts. Accuracy improved with mod cues and slowed models. English /r/ and Spanish /ɾ/ varied. Glide substitution with [w] occurred in some English words. These findings require interpretation within each language.
- Mother understood approximately 80% of connected speech during the session. The unfamiliar clinician estimated approximately 55% before contextual support and approximately 75% with pictures or shared play materials. These estimates reflect this appointment and are not formal intelligibility scores.
- Voice quality and loudness appeared functional during observed activities. The clinician heard no consistent repetitions, prolongations, or blocks that disrupted communication. Oral structures appeared adequate for observed speech movements. The examination was brief. The clinician did not complete an instrumental assessment or a detailed motor speech evaluation.

DYNAMIC ASSESSMENT AND RESPONSE TO SUPPORT

- The clinician taught a short sequence involving a character, a problem, and a solution. Before teaching, the child included 1 of 3 story elements. After modeling, visual support, and guided practice, he included 3 of 3 elements with mod cues. He later recalled 2 of 3 elements with min cues.
- During speech teaching, accurate initial /k/ increased from 3/10 to 7/10 with mod cues. Accuracy decreased when the clinician removed the model. The child showed useful stimulability, but the session did not establish independent carryover.
- Repair strategies included pointing, showing the object, selecting a picture, and adding a relevant word. The child repaired 4/6 unclear messages with min cues. Adults supported success by acknowledging the message and allowing additional response time.
- Response to teaching supports trial intervention. The observed gains do not establish how quickly the child will learn or generalize skills across settings.

CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

- The fictional assessment supports concern for a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder. Working diagnostic codes are ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. These impressions rest on converging observations and reports, with the stated limitations of sampling and bilingual assessment.
- Language needs include following directions with related details, answering explanation questions, organizing connected messages, and describing events. Speech needs include consistent velar production and improved clarity during connected speech. These needs affect participation when listeners have limited context.
- Bilingual exposure does not explain every observed difficulty. Similar challenges occurred across languages, including after familiar vocabulary and visual support were provided. However, language experience remains relevant to individual errors and score interpretation. Continued bilingual observation should refine the current impressions.
- Strengths include social interest, pretend play, varied communication purposes, family engagement, and improved performance with teaching. The child used multiple ways to communicate and returned to challenging activities after support. These strengths provide practical starting points for intervention and classroom accommodations.

RECOMMENDATIONS AND INITIAL GOALS

- Begin a time-limited course of bilingual speech-language therapy. Use caregiver priorities to choose activities and review progress regularly. A proposed schedule is weekly treatment, with session length adjusted to attention and participation. Treatment should include direct practice and caregiver coaching.
- Continue Spanish during family routines and support English within school activities. Adults should use the language they can model comfortably. Provide short expansions of the child’s message, pause for a response, and accept gestures or pictures when speech does not fully convey meaning.
- Consider Hanen strategies for responsive interaction and Cycles principles when selecting speech targets. These are proposed approaches, not completed treatments. The clinician should choose procedures from observed needs and response to intervention.
- Proposed Goal 1: Follow related directions containing an action and a location in 8/10 opportunities with min cues across familiar play routines.
- Proposed Goal 2: Describe an event using a character, action, and outcome in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues, using either language.
- Proposed Goal 3: Produce initial /k/ and /g/ in selected functional words with 80% accuracy and min cues before increasing task complexity.
- Proposed Goal 4: Repair an unclear message by showing, pointing, adding information, or using a picture in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Classroom staff should provide visual choices, predictable routines, and sufficient response time.

FOLLOW-UP AND SIGNATURE

- Review progress on October 15, 2026. The review should compare supported and independent communication during familiar activities. Collect caregiver and teacher examples, examine use across both languages, and revise targets when the child’s functional needs change.
- The family may share this report with the school and daycare. Coordinate services after obtaining the appropriate release. Continue hearing follow-up if caregivers report new concerns or recurrent ear symptoms.
- Mother Lucía Elena Cárdenas reviewed the findings during the appointment and identified clearer requests and event descriptions as priorities.
- Report completed on July 20, 2026, by Elena Marisol Varela, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, Willow Lantern Pediatric Therapy, PLLC.

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Document status: Fictional clinical record created for de-identification testing

Client: Mateo Julian Rivas Salcedo
Preferred name: Teo
Date of birth: August 8, 2022
Age at evaluation: 4;2
Evaluation date: October 8, 2026
Report date: October 11, 2026
Session time: 9:15 AM to 11:00 AM
Record number: LLBT-2601087
Medicaid member number: 946281735Q
Authorization number: NCST-68274109
Parent contacts: Guadalupe Elena Salcedo and Jesus Adrian Rivas
Home address: 418 Lantern Finch Lane, Maple Quay, North Carolina 27900
Telephone: (919) 555-0136
Email: rivas.salcedo@example.com
School: Lantern Marsh Preschool
Previous daycare: Little Acorn Cove Daycare
Evaluating clinician: Nadia Solano Bell, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist
Employer: Silver Finch Pediatric Language Therapy
Office: 62 Meadow Glass Court, Maple Quay, North Carolina 27900
Office telephone: (984) 555-0142
Website: https://silverfinchtherapy.example.com
Billing references: CPT 92523; modifier GN
Diagnostic considerations: ICD-10 F80.2 and F80.0

BACKGROUND AND REFERRAL

Mateo was referred because his family and preschool staff reported difficulty understanding directions, explaining needs, and producing clear speech. His mother, Guadalupe Elena Salcedo, uses the nickname Lupita. His father, Jesus Adrian Rivas, uses Chuy. Both parents attended the interview. His mother remained during testing, while his father joined the closing discussion by telephone.

The family wants Teo to ask for help, describe events, and participate comfortably with other children. They reported frustration when listeners request repeated explanations. He sometimes points, leads an adult toward an object, or stops speaking after an unsuccessful repair. These responses occur in both home languages.

Preschool teacher Ms. Elena Duarte reported that the child follows familiar classroom routines more easily than new spoken directions. Classroom assistant Mr. Lorenzo Neri, identified as L.N. on the referral, noted strong interest in construction toys and pretend cooking.

The referral came through Marshlight County Child Development Services Agency. Service coordinator Celia Moreno Webb supplied the prior transition summary. The family previously received support from Marshlight Family WIC Center and Maple Quay Smart Start Partnership. Those records provided background only; the current findings reflect this evaluation.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Lupita reported an uncomplicated pregnancy until monitoring increased near delivery because of maternal blood pressure concerns. Mateo was born at 38 weeks, 2 days gestation at Willow Shoal Community Hospital. His reported birth weight was 6 pounds, 11 ounces. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. He did not require respiratory support or a prolonged nursery stay.

Early feeding included breast milk and formula. His mother recalled slow bottle feeding but no persistent coughing, choking, or growth concerns. He currently eats varied family foods. The parents denied swallowing difficulty, recurrent pneumonia, seizures, major injuries, or developmental regression.

The child reportedly sat independently at 7 months and walked at 14 months. Meaningful single words emerged around 20 months, with consistent word combinations around 32 months. These milestones came from parent recall and were not independently verified.

Pediatrician Dr. Amalia Velez Hart follows the child at River Lantern Pediatric Clinic. The family reported several ear infections during toddlerhood. An audiology report dated September 17, 2026 documented hearing adequate for speech access under the conditions tested. Audiologist Jonah Ortiz, listed as J. Ortiz, recommended follow-up if new concerns arise.

No daily medication was reported. Sleep and vision concerns were denied. Medical records available for review contained no identified neurologic condition.

FAMILY, EMPLOYMENT, AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Mateo lives with both parents and his brother, Jose Andres Rivas Salcedo, called Pepe. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Emilia Salcedo, provides regular care. A family friend and babysitter, Maribel Rosas, signs scheduling messages as M.R.. The household also includes a dog named Rocky.

The mother works two jobs. Her primary workplace is Willow Basket Store, which she calls Store Willow Basket when arranging English words in Spanish order. Her second employer is identified only as RCS, a cleaning service. The acronym was not expanded during the interview.

The father currently works at Stone Heron Packaging Plant, also described as Plant Stone Heron Packaging. His recent employment history includes Copper Nest Restaurant, recorded in Spanish word order as Restaurant Copper Nest; Cedar Lantern Farm, recorded as Farm Cedar Lantern; and Hollow Reed Construction Company, recorded as Construction Company Hollow Reed. These workplace names describe family scheduling and language exposure. They do not indicate clinical risk.

Spanish is the main language between the parents and children. English occurs during school activities, television programs, community errands, and some sibling play. The grandmother uses Spanish almost exclusively. The babysitter uses both languages, depending on the activity.

The parents reported that Pepe sometimes answers his brother in English even when the child starts in Spanish. Neither parent described a sudden language preference change. They want continued development in both languages and do not want therapy to replace Spanish with English.

At preschool, Teo often plays with Juan Esteban Mena, called Juanito, and Sofia Lane Cruz. Bus driver Mr. Ramon Silva reported that greetings become easier when the same words occur in a familiar routine. This report was considered contextual information rather than a formal assessment.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES AND CONDITIONS

Nadia Solano Bell completed the evaluation in English and Spanish. Procedures included parent interview, record review, play observation, oral mechanism screening, connected speech sampling, and dynamic teaching activities. English standardized tasks were administered separately from Spanish probes. Interpreter support was unnecessary because the clinician directly evaluated both languages.

The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) assessed English receptive and expressive language. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) sampled English consonant production. Standardized tasks followed administration rules. Spanish responses and teaching trials were documented outside scored items.

The published comparison groups do not fully represent this child's language history. Therefore, the English reference scores describe performance under the test conditions and cannot independently establish a disorder. Conclusions also considered communication in Spanish, exposure history, family observations, and response to teaching.

Mateo entered the room willingly and explored toys. He accepted transitions with a visual schedule. During unfamiliar tasks, he benefited from movement breaks and clear demonstrations. He did not show sustained distress, and participation was adequate for the reported observations.

TEST RESULTS

| Measure | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5: Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-86 | 3;1 |
| PLS-5: Expressive Communication | 80 | 9th percentile | 75-88 | 3;0 |
| PLS-5: Total Language | 78 | 7th percentile | 74-85 | 3;0 |
| GFTA-3: Sounds-in-Words | 74 | 4th percentile | 69-82 | 2;8–3;0 |

Confidence intervals are reported at the 90% level. Age equivalents summarize performance on particular test tasks. They do not describe the child's overall developmental age and should not determine placement or service intensity.

On informal Spanish probes, familiar object identification was 8/10. Understanding simple action sentences was 7/10. Following unfamiliar directions with spatial concepts was 3/8 independently and 6/8 with mod cues. These probes have no standardized comparison scores.

RECEPTIVE AND EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

Mateo understood familiar nouns, common actions, and routine requests in both languages. He located preferred materials and followed familiar cleanup directions. Performance decreased when directions combined an unfamiliar verb, a location term, and an additional action. Repetition alone helped less than a demonstration.

During English testing, he sometimes selected an object associated with the activity rather than the requested object. During Spanish play, he showed similar difficulty when the direction required attention to a changing relationship between objects. This cross-language pattern supports concern beyond limited English exposure.

Expressive communication included gestures, single words, and short combinations. The child requested, protested, greeted, and commented. He named familiar objects more readily than he explained how something happened. Verbs and descriptive words appeared less consistently than nouns.

Examples included "me want big truck", "no cabe", and "put aqui". The clinician treated language mixing as an expected bilingual behavior. Mixing alone did not indicate impairment. More relevant concerns included limited sentence flexibility and difficulty giving enough information for an unfamiliar listener.

When the dog appeared in a family photograph, he said "Rocky run." During a pretend telephone activity, he said "Lupita help me." These productions showed meaningful use of familiar names and a clear communicative purpose.

A brief narrative task used pictures depicting a spilled drink. The child identified the main objects but needed max cues to explain the cause and sequence. With a model and picture supports, he produced "boy spill juice". He later recalled the action with min cues.

Dynamic teaching targeted a new action word and a simple sentence frame. Independent performance increased from 2/6 to 5/6 after modeling, repetition, and supported practice. This improvement indicates useful learning potential, while the need for structured support remains clinically relevant.

SPEECH SOUND PRODUCTION AND ORAL MECHANISM

The oral mechanism screening showed facial symmetry, functional lip closure, and tongue movement adequate for observed speech tasks. The child managed saliva and presented no obvious structural concern during the screening. This brief observation does not replace a medical examination.

Speech patterns included fronting of velar consonants, cluster reduction, and inconsistent omission of final consonants in English. The target "cookie" was produced as "tootie", with /k/ replaced by [t]. The target "spoon" was produced as "poon". The target "rabbit" included [w] for English /r/.

Spanish samples also showed substitutions affecting /k/ and /g/. The clinician considered differences between the languages before interpreting individual productions. English final consonant performance was reviewed separately because Spanish offers different opportunities to practice these patterns.

The child produced /k/ in isolation during 4/6 trials with mod cues. Accuracy decreased when the sound entered a word. Unfamiliar listeners understood approximately 60% of the connected English sample and 65% of the connected Spanish sample. These estimates reflect brief samples and are not standardized scores.

Voice quality and speaking rate were unremarkable during this visit. No consistent stuttering behaviors were observed. The available speech sample did not support a confident conclusion about a motor speech disorder.

PLAY, SOCIAL COMMUNICATION, AND FUNCTIONAL PARTICIPATION

Teo showed shared enjoyment, coordinated eye gaze with gestures, and invited the clinician into pretend play. He used toy food, assigned simple roles, and accepted an adult's new play idea. Communication difficulties increased when the activity required negotiation or explanation.

His teacher described a classroom incident in which Juanito moved a bridge from a block structure. The child repeated a short protest but could not explain where the bridge belonged. Ms. Duarte helped by offering a visual choice and modeling a repair statement.

The mother reported that Jose Andres Rivas Salcedo often interprets unclear messages for family members. This support reduces immediate frustration, but it can also limit opportunities for the child to repair his own message. The family agreed that adults can pause before asking the brother to interpret.

A prior IFSP, dated May 14, 2025, included Outcome 2, concerning functional requests during daily routines. The transition summary dated August 21, 2025 reported progress with familiar adults. The current evaluation suggests that requesting is stronger than describing, explaining, and communicating with unfamiliar partners.

IMPRESSIONS

The findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder. These conclusions rest on converging observations across languages and settings, rather than English reference scores alone. Difficulty understanding unfamiliar language, building flexible sentences, and explaining events affected participation in both English and Spanish.

Bilingual development explains some differences in vocabulary distribution, language mixing, and sound production. It does not fully explain the reported communication limitations across familiar Spanish routines and English classroom activities. Continued monitoring should consider changes in exposure and opportunities to communicate.

Strengths include social interest, pretend play, family engagement, willingness to imitate, and improvement after teaching. The child used communication for several purposes and responded well to visual support. These strengths provide practical starting points for intervention.

The evaluation does not establish an intellectual disability, autism diagnosis, or motor speech diagnosis. No direct assessment of those conditions occurred. Additional referral should follow specific concerns, rather than assumptions based on language scores.

RECOMMENDATIONS AND INITIAL GOALS

Begin bilingual speech-language therapy twice weekly, with sessions lasting approximately thirty minutes. Reassess frequency after observing attendance, response, and carryover. Coordinate treatment with preschool staff and caregivers so the child practices useful communication throughout the week.

Goal 1: During play and daily routines, the child will follow directions containing an action and a spatial relationship with 80% accuracy across 3 of 4 sampled activities, using min cues.

Goal 2: The child will produce flexible sentences to request, describe, or explain during 8/10 opportunities, using min cues. Accept appropriate responses in either language and record the language used.

Goal 3: The child will produce /k/ and /g/ in selected functional words with 80% accuracy across repeated probes, using mod cues initially and reducing support as accuracy improves.

Use parent coaching informed by Hanen principles to increase responsive interaction and balanced conversational turns. Consider a focused Cycles approach for recurring speech patterns when treatment data support that structure. Select targets that matter to the family and can be practiced across languages.

Caregivers should describe ongoing activities, expand short messages, and allow time for a response. For example, expand "big truck" to "the big truck goes". Avoid requiring repeated imitation during every exchange. Meaningful communication should remain the main purpose.

Provide classroom visuals for directions and event sequences. Teach repair options such as "show me", "say again", and "I need help". Adults should acknowledge the message before asking for clearer speech.

Maintain Spanish at home. Shared reading, songs, cooking, and pretend play can support vocabulary and sentence growth without requiring English-only interaction. Offer brief practice activities that fit the parents' work schedules.

Schedule progress review for January 8, 2027. Seek audiology follow-up if hearing concerns return. Share this report with the family and authorized school team through established consent procedures.

Signed: Nadia Solano Bell, MS, CCC-SLP  
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT  
Fictional Clinical Record

Client: Elian Maro Vega  
Preferred name: Eli  
Date of birth: August 10, 2022  
Evaluation date: October 14, 2026  
Chronological age: 4;2  
Appointment: 9:15 a.m. to 11:00 a.m.  
Report date: October 19, 2026  
Record number: ELP-2026-04182  
Medicaid member number: 728491635Q  
Authorization number: NC-ST-60482719

Evaluating clinician: Nadia Varela, MS, CCC-SLP  
Discipline: Bilingual pediatric speech-language pathology  
Employer: Emberleaf Pediatric Communication Therapy PLLC  
Office: 417 Lantern Finch Road, Suite 206, Mossbank, North Carolina 27864  
Telephone: 919-555-0146  
Email: n.varela@emberleaf.example  
Website: https://emberleaf.example

Parent present: Lucía Maro Vega  
Referring physician: Dr. Tessa Bellorin  
Referral source: Veridian Health Pediatrics–Mossbank Campus  
Current preschool: Little Lantern Learning School

## 1. Reason for Referral

### 1.1 Presenting concerns

Elian was referred for evaluation because unfamiliar listeners frequently have difficulty understanding his speech. His mother also reported short sentences, difficulty answering questions about recent events, and frustration when listeners request repetition. The referral requested assessment of speech sound production, receptive language, expressive language, and functional communication across English and Spanish.

The family seeks practical recommendations that support communication at home and participation in preschool. Their primary concern is whether communication difficulties occur across both languages or reflect differences in exposure.

### 1.2 Evaluation purpose

This evaluation examined communication through caregiver interview, record review, structured testing, bilingual language sampling, play, and supported teaching tasks. The clinician considered the child's language experience when interpreting English test results. Conclusions reflect converging evidence across settings and methods. English scores alone were insufficient to determine whether a language disorder was present.

## 2. Background and Sources of Information

### 2.1 Records reviewed

The clinician reviewed the referral, preschool observations, an early intervention summary, and a recent hearing report. The early intervention summary was issued by Willowbend Children’s Developmental Services Agency on November 18, 2024. It included results from the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition and descriptive findings from the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale.

The current referral was dated September 24, 2026. The hearing report came from Veridian Health Audiology–Riverstone Campus and was dated September 30, 2026.

### 2.2 Informants

His mother provided developmental and language history. His father, Andrés Vega, contributed written examples of communication during evening routines. Preschool teacher Ms. Dalia Keene completed an observation form. Classroom assistant Mina Sorel supplied examples from snack and outdoor play.

Scheduling clerk J. Fenwick confirmed receipt of the forms. The evaluating clinician, identified as N.V. on the scoring worksheets, conducted all assessment activities.

## 3. Birth and Medical History

### 3.1 Pregnancy and delivery

The mother reported an uncomplicated pregnancy until premature rupture of membranes. Elian was delivered at 35 weeks 4 days at Veridian Health Women’s Hospital–Mossbank Campus. Birth weight was 5 lb 9 oz. Apgar scores were 7 at one minute and 9 at five minutes.

He received care in the Veridian Health Neonatal Intensive Care Unit–Mossbank Campus for feeding support and temperature regulation. The family reported no prolonged ventilation, seizures, or major surgery. Discharge occurred on August 19, 2022.

### 3.2 Subsequent health

Medical history includes recurrent middle ear infections and seasonal nasal congestion. Dr. Owen Sayer evaluated these concerns at Veridian Health Ear, Nose and Throat–Riverstone Campus. The family reported no current medication that affects alertness.

Recent audiology findings indicated hearing adequate for the speech frequencies tested, with normal tympanometry on the examination date. These findings describe that visit and do not establish hearing status during earlier infections. The parent denied current swallowing concerns, choking, or restricted food textures. Sleep and appetite were described as stable.

## 4. Developmental and Service History

### 4.1 Early development

The caregiver reported independent walking at 15 months and consistent meaningful words at approximately 20 months. Word combinations emerged near 30 months. These ages reflect caregiver recall.

Early intervention began at 26 months. Service coordinator Iris Pell helped the family develop an individualized family service plan. The plan dated December 2, 2024 included IFSP Outcome 2, which addressed requesting help during familiar routines.

### 4.2 Previous intervention

Speech-language pathologist Marco Duran provided home visits through Willowbend CDSA. Records described gains in gestures, turn taking, and functional requesting. Services ended during transition to preschool.

The historical Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale findings were descriptive rather than standard scores. They documented uneven development across interaction, comprehension, and expression. The present evaluation did not administer that instrument outside its intended developmental range.

No outpatient speech therapy was reported between preschool entry and this assessment. The family described continued progress, with persistent difficulty explaining problems and making speech understood.

## 5. Family, Caregiving, and Language History

### 5.1 Household and routines

Eli lives with both parents and his sister, Luz. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Maro, provides care after preschool. A family friend, Paz Neri, occasionally babysits. The household dog is named Miso.

His father works at Hearthline Cartography Cooperative. His mother works at Silver Kite Packaging Studio. Work schedules influence which caregiver manages pickup, meals, and bedtime.

### 5.2 Language exposure

Spanish is the main language used by his mother and grandmother. His father uses both languages. English is the primary language at preschool. Estimated current exposure was 60% Spanish and 40% English, based on caregiver descriptions rather than direct measurement.

The family reported that he understands familiar routines in both languages. He usually speaks Spanish with his grandmother and English with classmates. Language mixing occurs naturally during play. The clinician treated mixing and language preference as features of bilingual development, while examining whether underlying difficulties appeared across languages.

## 6. Educational Participation and Functional Communication

### 6.1 Classroom observations

Ms. Keene reported that Elian participates readily in songs, construction play, and familiar routines. He sometimes watches classmates before following an unfamiliar direction. He benefits when an adult demonstrates the action and checks understanding.

He plays frequently with Mara Tovin and Nico Bell. During pretend play, he initiates by offering objects or assigning a role. Breakdowns occur when he needs to explain a change in the game. He may repeat the same phrase more loudly.

### 6.2 Home observations

His mother described successful requests for familiar foods and toys. Longer explanations require follow-up questions. During a recent home interaction, he said, "Luz come here," while pointing toward a fallen block tower.

He also said, "Miso run," when the dog crossed the room. These examples show purposeful communication, but they do not independently establish sentence complexity. The family wants him to describe what happened, request help clearly, and repair misunderstandings without becoming upset.

## 7. Assessment Procedures and Behavioral Observations

### 7.1 Procedures

The clinician administered English items from the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition and the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition. The Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition provided an additional English vocabulary measure.

Spanish probes examined comparable concepts through familiar objects, pictures, and conversation. These probes were informal and did not generate standardized Spanish scores. The clinician also collected play samples, examined oral structures, and used brief teaching trials to assess response to support.

### 7.2 Participation

Elian entered the room comfortably and explored the materials. He separated from his mother for short activities while she remained nearby. Attention improved when the clinician alternated seated tasks with movement and pretend play.

He occasionally declined unfamiliar naming items but returned with encouragement. No behavior suggested that refusal alone explained the overall pattern. He responded well to min cues for turn taking and needed mod cues during unfamiliar picture sequences.

The bilingual clinician conducted the evaluation directly. No interpreter was required. Breaks, item familiarity, and changes to standardized procedures were documented during scoring.

## 8. Test Results and Interpretation Limits

### 8.1 Score table

English norm comparisons below are descriptive. The normative groups do not fully represent this child's bilingual experience. Confidence intervals are reported at the 90% level where available.

| Measure | Subtest or domain | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition | Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 73–85 | 3;2 |
| Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition | Expressive Communication | 75 | 5th percentile | 70–83 | 2;11 |
| Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition | Total Language | 75 | 5th percentile | 71–82 | 3;0 |
| Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition | Sounds-in-Words | 74 | 4th percentile | 70–81 | Not interpreted |
| Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition | Receptive Vocabulary | 80 | 9th percentile | 75–87 | 3;3 |

### 8.2 Interpretation

Age equivalents describe performance on particular test items. They do not indicate that the child functions globally at that age. Informal skill estimates ranged from 2;10–3;4 across the language tasks sampled.

Performance varied with vocabulary familiarity, sentence length, and visual support. Items translated or taught after standardized administration were excluded from norm scoring. These supported responses informed the functional analysis.

The clinician gave greater weight to patterns repeated in both languages, caregiver reports, classroom impact, and learning response. Historical scores were not combined with current scores because the measures and testing conditions differed.

## 9. Receptive and Expressive Language Findings

### 9.1 Understanding language

Elian identified familiar objects, actions, and basic spatial concepts. He followed routine directions involving related actions. Performance decreased when directions included unfamiliar vocabulary, temporal concepts, or information that required inference.

During informal bilingual probes, he followed related directions in 8/10 opportunities with visual context. Without visual context, he followed 5/10. He answered concrete picture questions in 7/10 opportunities and explanation questions in 3/10.

### 9.2 Spoken language

He used speech, pointing, facial expression, and gesture together. Spontaneous productions included "I want the big truck", "se cayó aquí", and "him not going". The clinician distinguished expected language differences from persistent difficulty organizing a complete message.

A conversational sample yielded a mean length of utterance of 3.1 morphemes under the stated sampling rules. Transcription included the SALT code [EW] for marked word errors. This value was descriptive because the sample included both languages and uneven conversational demands.

He often omitted information about who acted or where an event occurred. Clarifying questions helped him add details. Longer messages remained difficult across languages, including during familiar play.

## 10. Speech Sound and Oral Mechanism Findings

### 10.1 Speech patterns

Speech was characterized by fronting of velar sounds, cluster reduction, and inconsistent omission of unstressed syllables. Examples included "tat" for "cat" and "poon" for "spoon". Substitution of [w] for /ɹ/ occurred in English words.

The clinician considered Spanish and English sound systems separately. Production of Spanish /ɾ/ remained variable. That finding alone did not determine disorder status. Errors affecting shared sounds, including /k/ and /g/, occurred in both languages.

### 10.2 Intelligibility and stimulability

Estimated intelligibility was 62% for an unfamiliar listener during connected speech and 78% for his mother. These estimates came from the evaluation samples and caregiver clarification.

He produced /k/ in isolation in 6/10 trials with mod cues. He produced initial /k/ in syllables in 3/10 trials with max cues.

Oral structures appeared adequate for speech. Facial movement was symmetric during observed tasks. Voice quality and fluency did not show a persistent concern. The examination did not include instrumental assessment of swallowing or resonance.

## 11. Dynamic Assessment and Clinical Impressions

### 11.1 Learning response

The clinician taught a short event sequence using pictures, gestures, and repeated models. Before teaching, Elian included the actor, action, and location in 2/6 opportunities. After teaching, he included those elements in 5/6 with min cues.

He retained the sequence after a play break but needed mod cues when the materials changed. This response showed useful learning potential. Continued support was necessary for transfer to unfamiliar tasks.

### 11.2 Impressions

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, ICD-10 F80.2, and a speech sound disorder, ICD-10 F80.0. The language conclusion rests on functional difficulties across languages, limited message organization, and agreement between caregiver and classroom observations.

Bilingual exposure does not explain the full pattern. English test scores likely reflect both language experience and communication difficulty. The clinician therefore avoids using those scores as the sole evidence for diagnosis.

Strengths include social interest, shared attention, imaginative play, gesture use, caregiver involvement, and response to teaching. Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable with consistent intervention and coordinated practice. The rate of progress will require direct measurement over time.

## 12. Recommendations and Initial Treatment Goals

### 12.1 Service plan

Initiate individual speech-language therapy twice weekly for 45 minutes, with caregiver participation during part of each visit. Services may use CPT 92507 with modifier GN when appropriate to the payer and service setting. This evaluation is recorded under CPT 92523.

Treatment should address speech clarity and functional language in both languages. The clinician may use Cycles for selected phonological patterns and Enhanced Milieu Teaching for spontaneous communication. Caregiver coaching may draw on Hanen It Takes Two to Talk.

### 12.2 Initial goals

1. Goal 1: Produce initial /k/ and /g/ in practiced words in 8/10 opportunities with mod cues across consecutive sessions.

2. Goal 2: Describe an event using an actor, action, and location in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

3. Goal 3: Follow unfamiliar related directions in 8/10 opportunities with visual support and min cues.

4. Goal 4: Repair a communication breakdown by adding information, pointing, or rephrasing in 4/5 opportunities with min cues.

These goals are provisional. The treating clinician should adjust targets after baseline collection and family consultation.

## 13. Home and Preschool Carryover

### 13.1 Caregiver strategies

Continue speaking the language each caregiver uses most comfortably. Offer clear models during meals, dressing, and play. Expand the child's message by adding a small amount of useful information. Allow time for a response before repeating a question.

Practice short contrasts such as "key", "tea", "go", and "dough", only when the treating clinician selects them. Keep practice brief and successful. Do not require repeated correction during every conversation.

### 13.2 Classroom strategies

Provide a visual example before unfamiliar directions. Check understanding through an action rather than a yes-or-no response. During storytelling, prompt for the person, action, and place. Accept gestures while supporting a clearer spoken message.

Emberleaf Therapy can provide a classroom summary after caregiver authorization. EPCT should coordinate targets with classroom staff to reduce competing prompts.

## 14. Follow-Up and Authentication

A progress review is recommended for January 14, 2027. Review functional communication samples, goal data, caregiver priorities, and classroom participation. Repeat standardized testing only when clinically useful and consistent with instrument guidance.

The mother reviewed the findings and requested examples for home practice. The clinician provided a written summary and explained the limits of English norm comparisons.

Electronically signed by Nadia Varela, MS, CCC-SLP  
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist  
Emberleaf Pediatric Communication Therapy PLLC

DOCUMENT HEADER

- Document status: Synthetic clinical record for offline de-identification testing. All people, organizations, identifiers, locations, events, and findings are fictional. Numerical test results are fabricated and do not represent authentic publisher norm conversions.
- Client: Mateo de la Cruz-Vega; preferred name: Teo.
