SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

- This fictional report was prepared for offline de-identification testing. All people, organizations, contact details, locations, and clinical findings are invented.
- Client: María José Valdés Cordero; preferred name: María José; family nickname: Marijó.
- Date of birth: August 9, 2021. Evaluation date: October 21, 2025. Chronological age: 4;2.
- Record number: LL-2025-04731. Medicaid member number: 847261905R. Authorization number: AUTH-58264017.
- Evaluator: Elena Marisol Fuentes, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist.
- Clinician employer: Willow Lantern Pediatric Therapy.
- Evaluation site: 318 Lantern Finch Lane, Cedarmist, North Carolina, 27863.
- Parent telephone: (919) 555-0148. Clinic telephone: (984) 555-0176.
- Parent email: lucia.cordero@example.invalid. Clinic website: https://willowlantern.example.invalid.

REFERRAL AND PURPOSE

- Dr. Adrián Solano referred María José because unfamiliar listeners frequently request repetition. Her parents also described difficulty answering questions, explaining events, and following directions during classroom routines.
- The evaluation examined communication across Spanish and English. Its purpose was to identify functional needs, describe strengths, and guide services without treating bilingual development as a disorder.
- Her mother, Lucía Cordero, attended the full evaluation. Her father, Rafael Valdés, contributed information by telephone. Both parents requested practical strategies that fit family routines.
- The family identified three priorities: clearer requests, successful participation with classmates, and fewer communication breakdowns during transitions. They want continued development of both languages and do not want Spanish use reduced.

BACKGROUND AND CURRENT SERVICES

- Marijó attends Little Learners Daycare in Cedarmist, within fictional Briarfern County. She entered the current classroom on September 2, 2025.
- She receives weekly communication support through the Little Learners Program, a therapy program operated by Willow Lantern Pediatric Therapy. The daycare and therapy program are separate services despite their shared name words.
- Service coordinator Nadia Bellamy previously worked with the family through Briarfern Children’s Developmental Services Agency. The archived IFSP is dated April 18, 2024.
- The current referral includes consultation about transition planning with Juniper Hollow Elementary School. Enrollment has not occurred. The family also receives resource information from Briarfern Family Start.
- No previous evaluation established performance across both languages. Earlier notes described short utterances but did not document language exposure or interpreter involvement.

BIRTH AND DEVELOPMENTAL HISTORY

- Lucía Cordero reported an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery at 39 weeks, 2 days of gestation. Birth occurred at Silver Wren Community Hospital.
- Reported birth weight was 7 pounds, 4 ounces. Apgar scores were 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. The newborn remained with her mother and went home after routine observation.
- Independent walking began at approximately 14 months. Consistent meaningful words emerged around 20 months, and combinations became frequent around 30 months.
- The parents reported no loss of communication, movement, play, or self-care skills. They described steady gains, with spoken language progressing more slowly than other daily skills.
- Early feeding included breastfeeding and bottle feeding. The family reported no persistent difficulty with sucking, chewing, swallowing, or growth. Current meals include varied textures, and the child usually eats with the family.

MEDICAL AND HEARING HISTORY

- Medical history includes occasional ear infections and seasonal nasal congestion. There is no reported history of seizures, major injury, prolonged hospitalization, or diagnosed neurological disease.
- Pediatric follow-up with Dr. Solano occurred on September 30, 2025. The referral record listed developmental communication concerns and requested comprehensive speech-language assessment.
- Audiologist Brenna Ives completed a hearing evaluation at Silver Wren Community Hospital on October 7, 2025. The fictional report documented hearing adequate for speech access during that visit.
- The parents reported no current prescription medication. Sleep is generally consistent, although congestion sometimes interrupts rest.
- Oral structures appeared symmetrical during observation. Functional lip closure, tongue movement, and chewing were observed. No feeding evaluation was completed, and these observations do not replace a medical examination.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

- Spanish is the primary language used by Lucía Cordero. Rafael Valdés uses Spanish and English. Their child hears English mainly at daycare and during community activities.
- Her sister, Ana Sofía Valdés Cordero, often reads picture books with her. Her brother, Mateo Valdés Cordero, called Teo, joins pretend cooking games.
- Grandmother Guadalupe Cordero, called Lupita, provides care twice weekly. Uncle Jesús Cordero, called Chuy, visits regularly.
- Grandfather José Valdés, called Pepe, and cousin Juan Valdés, called Juanito, participate in family gatherings. Babysitter Alma Rentería uses Spanish during care.
- The household dog is named Mochi. Her mother works at Copper Fern Packaging. Her father works at Cedar Lantern Bicycle Works.
- Estimated language exposure is 65% Spanish and 35% English. These estimates reflect parent report, not direct measurement.

CLASSROOM AND PEER INFORMATION

- Lead teacher Ms. Nora Pell described a child who enjoys songs, puzzles, outdoor play, and helping distribute materials. Classroom assistant J. Ortiz reported that visual reminders improve transitions.
- Classmates Camila Duarte and Owen Vela frequently invite her into pretend play. She sometimes watches before joining and then uses gestures or brief phrases.
- Staff reported stronger understanding during familiar routines than during new group instructions. Noise, rapid speech, and multiple competing directions increase her need for support.
- Community volunteer M.R. assists with the classroom lending library but provides no clinical services. Staff did not identify persistent behavior concerns; frustration most often followed misunderstood messages.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES AND PARTICIPATION

- Elena Marisol Fuentes conducted parent interviewing, play observation, structured probes, speech sampling, and administration of the Preschool Language Scales–Fifth Edition (PLS-5).
- English standardized administration was completed before bilingual teaching probes. Spanish observations and mediated tasks informed interpretation but were not converted into additional standardized scores.
- Testing occurred across two visits, on October 21, 2025 and October 23, 2025. The child participated best when movement breaks and predictable choices were available.
- Attention fluctuated during lengthy verbal tasks. She responded to encouragement and accepted correction without distress. Fatigue increased near the end of each visit.
- Results describe this sample of performance. English scores require caution because the normative comparison does not fully represent her language history. Conclusions therefore integrate caregiver reports, classroom observations, and performance across languages.

STANDARDIZED TEST RESULTS

- The following results summarize English administration. Confidence intervals are reported at the 90% level. Age equivalents are descriptive and must not determine placement independently.

  | Test or subtest | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th | 73-85 | 3;2 |
  | PLS-5 Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th | 69-82 | 2;11 |
  | PLS-5 Total Language | 75 | 5th | 70-83 | 3;0 |

- Scaled scores were not generated by this measure. The examiner did not substitute raw performance counts for standard scores.
- Differences between receptive and expressive results were interpreted descriptively. The small separation does not establish a meaningful difference by itself.

RECEPTIVE AND EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE FINDINGS

- María José identified familiar objects, actions, and basic body parts in both languages. She followed familiar one-step directions with min cues.
- Novel two-step directions were completed in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Accuracy improved when the examiner demonstrated the sequence and reduced competing materials.
- Understanding of location concepts was inconsistent. She benefited from contrasting examples and repeated opportunities to act out the instruction.
- Expressive strengths included requesting, labeling, protesting, and commenting. Spontaneous phrases were usually brief, with more varied vocabulary during Spanish play.
- She omitted grammatical elements in both languages. Difficulty explaining causes and describing completed events remained evident after familiar vocabulary was supplied.
- During mediated learning, she applied a newly taught sentence pattern in 6/10 opportunities with mod cues. This responsiveness supports intervention using repeated models and meaningful practice.

SPEECH SOUND AND INTELLIGIBILITY FINDINGS

- Connected speech included reduced consonant precision and variable syllable shapes. Errors occurred in familiar Spanish words and English words, although individual patterns differed between languages.
- English /k/ was sometimes replaced by [t], and /g/ by [d]. Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent. These findings require continued sampling in both languages.
- Examples included "tat" for "cat", "do" for "go", and "pato" for "plato". The examiner recorded the intended words after checking context.
- Unfamiliar-listener intelligibility was estimated at 55% in a brief connected-speech sample. Familiar listeners understood approximately 75%, based on caregiver report.
- Production of /k/ improved in 8/10 structured trials with max cues. Generalization to spontaneous speech was not demonstrated during this evaluation.

LANGUAGE SAMPLE AND SOCIAL COMMUNICATION

- A play sample included requests, comments, questions, and attempts to repair misunderstood messages. Marijó coordinated gaze, gestures, and speech during shared activities.
- Recorded productions included "yo quiero otro", "baby sleeping", and "no cabe aquí". Mixed-language utterances were treated as part of bilingual communication.
- During animal play, she said "Mochi run." During family pretend play, she said "Teo help me." These productions contained names and were preserved as separate identifier spans.
- The sample included the SALT notation [EW] for an extraneous word and [EU] for an extraneous utterance. Codes describe transcription decisions, not independent diagnoses.
- She sustained reciprocal play and accepted peer ideas. Communication repair often relied on pointing, repeating, or bringing an object to the listener.

CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

- Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder with accompanying speech sound difficulty. Challenges affected participation across languages and settings, beyond the expected effects of learning English.
- Strengths include social interest, symbolic play, family engagement, response to teaching, and willingness to communicate. These strengths provide useful foundations for intervention.
- Working diagnostic codes are F80.2 and F80.0. Final coding should remain consistent with the treating clinician’s complete record.
- Assessment billing code: CPT 92523. Anticipated individual treatment code: CPT 92507, with modifier GN when required by the payer.
- Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable with consistent attendance, bilingual support, and coordinated practice. Specific progress rates cannot be predicted from this evaluation alone.

RECOMMENDED GOALS AND APPROACHES

- Update IFSP outcome 2 to address functional requests and message repair during home routines. Retain family priorities when transferring goals into the next service plan.
- Goal 1: Follow related two-step directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues, across play and classroom activities.
- Goal 2: Produce expanded functional utterances in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues, using either language as appropriate.
- Goal 3: Produce selected speech targets with 80% accuracy in structured phrases with mod cues, then monitor spontaneous use.
- Goal 4: Repair a misunderstood message in 3 of 4 opportunities with min cues.
- Consider Hanen caregiver strategies and selected elements of Cycles. PROMPT or PECS may be considered only after individualized assessment establishes a relevant need.

PROPOSED SESSION SCHEDULE

- The schedule begins on November 3, 2025, subject to authorization and caregiver coordination. Travel time is outside treatment time.

  | Day | Start | Stop | Location |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Monday | 9:10 a.m. | 9:40 a.m. | Little Learners Daycare, classroom consultation |
  | Wednesday | 3:20 p.m. | 4:00 p.m. | Willow Lantern Pediatric Therapy, 318 Lantern Finch Lane |
  | Friday | 10:00 a.m. | 10:20 a.m. | Home coaching, 72 Sparrowglass Court, Cedarmist |

HOME AND CLASSROOM RECOMMENDATIONS

- Continue Spanish and English in natural routines. Adults should use the language in which they can provide clear, comfortable models.
- Follow the child’s interests, pause for a response, and expand short messages by adding useful information. Accept gestures while supplying a spoken model.
- Present new directions in manageable steps. Pair spoken instructions with objects, gestures, or pictures, then gradually reduce support as understanding improves.
- Practice communication during meals, dressing, book sharing, and pretend play. Short, successful exchanges are more useful than repeated correction during every conversation.
- Classroom staff should provide a predictable way to request help and enough time to respond. Record which supports improve participation across activities.
- Review progress on January 15, 2026. Repeat broader assessment if progress remains limited or new concerns emerge.
- Report prepared and signed by Elena Marisol Fuentes, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, on October 27, 2025.

Employer: Fernlight Pediatric Speech Services
Office: 72 Juniper Bell Court, Briarhaven, North Carolina 27963
Office phone: 252-555-0182
Service coding: CPT 92523; modifier GN
Referral diagnosis: ICD-10 F80.2

S:

Reason for referral. Mother reports limited spontaneous combinations, reduced intelligibility, and frustration during transitions. Family seeks functional communication across Spanish-speaking home routines and English-speaking classroom activities. Main priorities: requesting help, sharing experiences, answering simple questions, and being understood without repeated guessing. Mother describes recent vocabulary growth but inconsistent use outside familiar routines.

Informants. Mother, Lucía Vela, attended throughout and provided developmental history. Father, Andrés Cárdenas, contributed a written questionnaire. Maternal grandmother, Teresa Vela, supplies regular afternoon care. Older sister, Inés Cárdenas Vela, often models play language. Family dog, Pipo, is a frequent topic of spontaneous speech.

Background. Child resides with both parents and sibling. Mother works at Moonspindle Textile Studio. Father works at Copper Heron Equipment Cooperative. Family reports stable housing and reliable transportation. No recent placement changes. Grandmother provides care on alternating afternoons; occasional babysitter, Alma Robles, uses Spanish. Family requested written home activities in English with Spanish examples.

Educational setting. Child attends The Upside-Down Acorn during weekday mornings. Lead teacher, Ms. Renata Moss, reports strong interest in blocks, animals, and songs. Assistant teacher, Mr. Caleb Finch, reports difficulty understanding requests during noisy group activities. Classmates Zuri Bell and Owen Pike frequently invite child into pretend play. Child usually joins through imitation, pointing, or handing over materials.

Birth history. Born at Silver Estuary Regional Hospital following maternal hypertension and spontaneous labor. Gestational age: 35 weeks, 6 days. Birth weight: 2.41 kg. Apgar scores: 7 and 9. Delivery attended by Dr. Elena Merrow. Mother reports no known prenatal substance exposure. Feeding initiation delayed by respiratory monitoring; expressed breast milk introduced during admission.

NICU history. Admitted to the NICU at Silver Estuary Regional Hospital for transient respiratory distress, temperature support, and feeding immaturity. Neonatologist Dr. Omar Vale supervised care. Discharged on February 18, 2024. Mother recalls brief oxygen support and no prolonged ventilation. Birth and discharge details are caregiver-reported; hospital records were unavailable for this evaluation.

Medical history. Primary care through Dr. Nadia Soler at Willow Lantern Children’s Hospital. Recurrent middle-ear fluid reported. Tympanostomy tubes placed on May 12, 2026, by Dr. Theo Larkin. Audiologist Celia Rowan reportedly documented hearing adequate for speech access on June 2, 2026. Audiology report pending. No known seizures, head injury, daily medication, or food allergy. Vision concerns denied.

Development. Sat independently at 8 months, walked at 16 months, and used first consistent words at 19 months. Word combinations emerged around 28 months. Mother reports no loss of skills. Feeding includes varied table foods; occasional refusal of mixed textures. No reported coughing, choking, or unexplained weight loss. Sleep generally consistent, with occasional waking during respiratory illness.

Language history. Spanish exposure estimated at 70% and English at 30%, based on caregiver interview. Mother and grandmother primarily use Spanish. Father uses both languages. Sister uses English during pretend play and Spanish during meals. Classroom instruction primarily English. Exposure estimates describe current routines; they do not represent measured proficiency or fixed language dominance.

Family history. Father reports childhood difficulty producing /r/, resolved with school services. Maternal uncle, Julián Vela, reportedly received early language intervention. No other diagnosed communication condition reported. Family views bilingual development as a priority. Parents request support for both languages and do not wish to replace Spanish with English.

Existing services. Service coordinator Lena Hartwell, with Pineglass Children’s Developmental Services Agency, supplied the current IFSP dated August 21, 2026. IFSP outcome 2 addresses expressing needs during daily routines. Developmental specialist Sofia Calder visits the home. Family reports no prior direct speech-language treatment. Parent consent obtained for evaluation and coordination with existing providers.

O:

Presentation. Child arrived alert, accompanied by mother, and transitioned with familiar toy support. Initial proximity-seeking decreased after shared play. Participation improved with movement breaks and predictable turn-taking. No marked distress during structured activities. Attention varied by task interest. Brief refusal occurred when preferred vehicles were removed; child returned after a visual choice.

Methods. Procedures included caregiver interview, classroom questionnaire, bilingual play observation, oral mechanism screening, language sampling, PLS-5 Spanish, and Dynamic Assessment. Directions followed the test manual where feasible. Informal English probes supplemented Spanish testing. Departures from standardized administration are identified below. No interpreter used; examiner provided direct assessment in both languages.

Test results. PLS-5 Spanish scores reflect the completed standardized portion. Confidence intervals are reported at 90%. Age equivalents are descriptive and must not determine placement or treatment intensity. Scores require integration with exposure history, functional observations, and response to teaching.

| Test/subtest | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | 79 | 8th | 74–86 | 2;2 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | 75 | 5th | 70–83 | 1;11 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Total Language | 76 | 5th | 71–83 | 2;0 |

Testing limitations. Standardized responses were scored before additional teaching. Repeated directions, gestures, and demonstration used afterward were recorded as informal probes. Several English responses occurred during Spanish tasks; these were handled according to applicable scoring rules. No separate English standard score generated. Reported scores do not quantify each language independently.

Receptive language. Identified familiar objects in 8/10 opportunities without added support. Identified pictured actions in 5/8. Followed related directions in 4/6 with min cues. Performance decreased when directions included unfamiliar location words or several competing objects. Identified "in", "out", and "on"; inconsistent with "under" and "behind".

Expressive language. Spontaneous speech consisted mainly of single words and short combinations. Functions included requesting, protesting, labeling, greeting, and commenting. Action vocabulary less varied than object vocabulary. English and Spanish sometimes appeared within the same utterance. This pattern alone was not scored as an error. Novel combinations increased during familiar pretend routines.

Representative productions. Child said "más carro", "no quiero", "baby sleep", and "help me open". During animal play, child said "Pipo corre". When discussing home, child said "Inés took my ball". Child identified self with "Milo turn". Names within these productions reflect referents documented in caregiver history.

Language sample. Conversational/play sample contained spontaneous, imitated, and prompted utterances. Spontaneous combinations occurred in 12/30 communicative turns. Verb-containing messages occurred in 7/30. Unintelligible segments limited reliable grammatical analysis. SALT transcription used [EW] for extraneous words and [EU] for utterance-level errors where coding criteria were met. No normative sample comparison completed.

Social communication. Shared attention, social referencing, showing, and reciprocal play observed. Child initiated interaction with examiner and mother. Responded to partner bids in 8/10 opportunities. Maintained a brief pretend feeding routine with min cues. Communication breakdowns often led to repetition or pointing. Repair through a different word occurred in 2/6 opportunities.

Speech production. Consonant inventory included /p/, /b/, /m/, /n/, /t/, /d/, /k/, and /g/. Some word-final consonants omitted in English. Spanish tap /ɾ/ not established in the sample. Occasional [w] substitution heard in English approximations. Connected speech clarity decreased with utterance length. Findings require language-specific monitoring.

Intelligibility. Familiar caregiver understood approximately 75% of sampled messages with context. Examiner understood approximately 55%. These estimates are informal and reflect this session only. Child produced target "car" as [kɑ] and target "pelota" as [pota]. Syllable reduction occurred inconsistently. No formal articulation standard score obtained.

Oral mechanism, voice, fluency. Facial symmetry and functional lip closure observed. Tongue movement adequate during imitation and feeding-related play. Palate visualization limited by cooperation. Voice judged appropriate for activity and setting. No consistent stuttering-like behavior observed. Screening findings do not replace medical examination or establish swallowing safety.

Learning response. During Dynamic Assessment, examiner used Focused Stimulation, modeling, and brief wait time. Independent action-word use increased from 2/8 before teaching to 5/8 afterward. Novel combinations occurred with mod cues. Child retained selected combinations after a short play break. Performance suggests benefit from responsive teaching and repeated practice.

A:

Clinical impression. Findings support mixed receptive-expressive language delay affecting participation across home and classroom routines. ICD-10 F80.2 is consistent with observed needs. Reduced speech intelligibility contributes to communication breakdowns. Present data are insufficient to establish a separate speech sound diagnosis. Monitor phonological development across languages as expressive output expands.

Diagnostic reasoning. Concerns extend beyond unfamiliar English vocabulary. Difficulties also occurred during familiar Spanish routines, caregiver-supported tasks, and low-demand play. Relative strengths include social engagement, gesture use, pretend play, and response to modeling. Bilingual exposure does not explain all observed functional limitations. Continued assessment should examine change with intervention and stable hearing access.

Interpretive limits. Findings represent a single visit. Fatigue, task familiarity, and inconsistent audibility may affect performance. Hearing information remains caregiver-reported. Standardized results support the overall impression but are not sufficient alone. Age-equivalent values should not be interpreted as a global developmental age. Classroom participation warrants direct follow-up.

Prognosis. Favorable for improved functional communication with consistent intervention and caregiver participation. Learning response and family engagement support treatment. Rate of progress cannot be predicted from this evaluation. Primary barriers include limited spontaneous language, variable intelligibility, and reduced repair skills. Preserve bilingual access when selecting materials, partners, and treatment contexts.

P:

Recommend skilled speech-language intervention targeting functional comprehension, spontaneous combinations, and communication repair. Coordinate scheduling through the current service team. Use bilingual activities tied to family priorities. Review progress after a defined treatment block and adjust frequency using participation, caregiver feedback, and measured change.

Initial objectives linked to IFSP outcome 2: follow familiar action-plus-location directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues; produce spontaneous combinations in 7/10 opportunities; and repair misunderstood messages in 4/5 opportunities with mod cues. Accept meaningful responses in either language. Track language, context, and assistance separately.

Use Enhanced Milieu Teaching, Focused Stimulation, and Recasting during play, dressing, meals, and book sharing. Consider caregiver coaching based on Hanen principles. Introduce simple visual choices when spoken requests fail. A formal PECS program is not indicated by this evaluation alone. Select supports according to functional response.

Parents should model brief messages slightly beyond the child’s current production. Pause to allow initiation. Expand messages without requiring immediate repetition. Offer meaningful choices and acknowledge gestures. Practice targets such as "help open", "more water", and "quiero otro". Keep practice brief and embedded in routines.

Classroom staff should reduce competing noise during instructions, pair directions with visible actions, and allow extra response time. Model useful peer-entry phrases such as "my turn" and "play with me". Record spontaneous successes and breakdown contexts. Obtain caregiver authorization before exchanging clinical documents or arranging classroom observation.

Request the audiology report and confirm recommended hearing follow-up. Send evaluation findings to the referring physician through authorized channels. Reassess speech production when a larger sample is available. Review the IFSP on December 18, 2026. Family received findings, demonstrated selected language models, and expressed agreement with the proposed priorities.

Signed: Marina Bellavista, M.S., CCC-SLP
Fernlight Pediatric Speech Services
Signature date: October 11, 2026

NC Infant-Toddler Program  
Individualized Family Service Plan Review and Communication Evaluation

Child: Elian Mateo Serrano, called Eli at home  
Birth date: January 14, 2024  
Age at evaluation: 32 months  
Evaluation date: September 18, 2026  
IFSP review date: October 2, 2026  
Next review: April 2, 2027  
Child record: ITP-260918-0472  
Medicaid member number: 845731206Q

This fictional review describes communication, participation, and family priorities. All personal details, organizations, locations, and clinical results are invented for testing.

The evaluation occurred at the family home in Willowmere, North Carolina. The session began at 9:10 a.m. and ended at 10:25 a.m.. The family approved observation during breakfast, play, dressing, and a transition outside.

The clinician was Marisol Vega, MS, CCC-SLP, a bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist employed by Little Lantern Pediatric Communication. The clinician used English and Spanish during play. Interpreter Celia Duarte supported the review discussion and checked the meaning of family statements.

Family information

Parents Lucía Serrano and Andrés Molina share care of Elian. The family lives at 418 Juniper Lantern Lane, Willowmere, North Carolina 27547, in Pine Harbor County. The preferred telephone number is 919-555-0147. The family email is lucia.serrano@example.com.

Mother Lucía Serrano works two jobs: an early shift at RVC and evening laundry work at Sunbasket Linen Services. The first workplace is recorded only by its acronym. Father Andrés Molina works variable daytime shifts at Copper Finch Packaging.

Sister Inés Molina joins evening play. Grandmother Rosa Serrano provides care when the parents’ shifts overlap. Babysitter Nadia Ponce helps on some Saturdays. The family dog, Tavi, often joins floor play.

Spanish is the main home language. English is common at daycare. The family wants services that support both languages and does not want either language removed from daily routines.

Service coordinator and CDSA office

Service coordinator Daniela Ríos works through Pine Harbor Children’s Developmental Services Agency, the local CDSA office. The office address is 72 Meadowglass Court, Willowmere, North Carolina 27547. Its telephone number is 984-555-0126.

The coordinator will arrange visits, check access to services, and help the family prepare for transition planning. The family prefers telephone contact after 1:30 p.m.. Written reminders may go to the family email. Visits should avoid the mother’s work changeover.

Background and health information

The parents reported a birth at Meadowglass Women’s and Children’s Hospital following 38 weeks, 2 days of gestation. Birth weight was 6 lb 14 oz. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. These details came from family history and were not verified against hospital records.

Pediatrician Dr. Owen Bell at Willowmere Children’s Health Center last saw Elian on August 21, 2026. The family reported no current feeding restrictions or prescribed mobility equipment. They described occasional ear infections and requested help arranging hearing follow-up.

Occupational therapist Priya Nand reviewed sensory participation during dressing. Physical therapist Marcus Hale reviewed playground access and stair use. Their observations support routine planning but do not constitute new standardized motor evaluations.

Family concerns and priorities

Mother Lucía Serrano said, “I want him to tell us what hurts and what he needs. When I come home tired, I guess too much.”

Father Andrés Molina said, “He understands our usual things, but new instructions are hard. I want him to ask for help before he throws something.”

Grandmother Rosa Serrano said, “I want breakfast to feel calm. He points at the cupboard, and I bring the wrong cup.”

The parents identified three priorities: clearer requests, easier transitions, and participation with other children. They want practical activities that fit work schedules. They prefer short practice within existing routines instead of separate homework.

The family values shared meals, music, outdoor play, and visits with relatives. They want adults to recognize communication through gestures, sounds, and words. They also want daycare staff to use familiar Spanish words when those words help participation.

The family requested an interpreter for planning meetings involving unfamiliar terms. They asked providers to explain recommendations in ordinary language and demonstrate them before leaving written instructions.

Daily routines and participation

Breakfast usually begins at 6:45 a.m.. Elian chooses between cups by reaching or pointing. He sometimes says “más” and “agua”. Adults often anticipate his request before he finishes communicating. The family plans to pause briefly and accept any clear attempt.

Daycare arrival is near 8:20 a.m.. Elian attends Bright Acorn Early Learning House, in Ms. Lopez’s room. Teacher Alicia Lopez reported that familiar arrival steps help him separate from caregivers.

Classroom assistant Benita Cole helps with coat storage and handwashing. Classmates Milo Chen and Sofia Patel often offer toy vehicles. Elian watches them closely but may take a vehicle without looking toward its owner.

Lunch occurs near 11:30 a.m.. He feeds himself familiar foods and requests preferred items through pointing. A rest period begins around 12:15 p.m.. Transitions improve when adults show the next object and give time to respond.

Evening play starts around 6:10 p.m.. Sister Inés Molina likes pretend cooking. Elian brings her plates and copies stirring. During dog play, he said, “Tavi go.” The family understood this as a request to continue the game.

Bath begins near 7:20 p.m., followed by books. Dressing can be difficult when sleeves catch on his hands. He pulls away instead of asking for assistance. Bedtime is usually 8:15 p.m., with songs in both languages.

Evaluation procedures and score summary

The clinician completed the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), caregiver interview, a bilingual play sample, and routine observation. English standardized administration preceded supported Spanish exploration. Spanish responses helped describe skills but did not replace standardized scoring rules.

The table presents fictional descriptive results. Confidence intervals use the 90% level.

| Test or subtest | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age-equivalent range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-83 | 1;10–2;2 |
| PLS-5 Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th percentile | 69–81 | 1;6–1;10 |
| PLS-5 Total Language | 75 | 5th percentile | 70-82 | 1;8–2;0 |

Age equivalents describe test performance and do not define the child’s overall developmental age. The ranges above are planning descriptors. They should not guide placement by themselves.

During supported pretend play, performance resembled tasks commonly associated with 2;6–3;0, although this was not a standardized age-equivalent result. The clinician considered both languages, learning opportunities, caregiver reports, and observed participation when interpreting the scores.

Communication findings

Elian followed familiar directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Novel directions were completed in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. He identified familiar objects more consistently when adults used gestures and allowed processing time.

He communicated requests in 60% of observed opportunities through a word, sound, point, or combined gesture. Spoken combinations occurred less often than single words. Examples included “more car”, “mamá ven”, and “no shoe”.

A brief speech sample included “wa” for “water” and “tat” for “cat”. The clinician heard [​w​] in several word attempts. Production of /k/ varied across familiar words. Spanish /ɾ/ was not a treatment priority.

A transcript included the SALT code [EW] for an extra word. This transcription detail did not determine eligibility.

Familiar adults understood approximately 70% of the observed sample. The interpreter understood approximately 45% without routine context. These estimates describe this visit and are not standardized scores.

The pattern supports communication intervention addressing functional understanding, expression, and repair. Working diagnosis: ICD-10 F80.2. Billing references include CPT 92523, CPT 92507, and modifier GN.

Outcomes and strategies

Outcome 1: During meals and play, Elian will communicate a request or refusal in 8/10 opportunities across three routine observations, with min cues.

Adults will offer meaningful choices, wait, and respond to gestures as well as words. Models may include “help”, “more”, “all done”, and “ayuda”. Providers will use responsive interaction strategies informed by Hanen. Picture choices may supplement speech without requiring imitation before access to an item.

Outcome 2: During dressing and daycare transitions, Elian will follow a familiar two-step routine in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

Adults will show a simple picture sequence, name the immediate step, and allow a pause. The occupational therapist will help adapt sleeves and seating. The physical therapist will review stable positioning when shoes go on. Staff will reduce spoken instructions when the child appears overwhelmed.

Outcome 3: During shared play, Elian will initiate or respond to a peer in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues.

Adults will arrange brief vehicle games and pretend cooking. Teacher Ms. Lopez will model “my turn” and “your turn”. Staff will support exchanges with Milo Chen and other willing classmates. Adults will accept pointing, offering an object, or looking toward a partner as participation.

Outcome 4: During frustrating routines, Elian will seek assistance or use a repair strategy in 80% of observed opportunities with min cues.

Adults will model “help me” and “otra vez”. They will acknowledge the difficulty, offer a choice, and wait. Providers will record whether the child repeats, points, shows an object, or changes his message. The family will select examples that reflect useful progress.

Services and dates

Speech-language services will begin on October 5, 2026 and continue through April 1, 2027. Visits will occur weekly for 45 minutes in the home or daycare. The usual session will run from 9:00 a.m. to 9:45 a.m..

Occupational therapy consultation will begin on October 12, 2026, monthly for 30 minutes. Physical therapy consultation will begin on October 19, 2026, monthly for 30 minutes. The team will adjust consultation frequency through a documented IFSP review if participation needs change.

Service coordination will continue from October 2, 2026 through April 2, 2027. Interpreter support will accompany planning meetings and visits when requested. The coordinator will confirm scheduling before each unfamiliar provider attends.

Other agencies and transition planning

The family receives nutrition support from Pine Harbor Family Nutrition Office. Willowmere Early Connections Partnership offers library playgroups. Pine Harbor Family Support Services provided information about childcare assistance; no application outcome was verified.

With family consent, the coordinator will contact Meadowglass Primary School about transition planning. Proposed planning date: December 4, 2026. Consent permits sharing this review with named providers and daycare staff for coordination. Any additional release requires family authorization.

The team will review routine examples, family satisfaction, and progress toward each outcome. The family approved this plan verbally with interpreter support. Their highest priority remains communication that works during ordinary family life.

NC INFANT-TODDLER PROGRAM — IFSP REVIEW
FICTIONAL TRAINING RECORD

Review date: October 10, 2026. Original IFSP: April 10, 2026. Pt: Nico del Río-Santos, DOB August 12, 2024, chronological age approx 26 months. Child ID: ITP-60428-NR. Medicaid ID: 582741936K. Review held in family home w/ CGs present. English documentation by bilingual pediatric SLP; Spanish used for CG discussion and selected play routines. All people, organizations, contact details, and events in this training record are invented.

FAMILY INFORMATION

Mother: Elena de la Cruz. Father: Tomás del Río-Santos. Sister: Sol del Río-Santos, age 6 years. Maternal grandmother: Luz de la Cruz, regular afternoon CG. Home: 184 Lantern Finch Lane, Briarhaven, North Carolina 27903, Mallow County. Family phone: 919-555-0148. Alternate: 252-555-0162. Email: elena.delacruz@example.invalid. CG requests calls after 4:30 p.m.; voicemail permitted. Preferred spoken language is Spanish; written materials may be bilingual. Both parents share decisions. Grandmother practices agreed strategies but does not independently authorize service changes.

Parents provided workplace names in English order and Spanish word order. Mother works at Cedar Lantern Store / Tienda Cedar Lantern, takes evening shifts with Clear Window Cleaning Service / Servicio de Limpieza Clear Window, and does seasonal packing at Blue Heron Farm / Granja Blue Heron. Father works at Copper Finch Plant / Planta Copper Finch, covers weekend shifts at Golden Spoon Restaurant / Restaurante Golden Spoon, and accepts occasional jobs with Oak Bridge Construction Company / Compañía de Construcción Oak Bridge. Shift changes affect visit scheduling. CGs request flexible home visits, b/c neither parent has a fixed weekly day off.

TEAM AND CONTACTS

Service coordinator: Tessa Morgan, Mallow County CDSA, 62 Willow Compass Drive, Briarhaven, North Carolina 27903. Phone: 919-555-0117. Email: tessa.morgan@example.invalid. Office information: https://mallowcdsa.example.invalid.

Review clinician: Adriana Vega-Morales, bilingual pediatric SLP, Little Lantern Pediatric Therapy. OT: Priya Nand. PT: Owen Bell. Pediatrician: Dr. Camila Serrano, Juniper Lantern Health Briarhaven Campus Pediatric Clinic. Interpreter: Mara Vélez, Mallow Language Access Service. Interpreter supported consent discussion and checked CG understanding; SLP directly provided bilingual language assessment. Daycare lead: Ms. Iris Dunn. Classroom aide: Mr. Ben Arroyo. CG authorized coordination with Little Acorn Nest Childcare for routine strategies and attendance updates.

FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES

Mother stated, “I want him to tell us what hurts and what he wants. We guess, and then everyone gets upset.” Father stated, “When I come home, I want to understand him without asking his sister every time.” Grandmother stated, “Meals take so long. He points, but I cannot tell whether he wants food, water, or to leave.”

CG priorities: functional requests, easier transitions, participation in meals, and clearer communication across languages. Family wants pt to retain Spanish while learning English at daycare. Mother stated, “Please give us a few things that fit our day. We cannot do a worksheet after every shift.” Father prefers demonstration w/ familiar objects. Both CGs request practical strategies they can repeat during dressing, snack, and outdoor play. Family selected communication first, with feeding and movement supports embedded in the same routines.

HEALTH AND DEVELOPMENT

CG reports birth at Juniper Lantern Health Riverglass Campus Hospital, followed by NICU stay at Juniper Lantern Health Riverglass Campus NICU. Gestational age: 34 weeks, 2 days. Birth weight: 2,180 g. Apgar scores: 7 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. These details come from fictional discharge records dated August 26, 2024.

Recent pediatric visit: September 18, 2026. Audiology appointment at Juniper Lantern Health Briarhaven Campus ENT and Audiology scheduled for October 22, 2026, with Dr. Elias Mercer. Hearing status remains pending; response to conversational speech alone does not establish normal hearing. No current CG report of coughing during meals. OT will review utensil use and food textures. PT follows balance during steps and uneven outdoor surfaces.

CURRENT COMMUNICATION

Evaluation on September 30, 2026 included PLS-5 Spanish, play observation, CG interview, and a bilingual language sample. Auditory Comprehension standard score: 77, percentile 6, confidence interval 73-83. Expressive Communication standard score: 74, percentile 4, confidence interval 70-81. Total Language standard score: 74, percentile 4. Age-equivalent ranges were 1;6–1;9 for receptive tasks and 1;3–1;6 for expressive tasks. Scores describe test performance; they do not replace bilingual functional observations.

Pt follows familiar directions in 8/10 opportunities w/ min cues and unfamiliar directions in 3 of 5 opportunities w/ mod cues. Independent requests occurred in 40% of observed opportunities. Sample included "agua", "más", "up", and "all done". Pt also said "Sol go" while pointing toward the door. Productions showed [w] substitutions, recorded as [w], with inconsistent attempts at /k/ and /ɾ/. No isolated articulation outcome selected. SALT notation included [EW] for an extra word.

DAILY ROUTINES

Wake-up approx 6:45 a.m.. Dressing occurs before breakfast; pt usually brings shoes but protests shirt changes. CG will offer a choice, pause, then accept a gesture, picture, or word. Breakfast approx 7:15 a.m.. Pt remains seated longer when utensils and cup are within reach. CG currently anticipates requests quickly; coaching will support a brief response window.

Daycare arrival approx 8:00 a.m.. Pt watches peers Mila Ferren and Jonah Wren before joining block play. Teacher reports sharing improves with adult demonstration and mod cues. Lunch approx 11:30 a.m.; nap begins approx 12:15 p.m.. Grandmother collects pt on variable afternoons. Outdoor play includes steps, bubbles, and following pet Miga. Bath approx 7:00 p.m. provides opportunities for body-part directions and requests. Bedtime approx 8:15 p.m.. CGs prefer short practice during these routines.

OTHER AGENCIES AND TRANSITION

Family receives food support through Mallow County WIC and scheduling assistance from Mallow County Family Support DSS. Briarhaven Smart Start Partnership offered a bilingual playgroup; enrollment is pending transportation arrangements. Service coordinator will check availability by October 20, 2026. Family may explore preschool services through Briarhaven Meadow Primary School. Transition discussion planned for May 12, 2027. No preschool eligibility decision has occurred. CG wants daycare observations included in future planning. Written releases identify the permitted contacts and purpose; family may revise them through the service coordinator.

OUTCOMES AND STRATEGIES

Outcome 1: During meals and play, pt will request an item, action, or help using a gesture, picture, or spoken word in 8/10 opportunities across home and daycare, w/ min cues, for consecutive weekly checks. Baseline: 4/10 opportunities w/ mod cues. SLP will use Enhanced Milieu Teaching and Hanen It Takes Two to Talk strategies: follow pt’s interest, pause, model briefly, and respond to attempts. Target words include "help", "more", and "abre". CG chooses useful words in either language. Pictures remain available when speech is difficult. Review on January 12, 2027.

Outcome 2: During dressing and cleanup, pt will follow a familiar direction and move to the next activity in 4 of 5 opportunities w/ min cues. Baseline: 2 of 5 opportunities w/ max cues. CG will show the needed object, state one direction, wait, and demonstrate if needed. Use "shoes on", "put in", and "vamos". OT will adapt clothing setup; PT will advise safe positioning near steps. Daycare staff will use the same sequence. Record whether pt understands the direction separately from willingness to stop preferred play. Review on January 12, 2027.

Outcome 3: During snack, pt will indicate a choice and participate in utensil use in 80% of opportunities w/ mod cues or less. Baseline: 30% w/ max cues. OT leads utensil and seating recommendations; SLP supports choice-making and requests. Offer manageable portions and familiar foods. Honor refusal signals. Targets include "water", "otra", and "finished". CG will note fatigue, distress, and duration. New coughing, choking, or respiratory concerns prompt contact with the pediatrician. Do not increase texture demands solely to obtain a spoken request. Review on January 12, 2027.

Outcome 4: During family play, CGs will demonstrate agreed communication strategies in 3 of 4 observed opportunities w/ min cues. Baseline: 1 of 4 w/ mod cues. SLP will use routines-based coaching: observe, demonstrate, invite practice, and reflect. Strategies include waiting, matching pt’s words, expanding a message, and accepting communication across languages. Sister may join ordinary play without responsibility for interpretation. CG will select one routine each week and describe what helped. Visits will adjust to shift schedules. Success includes CG confidence and pt participation, with review on January 12, 2027.

SERVICE PLAN AND FOLLOW-UP

SLP: weekly, forty-five minutes, home or daycare; October 15, 2026 through January 14, 2027. CPT 92507, modifier GN, ICD-10 F80.2. OT: twice monthly, forty-five minutes; same service period, CPT 97530, modifier GO, ICD-10 R63.32. PT: monthly, thirty minutes; same service period, CPT 97530, modifier GP, ICD-10 R26.89. Coordination: monthly contact plus scheduling support as needed. Authorization: AUTH-672804-SLP. Proposed visit time: 4:45 p.m., subject to CG shift confirmation.

CGs received the review in English and Spanish. Interpreter checked understanding through teach-back. Both parents agreed to the listed priorities, strategies, settings, and service dates. Service coordinator will confirm audiology attendance and share permitted recommendations. Clinician will collect routine examples before the next review. Written by Adriana Vega-Morales on October 10, 2026. Next IFSP review: January 12, 2027.

Initial IFSP and family review

This synthetic record describes a fictional family receiving services through the Larkhaven NC Infant-Toddler Program. The meeting occurred on September 17, 2026, at the family’s apartment in Larkhaven, North Carolina. The client, Gabriel Santos Rivera, was born on May 9, 2024, and was 28 months old at this review. The child record number is ITP-604281, and the Medicaid member number is 482761930Q. I am Elena Varela, a bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist with Cedar Lantern Pediatric Therapy. I conducted the visit in Spanish and English, following the family’s preferences for each discussion.

The parents are Marisol Rivera and Daniel Santos. Their home address is 218 Finch Hollow Lane, Apartment 3B, Larkhaven, North Carolina 27587. The preferred telephone number is 919-555-0146, and the family’s email address is marisol.rivera@example.com. The mother prefers telephone calls after 6:15 p.m. and written summaries in Spanish. The father prefers English for scheduling and Spanish when discussing home routines. Both parents participated in the meeting and agreed that communication support should fit their existing routines.

The mother works two jobs: a morning stocking position at RFS and evening kitchen work at Juniper Table Café. Her changing shifts make separate home practice periods difficult. The father repairs equipment at Hollow Creek Toolworks and usually handles daycare pickup. The older sister, Ariana Santos Rivera, enjoys helping with songs but should not be responsible for interpreting or providing therapy. The maternal grandmother, Rosa Rivera, provides care on some evenings. A family friend, Nadia Fuentes, occasionally babysits when work schedules overlap. The family’s dog is named Pico.

The assigned service coordinator is J. Ortiz from Juniper Children’s Developmental Services Agency, commonly called Juniper CDSA. The coordinator can be reached at 919-555-0183 or j.ortiz@example.com. The office is at 64 Meadow Crossing Road, Larkhaven, North Carolina 27587. The coordinator will arrange visits, monitor service delivery, and help the family review options. The parents requested one consistent contact because they have previously received appointment messages from several offices without knowing which response was needed.

Family concerns, priorities, and routines

The mother said, “I want Gabriel to tell us what he needs before he gets upset. I work two jobs, and I cannot make every evening into another appointment.” The father said, “We understand many of his gestures, but other people guess. I want him to ask for help and tell someone when something hurts.” Both parents described their child as affectionate, curious, and persistent. Their main priorities are easier mealtimes, calmer transitions, and communication that works with familiar adults outside the home. They want both family languages supported.

The grandmother said, “When Gabi brings me a shoe, I know he wants outside. I want him to have another way when I do not understand.” The parents reported that their child uses gestures, sounds, and several words across languages. Recent productions included "agua", "more", and "no". During the visit, he pointed toward the doorway and said, “Pico run.” That phrase showed a meaningful attempt to combine information about a familiar animal and an action. The family prefers useful words and short phrases over repeated requests to copy isolated sounds.

Morning routines begin around 6:30 a.m.. Breakfast usually includes fruit, toast, or oatmeal while a parent prepares for work. The child often reaches toward food without naming it. When adults offer several questions quickly, he may push the bowl away or leave the table. The family will try offering two visible choices, pausing, and accepting a gesture, picture, sound, or word. Meals should remain comfortable. Adults will model one short phrase and respond to the child’s message without requiring a spoken answer before providing food.

The child attends Little Heron Early Learning Center in Ms. Lopez’s room. Ms. Lopez reported that Gabriel joins music activities and watches other children closely. He sometimes takes a toy when he cannot request a turn. Classmates Nora Bell and Eli Navarro frequently play beside him at the block shelf. The classroom assistant, Tessa Morgan, uses pictures during cleanup. Staff requested shared words and gestures for requesting help, joining play, and moving between activities. The parents approved coordination with the classroom team.

Afternoon pickup occurs around 4:45 p.m., followed by a snack and outdoor play. The father reported that the transition into the car is harder when the child is tired. A small picture card showing the car and home may help make the next activity clear. During bath time, the child enjoys pouring water and naming body parts with an adult. Bedtime starts near 8:00 p.m.. The family prefers a short book and familiar song, with communication practice embedded in these activities.

Other involved agencies include Juniper County DSS, Larkhaven WIC, Juniper Smart Start, and Meadow Bridge Early Head Start. The family also receives occasional transportation and parent support through Centro Comunitario de Apoyo Integral para Familias y Niños de Juniper (CCAIFNJ). The mother said CCAIFNJ helped her understand an enrollment letter and arrange a ride. Driver Mr. Luis Benton is a transportation contact, not a clinical team member. The coordinator will confirm which supports remain active before requesting further referrals, so the family does not repeat paperwork unnecessarily.

The parents reported an uncomplicated delivery at Juniper Valley Community Hospital. Gestational age was 39 weeks, 2 days, birth weight was 3.2 kg, and Apgar scores were 8 and 9. These details come from family report and were not independently verified during this visit. Pediatrician Dr. Mina Salcedo follows routine health needs. The family reported no current feeding safety concerns. They described a prior hearing screening as satisfactory; the coordinator will request the actual result with parental consent before documenting it as verified.

An evaluation on September 3, 2026, included the PLS-5 Spanish, caregiver interview, play observation, and a bilingual language sample. The Auditory Comprehension standard score was 84, with a percentile rank of 14 and confidence interval of 78–92. The Expressive Communication standard score was 78, with a percentile rank of 7 and confidence interval of 73–86. The Total Language standard score was 80. These scores describe performance under the assessment conditions. They do not capture every skill used with familiar people or establish a language difference as a disorder.

The Expressive Communication age equivalent was 1;10. This estimate is descriptive and does not mean that the child functions at that age across activities. During play, he followed familiar directions in 8/10 opportunities when objects were visible. He requested assistance in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Speech included [w] in several productions, documented here as [w], and an emerging /k/ in a familiar word. A sample utterance, "me agua", was retained with the SALT code [EW] for analysis without treating bilingual variation alone as an error.

Outcomes, strategies, and services

IFSP outcome 1 addresses requesting during meals and play. By December 17, 2026, Gabriel will communicate a choice, request, or need for help using a gesture, picture, word, or short phrase in 4 of 5 natural opportunities across two routines. Adults will keep desired items visible, offer an understandable choice, and pause before helping. Models may include "help", "ayuda", "more water", and "más agua". The family will accept either language and will not withhold necessary items to force speech.

We will use Hanen strategies and focused stimulation within activities the family already enjoys. During visits, I will demonstrate a strategy, invite a caregiver to try it, and discuss what happened. The mother requested examples that take less than a minute to use. The father will place two snack choices within view and model a short request once. The grandmother will use the same approach during evening care. Progress notes will describe the child’s message, the adult’s response, and whether min cues, mod cues, or max cues were needed.

IFSP outcome 2 addresses participation in classroom play. By January 14, 2027, the child will communicate with an adult or peer to enter play, request a turn, or obtain help in 3 of 4 observed opportunities across classroom activities. Ms. Lopez will pair simple gestures with "my turn", "turno", and "help me". Staff will arrange brief shared activities with willing peers and respond to gestures as meaningful communication. Adults will support access to toys while teaching a clearer request.

Classroom strategies will begin during blocks and music because these routines already hold the child’s attention. Ms. Morgan will show the same pictures used at home when practical. The team will avoid requiring eye contact or repeated imitation before responding. A successful interaction may be a point followed by an adult model and a peer’s response. Once each week, staff will note one example of independent communication and one situation that remains difficult. The coordinator will help share those observations without adding a lengthy reporting task.

IFSP outcome 3 addresses transitions. By January 14, 2027, the child will participate in moving from a preferred activity to the next routine with a clear advance signal and communicate acceptance, protest, or a request for help in 4 of 5 opportunities. Adults will show a picture, name the next activity, and allow a brief response. Useful models include "all done", "finished", and "one more". The family wants the child’s protest acknowledged while adults maintain necessary limits.

The father will try the transition strategy at daycare pickup. The grandmother will try it before bath time. Adults will note whether tiredness, hunger, noise, or an unexpected change affected participation. The team will review patterns rather than interpreting every difficult transition as a communication failure. If a picture adds confusion, we will simplify the support and use an object or consistent gesture. The parents chose these routines because improvements would reduce stress during the busiest parts of their day.

Speech-language services will start on September 24, 2026, and continue through March 17, 2027, pending the next team review. Visits will occur once weekly for forty-five minutes in the home or daycare, according to family priorities. The planned home appointment is Thursday at 5:30 p.m.. Service documentation lists CPT 92507, modifier GN, and ICD-10 F80.2. Authorization number AUTH-620947 covers the stated service period. Any schedule change will be discussed with the family and documented before the revised schedule begins.

The next IFSP review is scheduled for December 17, 2026. J. Ortiz will contact the family before that meeting and confirm participation by relevant providers and classroom staff. We will review routine observations, caregiver priorities, service attendance, and progress toward each outcome. The parents received a summary in their preferred languages and agreed with the proposed services. They emphasized that successful support means their child can communicate during ordinary family life. No additional referrals were finalized at this meeting; hearing documentation and agency coordination remain assigned to the service coordinator.

North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program
Fictional IFSP Review and Bilingual Communication Evaluation

Review date: October 14, 2026
Evaluation date: October 14, 2026
Initial IFSP date: April 14, 2026
Child record: NCIT-60482917
Medicaid member number: 604829173K

Family information and review participants

Mateo Adrián Solís, called Teo at home, was born on August 14, 2024. His chronological age is 26 months. He lives with his mother, Guadalupe Elena Solís, called Lupita; his father, Jesús Rafael Solís, called Chuy; and his brother, José Emiliano Solís, called Pepe, age 6 years. The family address is 418 Willow Lantern Lane, Bellhaven, North Carolina 27864. The primary telephone number is (919) 555-0147. The family email is solis.family@example.org.

The family uses Spanish during most home routines and English during some community activities. The parents requested this written review in English. The clinician discussed findings and recommendations in both languages.

Mother works morning shifts at Marigold Linen Services and evening shifts at NHC. Father repairs equipment for Cedar Basket Packing. Maternal grandmother Rosa Inés Valverde provides care between shifts. She previously lived at Calle Jacaranda 27, in the village of San Lucero del Monte, Mexico. The family maintains contact with relatives there through video calls.

Service coordination and participating agencies

The service coordinator is Marisol Reyes, identified as M.R. on scheduling notes. She works through Lantern County CDSA, located at 72 Orchard Commons Drive, Bellhaven, North Carolina 27864. Her telephone number is (919) 555-0162.

The evaluating bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist is Elena Marín Brooks, MS, CCC-SLP, employed by Juniper Bridge Pediatric Speech. She completed the family interview, direct assessment, language sampling, and routine observation.

The primary care physician is Dr. Anika Desai at Blue Heron Children’s Hospital. An occupational therapist, J. Ortiz, provides consultation about seating and participation during meals.

The family also receives support from Centro Comunitario de Apoyo Integral para Familias Migrantes y Desarrollo Infantil Temprano (CCAIFMDIT). Its family navigator, Dalia Fuentes, helped arrange transportation. CCAIFMDIT does not provide clinical treatment. Lantern County Family Nutrition Office supports food access. The coordinator will contact these agencies only within the family’s documented releases.

Family concerns and priorities

Mother stated, “I understand his looks, but other people do not. I want him to tell Grandma when he needs something.”

Father stated, “When I get home, he brings me things. I want to know what he wants before he gets upset.”

Mother added, “I work two jobs. Please give us things we can do while we eat or get dressed. We cannot make another homework time.”

The parents identified communication during meals, transitions, and play as their main priorities. They want both languages supported. They do not want relatives to stop speaking Spanish.

Grandmother stated, “He listens when we sing. If I wait, he sometimes tries a word. I need to remember to wait.”

The family described strengths in affection, movement, imitation of familiar actions, and interest in people. Mateo enjoys placing toy animals in containers and bringing books to adults. He often seeks his brother’s attention by offering a car.

The parents reported fewer prolonged protests since the initial plan. They still need help identifying whether a protest means refusal, discomfort, or a request for assistance. They want daycare staff to use the same simple choices that work at home.

Relevant history and current participation

Mother reported birth at 38 weeks gestation, birth weight 3,180 grams, and Apgar scores of 8 and 9. No neonatal admission was reported. These details came from the family interview; hospital birth records were unavailable for this review.

The family reported no recent loss of communication skills. Hearing screening documentation dated September 22, 2026 indicated a pass in both ears. The clinician reviewed that report. Feeding concerns involve limited food variety and difficulty requesting another serving. The family did not report coughing or choking during meals.

Teo attends Little Acorn Harbor on weekdays. Teacher Ms. Nora Velásquez reported that he watches familiar songs, joins movement activities, and needs adult help when another child takes a preferred toy. Classroom assistant Evan Pierce described improved participation when adults show an object before giving a direction.

A familiar peer, Juan Esteban Molina, called Juanito, often plays beside him at the vehicle shelf. Staff described brief exchanges of cars. They did not report sustained conversation between the children.

Daily routines and natural learning opportunities

Breakfast usually begins at 7:15 a.m.. Grandmother offers familiar foods while mother prepares for work. Adults often anticipate requests, which reduces opportunities for communication. The family agreed to pause before opening containers or giving another serving.

Daycare arrival is near 8:10 a.m.. A picture showing the next activity helps with separation. Staff will pair a brief spoken message with the picture and allow extra processing time.

Lunch provides opportunities to request, reject, and ask for help. Adults will accept a gesture, picture, sign, or spoken attempt. Food access will not depend on producing a word.

After daycare, the family walks near home. Mateo points toward moving vehicles and the family dog, Canela. Adults can describe his focus and add a short phrase without asking repeated questions.

Bathing and dressing provide predictable action words. Brother Pepe can offer a choice between two shirts with adult support. The parents will keep sibling participation playful and voluntary.

Bedtime begins around 8:30 p.m.. A short book and familiar song are practical opportunities for shared attention. The clinician recommended repeating enjoyable books rather than changing materials each night.

Evaluation procedures and results

The clinician administered PLS-5 Spanish using the instrument’s bilingual administration procedures. She also observed caregiver interaction, collected a spontaneous language sample, and reviewed daycare information. Family reports supported interpretation across settings.

The table presents standard scores, percentile ranks, confidence intervals, and age-equivalent ranges. Confidence intervals reflect measurement uncertainty. Age-equivalent ranges provide descriptive context and do not establish an instructional placement.

| Measure | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age-equivalent range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auditory Comprehension | 79 | 8th percentile | 74–87 | 1;8–1;11 |
| Expressive Communication | 76 | 5th percentile | 71–84 | 1;5–1;8 |
| Total Language | 76 | 5th percentile | 72–83 | 1;6–1;9 |

Mateo followed familiar directions in 7/10 opportunities when objects and gestures supported the message. Performance decreased when directions lacked context. He identified familiar pictured objects in 6/10 opportunities across both languages.

He communicated spontaneously in 8/15 observed opportunities through pointing, reaching, vocalizing, or words. He combined a gesture with a vocalization in 5 of 8 supported exchanges. These observations describe this session and are not additional standardized scores.

Clinical interpretation

Observed productions included "agua", "más", "go", and "no". A request for a toy car sounded like [ka]. The clinician heard emerging /k/ in familiar words and frequent [w] during excited play.

During a pet-related exchange, he said "Canela come". This phrase occurred once and was not treated as an established skill.

The language sample contained frequent gestures and limited word combinations. No consistent use of /ɾ/ was observed. Speech sound findings remain descriptive because the sample was small and language development limits formal interpretation.

The clinician used min cues for familiar gestures, mod cues for supported choices, and max cues when introducing a new picture request. Participation improved when adults followed the child’s interest.

Findings support continued intervention for receptive and expressive language needs. Bilingual exposure does not explain the observed difficulty across languages. The working treatment diagnosis is F80.2. Planned individual communication treatment uses CPT 92507 with modifier GN, subject to payer requirements.

Outcomes, strategies, and progress measures

Outcome 1: During meals and snacks, Teo will communicate a request, rejection, or need for help in 8/10 natural opportunities across consecutive caregiver observations.

Current performance is 4/10 opportunities with mod cues. Caregivers will offer meaningful choices, model "más", "help", and "all done", then pause. They will respond to gestures and word attempts. The clinician will coach responsive interaction using Hanen principles. The family will record examples with brief check marks.

Outcome 2: During dressing, cleanup, and daycare transitions, Mateo will follow familiar directions in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

Current performance is 3 of 5 opportunities with gestures and mod cues. Adults will use one brief direction, show the relevant object, and wait. They will reduce gestures gradually as understanding improves. Practice will occur within existing routines. Adults will avoid repeating a direction rapidly or adding several new instructions.

Outcome 3: During play and books, Mateo will initiate or respond within reciprocal interaction for 3 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

Current performance is 2 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Adults will imitate his actions, add a simple word, and leave space for a response. Target phrases include "my turn", "go car", and "abre". Daycare staff will support brief exchanges with Juanito without requiring spoken performance before access to toys.

Outcome 4: During familiar routines, caregivers will identify and use a communication strategy in 80% of sampled opportunities.

Current observed use is 50%. The clinician will demonstrate a strategy, observe caregiver practice, and give specific feedback. Parents selected waiting, offering choices, and expanding attempts. Coaching will use routines that fit changing work schedules. The family may decline a proposed activity and choose another routine that serves the same outcome.

Services, dates, and responsibilities

Speech-language services will occur weekly for 45 minutes in the home or daycare from October 19, 2026 through April 13, 2027. The first home visit is scheduled for October 19, 2026 at 4:15 p.m..

Monthly occupational therapy consultation will continue from October 21, 2026 through April 13, 2027. Consultation will address positioning and participation within family routines.

The service coordinator will contact the family monthly and help resolve scheduling barriers. A progress discussion is planned for January 14, 2027. The next formal review is scheduled for April 14, 2027.

The clinician will document communication opportunities, caregiver observations, cueing needs, and generalization between settings. Progress decisions will use repeated routine observations, family priorities, and direct assessment when appropriate.

Family participation and review agreement

The parents confirmed that the outcomes reflect their priorities. They requested late afternoon visits and advance notice of schedule changes. They agreed to share a brief strategy sheet with daycare staff.

Mother Lupita stated, “This feels possible because we can do it during things we already do.” Father Chuy requested examples in both languages. The clinician provided verbal examples and will bring a bilingual routine sheet to the first visit.

The team will revise strategies when routines change. The family can request an earlier review through the coordinator.

Prepared by Elena Marín Brooks, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, on October 14, 2026.

Strategies: Offer two visible choices. Name each choice once, then wait. Accept pointing, reaching with shared attention, pictures, and spoken attempts. Model "more water", "más agua", or "help" after the child's message. Provide the requested item without demanding repetition.

The clinician will use Hanen interaction strategies to coach waiting, following the child's interest, and responding to attempts. Pictures will remain available beside the table. Adults will avoid turning every bite into a communication test.

Strategies: Sit nearby, use matching toys, and copy the child's action before adding a new action. Model "my turn", "your turn", "mi turno", and "otra vez". Pause after a short model. Let gestures count as participation.

Success criterion: The child uses an agreed signal in 4 of 5 transition opportunities across home and daycare, with mod cues or less. Target date: 06-03-2025.

Strategies: Show a simple picture before the change. Offer one concrete next step. Model "help me", "all done", "ayuda", and "terminé". Recognize body movements and vocalizations as possible messages, then confirm the meaning.

Adults will give time to finish a small action when practical. The clinician will coach repair by acknowledging the attempt, offering a choice, and checking the child's response. Caregivers will use consistent pictures without requiring identical words in both languages.

Progress today: A picture and a short verbal warning supported cleanup. Repeated questions increased frustration.
