Client: María José Valdés Ortega
Preferred name: Majo
DOB: May 18, 2023
Chronological age: 3;4
Evaluation date: September 18, 2026
Session: 9:10 a.m.–10:35 a.m.
Record: SLP-260918-047
Medicaid member: 836204719Q
Authorization: NC-SL-482716
Referral: Mixed receptive-expressive language concerns; ICD-10 F80.2.
Evaluation service: CPT 92523; modifier GN.
Proposed treatment: CPT 92507; modifier GN.
Clinician: Elena Marisol Cárdenas, MS, CCC-SLP; bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist.
Employer: Sendero Bilingual Pediatric Therapies
Office: 418 Lantern Finch Lane, Suite B, Loma Serena, North Carolina 27846.
Phone: 919-555-0148
Email: ecardenas@senderopeds.example
Website: https://senderopeds.example
Parent contact: Lucía Valdés Romero; 984-555-0173.
School: Willow Lantern Early Learning School.
Classroom: Ms. Lopez's room.
CDSA office: Agencia de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil de Arroyo Cedro, short form CDSA-AC.
Service coordinator: Nora Isabel Peña, with Agencia Puentes de Familia para Coordinación de Servicios Infantiles de Loma Serena, short form APF-LS.

S: SUBJETIVO / ANTECEDENTES

Referral concerns: Limited sentence length, difficulty following unfamiliar directions, and frustration during peer play. Mother requested evaluation because familiar adults often anticipate needs. At school, adults report reduced independent communication during transitions. Family seeks functional bilingual communication; no request to replace Spanish with English. Evaluation addressed comprehension, expression, speech sound production, play, and participation. Parent consent obtained verbally and in writing. No interpreter used; clinician completed interview and assessment directly in both languages.

Present with child: Mother Lucía Valdés Romero and father Gabriel Ortega Salcedo. Mother stated, “En casa nos entiende cuando hacemos lo mismo cada día, pero si cambiamos algo, se pierde.” Father stated, “Queremos que pueda pedir ayuda sin llorar, en español o English.” Both described frequent pointing, pulling an adult toward an object, and short verbal requests. Parents reported that María José speaks more during familiar songs and pretend cooking than during direct questions.

Birth history / nacimiento: Born at Arroyo Cedro Family Birth Hospital in Arroyo Cedro, North Carolina. Gestational age 36 weeks, 5 days; birth weight 2.68 kg. Apgar scores 8 and 9. Parent reported brief observation for feeding endurance and temperature regulation. No respiratory support reported. Discharged home with parents after routine monitoring. Pregnancy history included maternal hypertension, per parent; no documented prenatal infection or exposure concerns available. Birth details came from parent interview and a fictional discharge summary supplied for this assessment.

Medical history: Primary care provider is Dr. Sofía Beltrán Vega at Lantern Creek Children's Medical Center. Parent reported recurrent middle-ear fluid during toddlerhood; no tubes placed. Audiologist Evan Calder Pike completed testing on August 21, 2026. Supplied report described hearing adequate for speech access during that visit. No current ear pain reported. No seizures, major surgery, regression, or known genetic condition reported. Child takes no daily medication, per parent. Seasonal congestion occurs intermittently; it did not visibly limit participation today.

Desarrollo temprano: Sat independently at 7 months, walked at 15 months, and used first consistent words near 19 months, per mother. Word combinations emerged near 30 months. Parents denied loss of previously established skills. Early words included "mamá", "agua", and "más". Family described steady but slow growth in vocabulary. Child now combines words mainly for requests and familiar routines. Novel descriptions, explanations, and repair after misunderstanding remain difficult. Parent estimates of early milestones were approximate; contemporaneous developmental records were unavailable.

Family history / familia: Lives with both parents and brother Diego Ortega Valdés, age 7 years. Maternal grandmother Teresa Romero Acosta provides after-school care. Aunt Inés Valdés Pardo helps during parent work shifts. Father works at Cedar Loom Packaging Cooperative; mother works at Brisa Orchard Catering Studio. Family dog is Tito. Mother reported that brother Diego received brief speech support for sound production. No additional family history of diagnosed language disorder was reported. Caregivers expressed willingness to practice short routines without turning play into repeated testing.

Language history: Spanish predominates during meals, caregiving, and extended-family contact. English exposure increased with school entry at 2;10. Parents estimated current waking exposure as 65% Spanish and 35% English; these are interview estimates. Father code-switches during books and outdoor play. Grandmother Teresa uses Spanish consistently. Brother Diego uses both languages during pretend play. Family has not stopped either language. Mother stated, “A veces mezcla, pero eso no nos preocupa; nos preocupa que no puede explicar qué pasó.”

School participation: Attends Willow Lantern Early Learning School on weekday mornings. Lead teacher Ms. Irene Lopez provided a written report dated September 12, 2026. In Ms. Lopez's room, the child follows cleanup routines with visual support but misses novel group directions. Classroom assistant Camila Reed Torres reported improved participation when adults demonstrate the first step. Peer Nico Serrano Bell often initiates block play. Peer Elena Cruz Finch shares pretend food. Child reportedly watches peers before joining and sometimes abandons an interaction after an unsuccessful request.

Daily routines: Family wakes around 6:45 a.m.; school arrival is near 8:15 a.m.. Bedtime routine begins around 8:00 p.m.. Parent described adequate sleep with occasional waking. Meals involve familiar foods; no coughing, choking, or prolonged chewing reported. Dressing and toileting create communication demands when an item is missing or help is needed. Child often uses "no puedo" but does not consistently identify the problem. Mother wants language practice embedded in these routines, “sin presión, poquito a poquito.”

Prior services / coordinación: Historical IFSP dated February 6, 2026 came from CDSA-AC. Service coordinator Nora Peña of APF-LS supported transition planning. Prior IFSP outcome 2 addressed functional requesting; goal 2.1 addressed combining words during familiar play. Home visits ended after transition from infant-toddler services. No current outpatient speech treatment reported. Parent priorities today: asking for help, understanding school directions, telling a simple event, and maintaining Spanish relationships. Family agreed that progress should be measured across settings and languages.

O: OBJETIVO / PROCEDIMIENTOS Y RESULTADOS

Assessment conditions: Quiet clinic room; parent nearby; floor play, tabletop activities, and movement breaks alternated. Child entered holding mother's hand, explored toys, and gradually initiated interaction. Attention varied with task novelty and language load. Participation improved when clinician reduced verbal length and allowed processing time. No acute distress observed. Fatigue appeared during later naming tasks. Results reflect today's performance under these conditions. Parent and teacher reports supplied complementary information about daily functioning. Testing did not establish performance across every possible setting.

Procedures included PLS-5 Spanish, a bilingual language sample, dynamic teaching probes, play observation, an informal oral mechanism screen, and an informal speech sound inventory. Clinician followed the dual-language administration rules for PLS-5 Spanish during scored items. Additional teaching occurred after scored responses and remained separate from standard scoring. No English-only standard score was generated. Spanish and English responses informed functional interpretation. Familiar vocabulary was checked with parents when regional wording differed. Parent familiarity with an item did not replace an observed child response.

Resultados estandarizados: PLS-5 Spanish

| Test/subtest | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auditory Comprehension | 31 | 78 | 7th | 73-83 | 2;6–3;0 |
| Expressive Communication | 29 | 82 | 12th | 77–87 | 2;8–3;1 |
| Total Language | 60 | 79 | 8th | 74–84 | 2;7–3;0 |

Confidence intervals above use the 90% level. Scores and age-equivalent ranges are fictional test data for this report. Age equivalents describe selected task performance; they do not assign the child a single developmental age. Interpretation considers bilingual exposure, task demands, and functional observations. The Total Language standard score of 79 indicates performance below the test's expected range. Its confidence interval, 74–84, reflects measurement uncertainty. Functional findings below provide the main basis for treatment priorities and participation planning.

Comprensión: Identified familiar objects and actions across languages. Followed familiar single-step directions in 8/10 opportunities, or 80%, with min cues. Unfamiliar single-step directions decreased to 5/10, or 50%, without a model. Two-step related directions were completed in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Errors increased when directions combined a location word, an unfamiliar noun, and an action. Child sometimes acted on the final noun while missing the relationship between objects. Demonstration supported performance, but repeated verbal directions alone offered limited benefit.

Conceptos y preguntas: Identified "in" and "dentro" reliably during familiar container play. Responses to "under", "debajo", "behind", and "detrás" were inconsistent across materials. Answered concrete object questions more readily than questions about events. For "¿Dónde está?", child often pointed without a verbal response. For "What happened?", child repeated part of the prompt or labeled one visible item. Accuracy improved when clinician provided an actual event to observe. Difficulty appeared in both languages and exceeded simple unfamiliarity with English classroom vocabulary.

Expresión: Spontaneous communication consisted mainly of short requests, labels, refusals, and comments. Sample included "más bubbles", "quiero la taza", "it fall down", and "no está aquí". Child used Spanish articles inconsistently and omitted some English grammatical markers. Several omissions occurred in both languages during longer utterances. Code-switching served a clear communicative purpose and was not counted as an error. Child used available vocabulary from either language to maintain play. Word retrieval pauses sometimes led to gesture, a general noun, or abandonment of the message.

Language sample / muestra: Collected during pretend cooking, blocks, and picture discussion. SALT code [EW] marked an extraneous word when it added no intended meaning. SALT code [EU] marked an extraneous utterance unrelated to the ongoing exchange. These codes describe sample transcription, not a diagnosis. Child produced "yo quiero ese grande" after a choice prompt, then used "big one aquí" independently. When the toy dog moved, child said "Tito run"; the named production was transcribed without treating the name as a clinical target.

Narrative and repair: Given a brief picture sequence, child labeled visible items but needed max cues to connect actions. With mod cues, child produced "baby cayó" and "mamá ayuda". Independent explanation of cause was absent during this probe. When clinician intentionally misunderstood a request, child repeated the same words, increased volume, or pointed. With min cues to show the needed object, repair improved in 4/6 opportunities. Functional repair remains a priority because communication breakdown affected persistence more than willingness to interact.

Dynamic learning: Clinician taught a simple help-request routine using Focused Stimulation and Enhanced Milieu Teaching. Initial independent use of "help me" or "ayúdame" occurred in 2/8 opportunities. After models and supported practice, use increased to 6/8 opportunities with mod cues. During a later toy change, child used "ayúdame abrir" with min cues. This response suggests useful learning potential. It does not erase the need for support or establish independent generalization. Parent observed the teaching sequence and practiced the same pause-and-model routine.

Habla / sonidos: Informal inventory included consonants /p/, /b/, /m/, /t/, /d/, /n/, /k/, and /g/ in familiar words. Productions of /ɾ/ varied; developmental interpretation considered language and age. Target "casa" was produced as "tasa" in one imitation trial but accurately during later play. Target "water" began with [w] in the sample. No single isolated substitution established a consistent pattern. Longer utterances reduced clarity, especially when volume decreased. Speech sound findings require continued observation as language output expands.

Oral mechanism and voice: Facial symmetry, lip closure, and tongue movement appeared adequate for observed speech tasks. Child followed imitation requests inconsistently; therefore, the screen was limited. Voice sounded clear during available speech. No persistent strain or unusual resonance observed. Fluency showed brief repetitions during formulation, without visible tension in this sample. Feeding and swallowing were not formally evaluated. Caregiver reported no current swallowing concern. Any future concern would require its own assessment rather than inference from today's brief speech-related observation.

Juego, pragmática y regulación: Shared attention, social interest, and symbolic play were present. Child offered pretend food, checked adult reactions, and accepted a partner's play idea. Initiated communication in 7/10 arranged opportunities with min cues. Turn-taking was stronger when language demands were low. During a simulated peer exchange, requests required mod cues. Child tolerated transitions with a visual warning and access to a familiar object. Parent reported similar strengths at home. Today’s pragmatic observations support language-focused intervention while leaving broader developmental questions open to continued team observation.

A: ANÁLISIS / IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Findings support mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, ICD-10 F80.2, within this fictional case. Comprehension weaknesses affect unfamiliar directions, relational concepts, and event questions. Expressive weaknesses affect flexible combinations, event descriptions, and repair. Evidence includes below-expected standardized performance, difficulty across both languages, functional caregiver concerns, and direct observation. Bilingual exposure alone does not explain the full pattern. English experience remains relevant to item familiarity and school performance. The clinician considered that context throughout interpretation.

Severity impression: Moderate functional language support need at present. This description reflects participation demands and cue dependence, not a fixed prediction. Child communicates many basic needs through words and gestures. Breakdowns increase when partners lack shared context or require an explanation. School group directions create added processing demands. At home, familiar routines can conceal comprehension gaps because caregivers anticipate the next step. Treatment should measure communication with less familiar materials and partners while preserving predictable supports for success.

Strengths / fortalezas: Social engagement, pretend play, persistence with preferred materials, and response to supported teaching. Parents notice communication attempts and accept both languages. Child uses code-switching purposefully and has meaningful vocabulary distributed across languages. A Spanish-only or English-only view would undercount some abilities. Dynamic improvement indicates capacity to learn with an appropriate model and practice. Generalization still requires verification. Team members should value a successful bilingual message even when it differs from the adult's preferred language.

Speech sound impression: No separate speech sound diagnosis assigned today. The available sample was limited, and observed variability did not establish a stable pattern. Some productions reduced intelligibility, but language formulation also contributed. Reassessment should examine repeated words and connected speech across languages. Current therapy should avoid assigning developmentally inappropriate sound expectations. A focused speech intervention such as Cycles or PROMPT is not selected from these data. Selection would require a clearer speech profile and a specific functional rationale.

Educational implications: Child may miss instructions even while appearing attentive. Repetition of the same long sentence may increase confusion. Short directions, visual information, and a check through action can improve access. Teachers should allow responses in either language when the activity permits. Peer support can help entry into play, but peers should not carry responsibility for communication. Adult modeling should show how to request, clarify, and repair. Participation data should include independent attempts and the amount of support required.

Limitations: Parent history includes recall estimates. Teacher information came from a written report, without direct classroom observation. Assessment occurred during one clinic visit. Standardized scores cannot fully describe bilingual communication in daily life. Age-equivalent ranges must not determine placement or replace functional judgment. Prognosis for useful progress is favorable with consistent support, based on observed learning and caregiver participation. Rate of progress remains uncertain. Continued data collection will test whether clinic gains transfer to home and school.

P: PLAN / RECOMENDACIONES

1. Begin individual speech-language therapy weekly, with a planned treatment block followed by review. Use CPT 92507 and modifier GN when applicable to the fictional authorization. Confirm scheduling and coverage before service begins. Treatment may include caregiver participation and coordination with school staff after consent. Keep sessions bilingual according to task, partner, and child response. Review progress on December 18, 2026. Proposed frequency is provisional and should change with attendance, response, and functional need.

2. Address historical IFSP outcome 2 through the current treatment plan. Treatment goal 1: Child will request help, an item, or a turn using a functional word combination in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Accept Spanish, English, and mixed-language responses that communicate the intended meaning. Record spontaneous responses separately from imitation. Use different objects and routines. A successful familiar phrase should be tested again when the partner or material changes.

3. Treatment goal 2: Follow related directions containing an action and location concept in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Begin with familiar materials, then vary the arrangement. Contrast targets "in"/"dentro" and "under"/"debajo" during actual play. Reduce verbal load before adding another step. Record errors by concept and language of presentation. Do not count a correct action after full demonstration as an independent comprehension response.

4. Treatment goal 3: Describe a recent play event with an agent and action in 80% of structured opportunities with mod cues. Support messages such as "el bebé cayó" and "the dog is running". Treatment goal 4: Repair a misunderstood message in 3 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Accept showing, adding a word, or using a different phrase. Fade adult guessing so the child has a real reason to clarify.

5. Use Focused Stimulation and Enhanced Milieu Teaching during motivating routines. Offer caregivers principles consistent with Hanen, using brief demonstrations and practice. Model one useful phrase, pause, and respond to the child's attempt. Expand a message without requiring repeated imitation. Low-tech picture choices may support access. A formal PECS program is not currently selected; assess need if functional communication remains insufficient. Program choice should follow the child's response, family priorities, and available training.

6. Home practice / práctica en casa: Choose a short daily routine such as snack, dressing, or toy cleanup. Mother Lucía and father Gabriel will model "ayúdame", "abre esto", or "help me open" when the need occurs. Grandmother Teresa may use the Spanish version naturally. Keep practice brief and enjoyable. Avoid withholding essential needs to create communication opportunities. Accept gesture plus speech while building more specific messages. Note one successful independent attempt for discussion at the next visit.

7. School support: Share a concise plan with Ms. Lopez at Willow Lantern Early Learning School after parent consent. Provide visual directions, processing time, and a model for joining play. Classroom assistant Camila can record cue levels during transitions. Invite peer Nico or peer Elena into ordinary supported play without assigning them a helper role. Ask staff to describe the situation, child message, and adult response. These observations will show whether communication gains improve participation.

8. Coordination / seguimiento: Send the signed assessment only through the family's approved route. Contact Dr. Beltrán Vega if parent reports new hearing concerns or regression. With consent, ask Nora Peña at Agencia Puentes de Familia para Coordinación de Servicios Infantiles de Loma Serena to clarify remaining transition records. Reference the historical office as Agencia de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil de Arroyo Cedro or CDSA-AC in record matching. Recheck speech clarity during treatment. Consider further assessment if a consistent speech pattern or broader developmental concern emerges.

Parent education completed; caregivers demonstrated the pause-and-model routine and stated priorities consistent with this plan. Mother stated, “Así sí podemos hacerlo en casa, durante lo que ya hacemos.” Written bilingual practice notes supplied. No outside communication completed during this evaluation.

Signed: Elena Marisol Cárdenas, MS, CCC-SLP
Sendero Bilingual Pediatric Therapies

Signature time: 4:20 p.m.

A transportation aide, Mr. Oliver Grant Hale, described successful greetings but limited conversation.

SESSION SCHEDULE / HORARIO

The following schedule lists completed assessment contacts and proposed treatment windows. Treatment appointments remain subject to family availability and authorization.

| Contact | Day | Date | Start | Stop | Location |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Caregiver interview | Tuesday | July 14, 2026 | 6:15 p.m. | 6:45 p.m. | Home telephone contact, Briarhaven |
| Direct evaluation | Thursday | July 16, 2026 | 9:00 a.m. | 10:25 a.m. | Lantern Finch Pediatric Communication |
| Classroom consultation | Friday | July 17, 2026 | 10:10 a.m. | 10:35 a.m. | Juniper Lantern Preschool |
| Proposed individual session | Tuesday | August 4, 2026 | 3:30 p.m. | 4:00 p.m. | Clinic, Briarhaven |
| Proposed caregiver session | Thursday | August 6, 2026 | 5:15 p.m. | 5:45 p.m. | Home, 418 Lantern Orchard Lane |

MÉTODOS / ASSESSMENT METHODS

The clinician used PLS-5 Spanish according to its bilingual administration framework. Credit reflected eligible responses across Spanish and English. The clinician recorded language choices separately. Informal activities examined skills that standardized scores alone cannot describe.

GFTA-3 items supported descriptive observation of English speech sounds. No norm-referenced score was assigned because interpretation required consideration of bilingual exposure and cross-language patterns. Connected speech, Spanish picture naming, play, and caregiver examples supplied additional evidence.

A language sample was transcribed using SALT conventions. Codes included [EW] for word errors and [EU] for utterance errors. These codes describe transcript features; they do not independently establish a diagnosis.

RESULTADOS / SCORE SUMMARY

The table contains invented results for this fictional assessment. Percentiles and confidence intervals are illustrative. Scores must be interpreted with observation, bilingual language experience, and family priorities.

| Measure | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish — Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 71–85, 90% interval | 3;2 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th percentile | 68–82, 90% interval | 2;10 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Total Language | 75 | 5th percentile | 69–83, 90% interval | 3;0 |

Age equivalents are descriptive estimates. They do not represent a developmental age for the whole child. Informal tasks showed uneven abilities, with stronger familiar vocabulary and social engagement than sentence organization and comprehension of less familiar directions.

COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

Mateo identified common objects and actions across both languages. He followed familiar single-step directions in 8/10 opportunities without added support. Performance decreased when directions included an unfamiliar spatial term or more than one action.

For related two-step directions, he completed 3 of 5 trials with min cues and 4 of 5 with mod cues. He benefited from a gesture and a pause between actions. Rapid repetition without visual information did not consistently improve performance.

He understood “inside” and “adentro” during container play. Responses to “behind” and “detrás” were inconsistent. He answered concrete identification questions more reliably than questions requiring a reason, prediction, or description of a past event.

During book sharing, he pointed to a character’s expression and selected a matching feeling picture. He needed mod cues to explain the cause. The difficulty appeared in Spanish and English, aunque conocía muchas de las palabras individuales.

EXPRESIÓN / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

The sample contained short combinations, occasional longer messages, and frequent language switching. Switching served communication and was not counted as an error. Examples included “quiero blue car”, “se cayó down”, and “yo no want ese”.

He used “más agua” independently and expanded to “quiero más agua” after a model. For the target “the dog is sleeping”, he produced “dog sleep”. For “el perro está durmiendo”, he produced “perro mimi”.

Messages containing names were transcribed without production-level protection: he said “Nube come aquí” and “Pepe my turn.” He called “Chuy help” when a container would not open. These examples showed intentional requesting and partner selection.

Spontaneous grammatical marking was inconsistent in both languages. He omitted some articles and auxiliary verbs, and he sometimes used a general word instead of a specific action. Word retrieval improved with an object cue or a choice between two familiar words.

A brief teaching probe increased successful action descriptions from 2/6 independently to 5/6 with mod cues. After a short delay, he retained 3/6 with min cues. This response supports learning potential, while continued support remains necessary.

HABLA / SPEECH SOUND FINDINGS

Oral structures appeared adequate for the observed tasks. Lip closure, tongue movement, and jaw stability supported eating-related movements and simple imitation. No obvious structural difference was observed. This screening did not replace a medical or dental examination.

Speech showed reduced precision in longer words and connected phrases. Frequent patterns included fronting of /k/ and /g/, cluster reduction, and inconsistent final consonant omission in English. Spanish observations included reduced syllables and substitutions affecting /ɾ/.

For “casa”, he produced “tasa”. For “go”, he produced “do”. For “spoon”, he produced “poon”. The target “pero” sometimes contained [w] in place of /ɾ/. No single example determined the clinical impression.

He imitated /k/ in isolation with max cues and in simple syllables with mod cues. Accuracy declined during spontaneous words. Familiar listeners understood approximately 75% of sampled messages; the clinician understood approximately 55% without contextual support.

Voice quality and fluency were functional during this session. No persistent strain or repetitive disruption was observed. Prosody varied with excitement. Findings did not establish childhood apraxia of speech; monitoring across repeated productions and treatment sessions is recommended.

IMPRESIONES / CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

The fictional findings support mixed receptive-expressive language difficulty and a speech sound disorder. Proposed diagnostic codes are F80.2 and F80.0. Communication differences affected participation across home and classroom activities, rather than appearing only in the less familiar language.

Bilingual exposure does not explain the full pattern. Difficulties appeared across both languages and included limited sentence organization, inconsistent comprehension of complex directions, and reduced intelligibility. Strengths included social motivation, shared attention, purposeful gestures, and a positive response to teaching.

Scores provide one part of the assessment. Fatigue, unfamiliar materials, and variable attention may have affected performance. Caregiver reports and classroom observations supported the same functional concerns. The clinician recommends intervention that preserves Spanish, supports English access, and measures progress across meaningful activities.

RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN

1. Begin individual speech-language therapy twice weekly, with caregiver participation when possible. Use play, familiar routines, and short practice blocks. Confirm appointments through the family’s preferred contact method. Offer flexible caregiver coaching around work schedules.

2. Address speech patterns through Cycles activities and meaningful contrasts. Select targets that improve everyday intelligibility. Consider PROMPT only after the clinician determines that its supports fit the observed needs. Do not select a motor-based program from this evaluation alone.

3. Use strategies drawn from Hanen to support shared attention, waiting, and expanded language models. Acknowledge the child’s message first. Then provide one natural expansion in the language used by the communication partner.

4. Support comprehension with pictures, gestures, and shorter directions. Reduce repeated questioning. Give processing time before offering min cues, then increase to mod cues if needed. Document the support required rather than recording success alone.

5. Encourage functional communication during meals, dressing, and play. Accept gestures and mixed-language messages. A simple picture board may support choices and repair. A formal PECS program is not currently required by the observed communication profile.

6. Coordinate strategies with the occupational therapist, physical therapist, pediatrician, and classroom team. Obtain family authorization before sharing the report. Review hearing again if ear symptoms return or listening behavior changes.

OBJETIVOS INICIALES / INITIAL GOALS

Goal 1: Follow related two-step directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues, across familiar Spanish and English routines.

Goal 2: Produce functional expanded messages in 4/5 opportunities with mod cues, using speech, gesture, or picture support.

Goal 3: Produce selected velar targets with 80% accuracy during structured play, initially with mod cues.

Goal 4: Repair an unclear message in 3 of 5 opportunities with min cues, by repeating, pointing, showing, or changing words.

Lupita selected snack preparation as the first practice routine. Chuy selected toy cleanup. Both parents agreed that successful communication matters more than perfect repetition. The clinician modeled one expansion and one pause, and each parent practiced during play.

Progress review is proposed for October 8, 2026. Review participation, intelligibility, comprehension, caregiver burden, and response to cueing. Adjust goals when the evidence supports a change. Reassessment timing should reflect treatment response and the family’s priorities.

text:
+ Name: Emilio Rafael Varela
+ Nickname: Milo
+ CA: 4;2
+ DOB: August 6, 2022
+ Evaluation date: October 8, 2026
+ Context: Bilingual pediatric speech-language assessment; clinic play, caregiver interview, school observation, and structured tasks.
+ Languages: Spanish and English.
+ Examiner: Marisol Vega, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist.
+ Employer: Juniper Lantern Pediatric Communication
+ Clinic: 1847 Lantern Finch Lane, Larkhaven, North Carolina 27864
+ Telephone: (919) 555-0142
+ Email: mvega@juniperlantern.example.invalid
+ Website: https://juniperlantern.example.invalid
+ Record: JLPC-26-0418
+ Medicaid member: 582640193K
+ Authorization: AUTH-NC-604218
+ Referral: Dr. Nadia Cordero, Willow Lantern Children’s Hospital
+ School district: Larkhaven Meadow School District
+ School: Copperleaf Early Learning School
+ Classroom: Elena Pardo’s bilingual preschool classroom.

Resumen / Summary

Emilio presents with reduced speech intelligibility and difficulty organizing longer messages across Spanish and English. He communicates readily through gestures, short sentences, facial expression, and shared play. His participation improves when the listener allows extra response time and offers visual support. His family identifies being understood during meals, school transitions, and sibling play as the main priorities.

Findings support a speech sound disorder and concern for an expressive language disorder. His skills vary across languages and activities. English scores describe performance under the stated conditions; they do not independently establish a disorder. The clinical conclusion also considers Spanish sampling, caregiver history, classroom participation, and response to teaching. Continued bilingual assessment will clarify his language profile.

Antecedentes / Background and referral

Su mamá, Lucía Varela, requested evaluation because familiar listeners sometimes need repeated attempts to understand daily requests. She explained, “Él tiene mucho que decir, pero la palabra sale cortita.” His father, Daniel Varela, reported that communication breakdowns occur most often when the topic is unexpected.

The family previously received early intervention through Piedra Clara Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Service coordinator Inés Mercado supplied a discharge summary dated September 2, 2025. The prior plan listed IFSP outcome 2, requesting help during routines, and IFSP outcome 4, combining words during shared play.

Current concerns increased after preschool entry. Ms. Pardo observes that Milo joins activities willingly but sometimes leaves a conversation when peers request clarification. The referral asks whether this pattern reflects language exposure, a communication disorder, or both. This report addresses communication access and treatment needs without treating bilingual development as a deficit.

Historia de nacimiento y salud / Birth and medical history

Caregivers reported delivery at 39 weeks, 1 day at Willow Lantern Children’s Hospital in Larkhaven, North Carolina. Birth weight was 3,280 g. Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The family reported no neonatal respiratory support, feeding tube, or prolonged admission.

Early feeding included breast and bottle feeding. Caregivers recalled comfortable swallowing and gradual acceptance of varied textures. Current concerns involve limited food preferences, without reported coughing, choking, or recurrent chest illness. Feeding was discussed but was not formally assessed.

Two episodes of middle-ear infection were reported during toddlerhood. Audiologist Teresa Neri documented hearing adequate for speech access on September 18, 2026. Caregivers reported no current medications or known allergies.

A developmental record from November 15, 2024 included the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition. An early communication note used the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale. These historical measures were reviewed for developmental context. Neither was administered today, and their earlier findings were not substituted for current results.

Historia familiar y de idiomas / Family and language history

Emilio lives with both parents and his sister, Sol, who is 7 years old. His grandmother, Beatriz Salcedo, provides care after school. A regular babysitter, Rosa Téllez, supports occasional evening routines. The family’s dog is named Chispa.

Spanish predominates during meals, family calls, and bedtime. English increases during preschool activities and neighborhood play. Caregivers estimate exposure at approximately 60% Spanish and 40% English, with substantial variation by day. These estimates describe opportunities for interaction, not language proficiency.

His mother works at Meadowglass Textile Cooperative. His father works at Cedar Finch Repair Works. Their schedules influence which caregiver attends appointments. The family prefers spoken explanations in Spanish and written summaries in both languages.

The family reported first meaningful words around 18 months and spontaneous combinations around 30 months. His grandmother noted, “Entiende lo de la casa; contar lo que pasó le cuesta.” Caregivers describe similar difficulty explaining events in either language. No family member was instructed to reduce Spanish use. Maintaining comfortable, responsive conversation in both languages remains a treatment priority.

Horario de sesiones / Session schedule

The following recurring schedule is proposed, subject to school and caregiver coordination.

| Day | Start | Stop | Location | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monday | 8:15 a.m. | 8:45 a.m. | Juniper Lantern Pediatric Communication, Larkhaven | Individual bilingual treatment |
| Wednesday | 10:10 a.m. | 10:40 a.m. | Copperleaf Early Learning School, Ms. Pardo’s classroom | Classroom participation |
| Friday | 3:30 p.m. | 4:00 p.m. | Juniper Lantern Pediatric Communication, Larkhaven | Caregiver coaching and play |

The evaluation began at 9:05 a.m. and ended at 10:25 a.m.. A movement break occurred at 9:45 a.m.. School observation occurred on October 7, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m.. Caregivers described communication during breakfast at 7:10 a.m. and bedtime reading at 7:45 p.m..

Procedimientos / Assessment conditions

Assessment included caregiver interview, oral mechanism screening, play observation, speech sampling, dynamic teaching, and selected standardized measures. Spanish and English were sampled in separate activities and in natural code-switching. The clinician accepted responses in either language during informal tasks.

The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) was administered in English under standard conditions. Its English normative comparisons have limited applicability to this bilingual child. Spanish explanations were offered after scored items, during separate teaching activities, and were excluded from standardized scoring.

The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) provided an English single-word sample. The Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition (PPVT-5) sampled English receptive vocabulary. These measures do not capture his full conceptual vocabulary across languages.

Milo initially watched quietly, then engaged with animals, blocks, and pretend cooking. He needed min cues to return after the break. Attention was sufficient for selected tasks, although fatigue increased near the end. The oral mechanism screening showed functional movement for sampled speech tasks; it was not an instrumental examination.

Resultados / Score table

Confidence intervals below use the 90% level. Age equivalents are descriptive estimates and should not guide placement or diagnosis alone.

| Measure | Test or subtest | Score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 | Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 84 | 14th percentile | 79–90 | 3;7 |
| PLS-5 | Expressive Communication | Standard score 76 | 5th percentile | 71–83 | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 | Total Language | Standard score 79 | 8th percentile | 74–85 | 3;3 |
| GFTA-3 | Sounds-in-Words | Standard score 71 | 3rd percentile | 67–78 | Not interpreted |
| PPVT-5 | Receptive vocabulary measure | Standard score 85 | 16th percentile | 80–91 | 3;6 |

Comprensión y expresión / Language findings

During familiar Spanish routines, Emilio followed related directions in 8/10 opportunities without repetition. Performance decreased to 3 of 5 when directions included an unfamiliar location term. Visual demonstration improved performance to 5 of 5. This suggests benefit from contextual support, rather than a uniform difficulty understanding spoken language.

English responses included labeling, requesting, and simple location information. Spanish responses showed broader vocabulary for household routines. He sometimes selected a word from the other language: "quiero more agua". This code-switching was accepted as meaningful communication.

Longer messages contained omissions and unclear references. During pretend cooking, he said "yo pon aquí", then pointed to a bowl. With mod cues, he expanded to "yo pongo sopa aquí". After a model, he produced "the dog is sleeping", but did not consistently generate similar sentence structures independently.

In a picture sequence, he identified the main event but needed max cues to explain the cause. He improved after demonstration and guided practice. The improvement shows learning potential, while continued support needs indicate that a single successful imitation should not be treated as mastery.

Habla y muestra SALT / Speech and language sample

Speech included inconsistent omissions of final consonants and reduced production of velar consonants. Substitutions of /t/ for /k/ occurred in both language samples. English /ɹ/ and Spanish /ɾ/ were observed separately; they were not treated as interchangeable targets.

Caregiver-estimated intelligibility was 75% for familiar listeners. The clinician understood approximately 55% of connected speech with contextual support. These estimates were informal and should not be compared directly with standardized scores.

A phonetic transcription documented [w] during an English liquid production. With mod cues, correct initial /k/ occurred in 6/10 attempts. Accuracy decreased during spontaneous phrases.

A sample entry recorded "him go home" with [EW]. Another recorded "yo quiero carro". The target word "sol" referred to the sun in a picture. His sister’s name, Sol, was discussed separately because the shared word form could affect interpretation.

During pet play, he said “Chispa corre.” During family play, he said “Sol come.” These productions demonstrated meaningful references to familiar individuals.

Participación / Classroom and social communication

Ms. Pardo reported that Milo responds to greetings, notices peers’ activities, and seeks shared materials. Classroom aide Joel Ledesma observed stronger participation when an adult previews the activity.

During observation, classmate Alma Ríos offered a pretend cup. Emilio accepted it and continued the play sequence. Classmate Nico Beltrán requested a block, and the child responded through pointing and a short verbal message. These exchanges showed social interest and reciprocal participation.

Communication breakdowns increased during rapid group discussion. A visual choice board helped him clarify his message with min cues. No diagnosis concerning social communication was established from this observation.

Impresiones clínicas / Clinical impressions

The combined evidence supports reduced speech clarity across languages, with errors that affect daily participation. Differences between Spanish and English sound systems were considered before selecting targets. Bilingual exposure alone does not explain the observed shared speech difficulties.

Expressive language concerns also appear across caregiver reports, language samples, and classroom activities. Receptive skills are stronger in familiar contexts. Additional Spanish assessment and repeated natural samples will help separate limited task familiarity from persistent language difficulty.

Working diagnostic codes are F80.0 for phonological disorder and provisional F80.1 for expressive language disorder. The second code remains subject to further bilingual evidence. Strengths include social engagement, gesture use, family participation, and improvement with supported teaching.

Recomendaciones / Recommendations

1. Begin bilingual treatment using the proposed schedule. Address functional speech clarity and sentence formulation through familiar play and routines. Use Cycles principles selectively for recurring sound patterns, with targets appropriate to each language.

2. Teach initial /k/ in meaningful words and short phrases. Establish baseline accuracy before setting the next criterion. A preliminary objective is 8/10 accurate productions with min cues, across repeated sessions.

3. Support descriptions of actions and recent events. Aim for complete messages in 4 of 5 structured opportunities with mod cues, then reduce assistance as independence improves.

4. Provide caregiver coaching informed by Hanen strategies. Follow the child’s interest, pause for a response, and expand the message naturally. Families may respond in the language that feels most comfortable.

5. Use classroom visuals, advance previews, and extra response time. Invite clarification without requiring repeated public correction. Practice repair phrases such as "otra vez", "quiero decir", and "let me show you".

6. Review progress on January 14, 2027. Compare spontaneous communication, caregiver priorities, and classroom access. Repeat formal testing only when clinically justified.

Documentación y cierre / Documentation and follow-up

Evaluation billing: CPT 92523 with modifier GN. Proposed treatment billing: CPT 92507 with modifier GN. Attendance and authorization limits require separate administrative verification.

The clinician reviewed findings with both parents in Spanish and English. The family requested examples they can use during meals and reading. They agreed that clearer everyday messages matter more than practicing isolated words alone.

Signed: Marisol Vega, MS, CCC-SLP  
Juniper Lantern Pediatric Communication  
Report completed: October 9, 2026

Evaluating clinician	Elena Marisol Duarte	919-555-0163; eduarte@puenteclaro.example
Practice website	Puente Claro Pediatric Communication Services	https://puenteclaro.example

REASON FOR REFERRAL / MOTIVO DE CONSULTA

Mateo Andrés Valverde was referred for a bilingual evaluation because his family and preschool staff report difficulty understanding directions, combining words, and repairing communication breakdowns. His mother stated, “Él sabe lo que quiere, pero nosotros tenemos que adivinar.” His father described frustration when familiar adults cannot determine whether he wants help, a different activity, or another serving of food.

The evaluation addressed whether the observed concerns reflect differences associated with bilingual development, a language disorder, a speech sound concern, or a combination of factors. The family requested practical strategies for both languages. They also wanted recommendations that fit everyday routines, porque en casa las conversaciones cambian entre español e inglés without a fixed schedule.

The referral came from Piedra Azul Health Pediatric Clinic, Vallebrisa Campus, where Dr. Nadia Salcedo documented communication concerns at a developmental follow-up. Preschool information came from Little Orchard Learning House. The classroom is commonly called Ms. Lopez's room. The teacher reported that visual demonstrations help substantially, but spoken group directions remain difficult.

This report integrates caregiver history, record review, structured assessment, play observations, and language samples. Findings describe performance under the conditions documented below. The recommendations consider participation at home and preschool, family priorities, and the child's access to both languages.

BACKGROUND / ANTECEDENTES

Mateo lives with his mother, Lucía Valverde, his father, Andrés Valverde, and his older sister, Sol Valverde, in Vallebrisa, Larkfern County, North Carolina. The family provided the mailing address 72 Meadow Lantern Lane, Vallebrisa, North Carolina 27903. His sister is 6;8 and often joins pretend play after school.

His maternal aunt, Paz Navarro, provides afternoon care when both parents work. His grandmother, Rosa Navarro, visits regularly and participates in meals and bedtime stories. The family dog, Nube, is a frequent topic during play. These familiar partners generally understand gestures and routines, although they still report difficulty understanding unfamiliar messages.

His mother works at Larkfern Packaging Cooperative, and his father works at Meadow Lantern Bicycle Works. The parents described variable work schedules and requested a service plan with predictable appointments. They can participate in caregiver coaching and prefer written summaries in Spanish with clear English terms for information shared with preschool staff.

Early intervention records identify the former office as Oficina de la Agencia de Servicios para el Desarrollo Infantil de Vallebrisa y el Condado de Larkfern, abbreviated CDSA de Vallebrisa. The former service coordinator was Marina Castañeda. Her employing agency appears as Agencia Comunitaria de Coordinación de Servicios y Apoyo a las Familias del Condado de Larkfern, abbreviated Apoyo Familiar Larkfern.

The available IFSP was dated May 16, 2025. Its communication outcome, IFSP Outcome 2, addressed requesting help during family routines. The transition record dated July 18, 2025 documented referral information for preschool services. These historical records support continuity of care; they do not establish current eligibility or authorization.

HISTORIA DEL NACIMIENTO Y DESARROLLO

The pregnancy history was provided by the mother and supplemented by a discharge summary. The family reported monitoring for maternal hypertension near delivery. Birth occurred at Piedra Azul Health Women and Children’s Hospital, Río Claro Campus in Río Claro, North Carolina. Gestational age was 36 weeks, 2 days, and birth weight was 2,480 g.

The recorded Apgar scores were 7 at the initial assessment and 9 at the later assessment. The infant received care in Piedra Azul Health Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, Río Claro Campus for feeding support and temperature monitoring. The discharge date was August 2, 2022. The available summary did not describe prolonged respiratory support.

His mother recalled that feeding initially required pacing and frequent pauses. The family reported no current coughing, choking, or persistent difficulty with ordinary food textures. Selective eating occurs, especially with mixed textures, but the child accepts familiar foods from several groups. Feeding concerns were discussed as background information and were not formally assessed during this language evaluation.

Reported developmental milestones included independent walking at approximately 15 months, recognizable first words near 20 months, and occasional word combinations around 31 months. The parents emphasized that these estimates are approximate. They recalled steady progress without a clear loss of previously established communication skills.

Early communication relied heavily on pointing, bringing objects to adults, and pulling a caregiver toward a desired activity. His father said, “Primero nos llevaba de la mano; ahora intenta decirlo, pero se queda corto.” Currently, gestures remain useful, especially when the message is unfamiliar or when the listener does not share the immediate context.

MEDICAL AND HEARING HISTORY / SALUD Y AUDICIÓN

The pediatric history includes recurrent middle-ear concerns during toddlerhood and seasonal nasal congestion. The family reported no seizures, major head injury, or known neurological diagnosis. No daily medication was reported at the evaluation. Sleep varies with congestion, and the parents notice less patience during communication tasks after disrupted nights.

An audiology visit occurred on August 19, 2026 at Piedra Azul Health Audiology and ENT, Cedarlight Campus. Audiologist Camila Brenner documented behavioral responses considered adequate for access to conversational speech under the test conditions. The record recommended continued monitoring because of the middle-ear history. This evaluation did not independently establish hearing status.

ENT physician Dr. Owen Serrano reviewed the child on August 26, 2026. The available note recommended follow-up if ear symptoms or listening concerns returned. During this session, responses to his name and environmental sounds were observed. Inconsistent responses to longer directions occurred even when he appeared attentive and could hear the speaker.

The oral mechanism screening showed facial symmetry at rest and functional movement during speech and play. The child tolerated a brief visual inspection but declined sustained imitation tasks. Findings support continued observation during therapy. The screening was insufficient for conclusions about subtle motor differences, and no swallowing assessment was completed.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY / IDIOMAS DE LA FAMILIA

Spanish is the primary language used by the mother, grandmother, and aunt. The father uses both languages, with English more common during errands and some play routines. The sister usually speaks English during pretend play and Spanish during meals. Family members described code-switching as natural and frequent, especially when discussing preschool experiences.

Caregiver estimates suggest approximately 65% Spanish and 35% English exposure across a typical week. These estimates describe opportunity, not proficiency. Preschool instruction occurs mainly in English, with Spanish greetings, songs, and individual support. The family reported that the child hears different vocabulary in each setting rather than equivalent input for every topic.

His mother stated, “No queremos quitarle el español; queremos que pueda hablar con su abuela.” The clinician supported continued use of the languages that caregivers speak comfortably. Adults should provide clear, meaningful models in their strongest language. The family does not need to translate every sentence or restrict conversation to a single language.

Reported family history includes a paternal uncle, Will Valverde, who received childhood speech therapy. The family could not provide his diagnosis or treatment records. No additional family history was established. This report treats that information as caregiver report and does not use it to determine the child's diagnosis.

Across interviews, the parents described communication difficulty in both languages. Familiar Spanish vocabulary was stronger for food and household routines. Familiar English vocabulary was stronger for classroom materials and vehicle play. Limited grammatical combinations and difficulty understanding relationships appeared across languages, which warrants evaluation beyond English vocabulary alone.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES / PROCEDIMIENTOS

The clinician administered Preschool Language Scales–Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) using its bilingual administration framework. Responses were considered across Spanish and English according to the instrument's procedures. Additional tasks included caregiver interviews, an oral mechanism screening, connected speech sampling, play-based probes, and Dynamic Assessment of selected language skills.

The assessment used familiar toys, pictures, books, and everyday objects. The clinician alternated languages according to the task and the child's responses. Brief movement breaks supported participation. The mother remained available for reassurance and history clarification. No separate interpreter participated because the evaluating clinician conducted the assessment directly in Spanish and English.

Attention was strongest during vehicle play and snack-related pretend routines. Participation decreased during repetitive picture tasks. The clinician used encouragement and breaks while preserving standardized conditions for scored items. Teaching trials occurred after standardized administration and were documented separately. Responses following instruction were not added to standardized scores.

The child initially stayed close to his mother, then approached the clinician and shared materials. He accepted changes in toys when adults explained the transition with gestures. Fatigue became apparent near the end of the session. Findings are considered a useful sample of current functioning, with performance variability related to attention, task familiarity, and language context.

RESULTADOS: STANDARDIZED LANGUAGE TESTING

The following results come from PLS-5 Spanish. Confidence intervals reflect the 90% level. Age equivalents are descriptive estimates and should not be interpreted as the child's overall developmental age.

Measure	Standard score	Percentile	Confidence interval	Age equivalent
Auditory Comprehension	76	5	71–84	2;10
Expressive Communication	73	4	68–82	2;8
Total Language Score	73	4	69–81	2;9

Performance showed strengths in familiar object identification, functional play, and recognizing common actions with contextual support. The child understood many routine requests when the object was visible. Difficulty increased when directions required interpreting spatial relationships, tracking several details, or responding without gestures and shared situational cues.

Expressive performance showed a functional vocabulary distributed across both languages. The child named familiar objects and used words to request, reject, and comment. Longer combinations were less consistent. Grammatical markers, descriptive detail, and explanations were limited in both languages, although the exact forms differed because Spanish and English have different grammatical systems.

The scores support concern when considered with caregiver reports and observed functioning. They do not explain the full bilingual profile by themselves. The diagnostic interpretation relies on converging evidence across languages, natural communication, learning trials, and participation demands. English-only performance was not used as the sole basis for identifying impairment.

FUNCTIONAL LANGUAGE PROBES / LENGUAJE FUNCIONAL

Probe	Observed performance	Support
Familiar object identification	8/10; 80%	min cues
Directions containing spatial relationships	4/10; 40%	mod cues
Novel word combinations during play	3 of 5 opportunities; 60%	mod cues
Communication repair after a misunderstanding	2/5; 40%	max cues
Action descriptions after teaching	7/10; 70%	mod cues

These probes were informal and were not norm-referenced. The child benefited from demonstrations, slowed presentation, and repetition within meaningful play. For spatial directions, he often selected the correct object but placed it incorrectly. This pattern suggests that understanding the relationship was harder than recognizing the object label.

During Dynamic Assessment, the clinician taught action descriptions through demonstration and recasting. The child began to combine an actor and action more consistently after repeated models. He needed continued support when the materials changed. His responsiveness supports a treatment approach that teaches within routines and checks whether learning transfers to new situations.

LANGUAGE SAMPLE / MUESTRA DE LENGUAJE

A play sample included Spanish, English, and mixed utterances. Productions included “más agua,” “car go,” “quiero blue,” and “no cabe.” These forms served clear purposes in context. The mixed utterances were accepted as meaningful bilingual communication. Code-switching itself was not counted as an error.

When a vehicle disappeared behind a box, the child said “where car” and pointed. When the clinician misunderstood a request, he repeated “ese” with greater volume but provided no additional description. During family play, he called “Sol ven.” While discussing the dog, he said “Nube run.” Names in those productions identify familiar communication partners.

The sample showed frequent omission of information needed by an unfamiliar listener. The clinician modeled “the car is under the box” and “el carro está debajo de la caja.” The child repeated shorter portions and then attempted related combinations during play. Repetition was documented separately from spontaneous language.

Selected utterances were reviewed using Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions. The code [EW] identified an extraneous word in a clearly interpretable English utterance. Mixed-language words were retained in the transcript. Spanish grammatical patterns were examined in Spanish context, and English grammatical patterns were examined in English context.

Speech was easier to understand when listeners knew the activity and could see his gestures. Short messages often communicated immediate wants effectively. Messages about absent objects or earlier events required substantial caregiver interpretation. The mother reported the same pattern at home: “Si yo vi lo que pasó, entiendo; si no, me cuesta.”

SPEECH SOUND OBSERVATIONS / SONIDOS DEL HABLA

The speech sample included a range of consonants and vowels across both languages. Fronting of /k/ to [t] occurred in some words, and /g/ was also inconsistent. The Spanish tap /ɾ/ varied across contexts. These observations require a larger sample before determining the extent of any separate speech sound disorder.

Target words included “casa,” “gato,” “car,” and “go.” The child produced “tasa” for “casa” during one naming opportunity. A model plus mod cues improved placement in an isolated attempt. The clinician did not interpret a single corrected response as established mastery.

Caregiver estimates placed intelligibility near 75% for familiar listeners and 50% for unfamiliar listeners during ordinary conversation. These are reported estimates, not measured scores. Speech clarity, short utterances, and missing context all contributed to misunderstandings. No standardized articulation score was obtained, and voice and fluency concerns were not prominent during observation.

SOCIAL COMMUNICATION AND PRESCHOOL PARTICIPATION

The child shared enjoyment, initiated interaction, and used coordinated pointing during preferred activities. He brought toys to adults and checked their reactions. He participated in simple reciprocal play when the language demand was manageable. These strengths provide useful starting points for treatment and should remain central to intervention planning.

Ms. Lopez reported that he seeks interaction with classmates Emilia Torres and Benji Cole. He follows their play themes but has difficulty negotiating roles. Classroom assistant Tessa Molina described successful participation when an adult models a short phrase and then gives him time to respond.

During small-group activities, classmate Nico Ferrer sometimes answers before he can formulate a response. Staff plan to provide wait time and visual choices. The classroom observations reported by staff were not directly verified through an onsite visit. A preschool observation would help determine how communication changes during group instruction and peer conflict.

IMPRESSIONS / IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

The combined findings support mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, coded F80.2. Difficulties affect understanding relationships in spoken messages, creating flexible word combinations, and adding information when communication breaks down. These concerns appear across Spanish and English and exceed differences explained by vocabulary exposure alone.

The child also shows speech sound patterns that reduce clarity. A separate speech sound diagnosis is deferred pending a broader bilingual sample and monitoring during treatment. Hearing history remains relevant because fluctuating access could affect listening. The current report does not establish a hearing disorder or attribute the language findings to hearing alone.

Strengths include social interest, meaningful gestures, functional vocabulary, family engagement, and learning with contextual teaching. Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable with consistent support, although the rate cannot be predicted from this session. Progress should be measured through communication across partners and settings, alongside structured treatment data.

RECOMMENDATIONS / RECOMENDACIONES

Begin bilingual speech-language treatment under 92507 with modifier GN, subject to coverage requirements. Initial treatment should combine direct interaction with caregiver coaching. Use Enhanced Milieu Teaching, Focused Stimulation, and principles from Hanen to increase meaningful practice during routines. Select strategies according to response and family preference.

Continue Spanish at home and provide English opportunities through preschool and community activities. Adults should use comfortable, natural language. Follow the child's focus, model a slightly longer message, and pause. For example, expand “agua” to “quiero agua” or “más agua fría” without requiring repeated correction before honoring the request.

Teach understanding of relationships through movement and objects before relying on picture worksheets. Practice “under,” “behind,” “debajo,” and “detrás” within play. Use mod cues initially, then reduce support as performance improves. Check the same concept with different materials and both familiar and unfamiliar partners.

Use shared books with Dialogic Reading strategies. Adults can comment, offer choices, and invite short descriptions. Questions should support participation rather than become a rapid test. Accept a gesture or mixed-language response, then provide a clear spoken model. Coordinate selected classroom vocabulary with home activities when the family finds that useful.

Proposed goals are listed below. These are treatment planning goals and do not amend the historical IFSP.

Goal	Functional target	Initial criterion
1	Follow directions containing a spatial relationship during play	8/10 opportunities with min cues
2	Combine words to request, comment, or describe an action	80% of sampled opportunities with mod cues
3	Add a word, gesture, or visual choice to repair a misunderstanding	4 of 5 opportunities with min cues
4	Produce selected familiar words with clearer consonant placement	70% accuracy with mod cues

Reassess speech targets after obtaining a broader sample. Begin with meaningful words that affect daily communication. If patterns remain consistent, consider a structured phonological approach such as Cycles. The current findings do not establish a need for PROMPT or a motor speech diagnosis.

SERVICE SCHEDULE / HORARIO PROPUESTO

Service	Frequency	Proposed appointment	Location or delivery
Bilingual individual speech-language therapy	Weekly	Tuesday, 4:15 p.m.–5:00 p.m.	Puente Claro Pediatric Communication Services
Caregiver coaching	Within each treatment visit	Final portion of the appointment	In person with written carryover notes
Preschool consultation	Monthly	Thursday, 12:10 p.m.–12:30 p.m.	With consent through Little Orchard Learning House
Initial progress review	After the introductory treatment block	December 17, 2026, 4:15 p.m.	Family and clinician review

Appointments are proposed and have not been confirmed. The clinician will document attendance, language used, cueing, independent responses, and carryover. Review should consider whether gains appear outside practiced activities. If participation or hearing concerns change, coordinate with the pediatrician and audiology practice.

The family identified requesting help and sharing preschool experiences as immediate priorities. The clinician will provide brief Spanish summaries and classroom suggestions in English. Release of information requires caregiver consent. No preschool contact or additional referral was completed during this evaluation.

Signed electronically on September 30, 2026

Elena Marisol Duarte, MS, CCC-SLP
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist
Puente Claro Pediatric Communication Services
Provider record: SLP-NC-604821
