Buenas tardes, señora Salcedo:

Below is the completed report, followed by the earlier scheduling messages. The family requested one email that includes the results, the home plan, and the questions discussed during the visit. Please share this copy with the classroom team through the agreed family communication process. The Spanish comments preserve the family’s wording where possible. All scores describe performance during this evaluation; the observations also include the child’s communication across people, languages, and routines.

EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE / SPEECH-LANGUAGE ASSESSMENT

Client: Nicolás Salcedo
Family nickname: Nico
Date of birth: May 14, 2023
Evaluation date: September 14, 2026
Chronological age: 3;4
Report date: September 22, 2026
Parent and legal guardian: Lucía Salcedo
Other parent: Andrés Beltrán
Home address: 418 Willow Lantern Lane, Brisaclara, North Carolina 27864
Family telephone: (252) 555-0147
Medical record: PV-260914-083
Medicaid member number: 583741926Q
Service authorization: SLP-26-48173
Evaluation location: Puentes de Voz Pediatric Therapy
Clinician: Elena Marisol Vega, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist
Interpreter: Inés Duarte
Service coordinator: Teresa Montalvo
Referring pediatrician: Dr. Samuel Rivas
Current childcare: Jardín de las Luciérnagas

MOTIVO DE REFERENCIA / FAMILY PRIORITIES

The family requested an evaluation because Nicolás uses short messages, becomes upset when listeners misunderstand him, and needs help following classroom directions. His mother stated, “Yo sé lo que quiere cuando estamos en casa, pero afuera necesita que yo traduzca lo que está tratando de decir.” His father’s main concern was helping him explain a problem before he cries or leaves the activity.

The family wants useful communication in Spanish and English. Their priorities are requesting help, joining play, and telling an adult when something hurts or feels difficult. They did not request that either language be removed. This evaluation therefore considered the child’s combined language resources, including gestures, words, shared context, and responses across both languages.

ANTECEDENTES / BACKGROUND

Nico lives with his mother and older sister, Valeria Salcedo. His father visits regularly and participates in evening routines when work permits. His maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, provides care on several afternoons. A neighbor, Mr. Tom, sometimes drives the family to appointments. He does not provide therapy or participate in assessment decisions.

The child attends Jardín de las Luciérnagas on weekdays. Miss Ana leads the morning classroom, and la maestra Carmen supports outdoor play and afternoon transitions. Staff describe him as curious, affectionate, and more comfortable beside another child than in a large group. He often watches before joining. Once familiar with an activity, he brings materials to peers and smiles to invite repetition.

The classroom report described frequent play with Emilia Torres and Julián Ponce. During pretend cooking, he reportedly offers plates and copies familiar actions. During noisy transitions, he may hold an adult’s sleeve instead of speaking. The teachers asked for a consistent way to acknowledge his gestures while helping him add a useful spoken message.

HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO Y SALUD

His mother reported delivery at 38 weeks, 2 days gestation at Hospital Infantil de Arroyo Claro. Birth weight was 6 lb 11 oz. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The family described an uncomplicated newborn stay. These details came from parent report; the birth discharge record was not available for review.

The pediatric referral listed recurrent middle-ear fluid and an expressive communication concern. Dr. Rivas documented a recent ear examination on August 28, 2026. The family reported no current medication and no known food allergy. An audiology appointment remains pending. No formal hearing result was supplied, so responses to speech during this visit cannot establish hearing status.

Occupational therapist Maya Cordero currently supports participation in dressing, utensil use, and transitions. Physical therapist Daniel Figueroa previously evaluated balance and playground access. His mother reported that he walks and runs independently but sometimes avoids climbing when other children move quickly nearby.

Feeding information was limited to interview. The family reported a narrow range of preferred textures, with no reported coughing during meals. A feeding assessment was outside this evaluation’s scope. The clinician asked the family to discuss any new swallowing concern with the pediatrician and the treating occupational therapist.

FAMILIA, IDIOMAS Y RUTINAS

Spanish is the main language between Lucía and the child. English occurs at childcare, during some sibling play, and in familiar songs. Andrés uses both languages. The family described language choice as natural and dependent on the person and activity. They do not use a fixed language schedule.

His sister, Valeria, is 7 years old. She often speaks English during games, then switches to Spanish when her brother appears confused. His aunt, Maribel Salcedo, reads picture books in Spanish during weekend visits. The family dog, Canela, is a frequent topic of conversation. The child said, “Canela ven,” while pointing toward a photograph; the name-containing production is preserved without a clinical-token span.

The mother works two jobs: an early shift at RLS and evening shifts at Mercado Luz de Patio. She stated, “No puedo agregar otra tarea larga; necesito algo que podamos hacer mientras comemos o nos ponemos los zapatos.” The recommended practice therefore uses existing routines and brief repetitions.

Doña Lupe reported that the child talks most while helping sort laundry. She said, “Cuando le doy tiempo, él me explica con sus manos y con palabritas.” The clinician encouraged all caregivers to notice those messages first. An immediate demand to repeat can interrupt the exchange, especially when the child is already frustrated.

The family’s care coordination involves Oficina de la Agencia de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil de Brisaclara, referred to locally as CDSA Brisaclara. The service coordinator works through Red Comunitaria de Coordinación de Servicios para Familias de Arroyo Claro, abbreviated RCCSFA. The coordinator is helping the family clarify transition records and current preschool service options.

PROCEDIMIENTOS / HOW INFORMATION WAS COLLECTED

The visit began at 9:10 AM and ended at 10:35 AM. The mother remained present. The bilingual clinician conducted the assessment in Spanish and English. Inés Duarte supported the family interview, clarified regional vocabulary, and helped confirm caregiver meanings. She did not independently administer or score standardized items.

Procedures included record review, caregiver interview, play observation, an oral mechanism screening, a speech sample, and Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish). Standardized items followed the instrument’s administration rules. Additional teaching trials occurred afterward and were recorded separately. The child’s performance during those trials did not change the standardized scores.

During play, the clinician offered familiar objects, paused for initiation, and followed the child’s interests. Instructions were presented without extra gestures when assessing independent understanding. Later trials added pointing, demonstration, or simplified wording to examine responsiveness to support. The clinician distinguished understanding the message from simply following another person’s action.

Attention varied with activity. The child remained engaged with pretend food and toy vehicles but moved away from lengthy picture tasks. A short movement break improved participation. He sometimes responded after a delay, so the clinician allowed additional processing time before repeating a direction. His mother confirmed that this pattern also occurs at home.

RESULTADOS / SCORE SUMMARY

| Measure or subtest | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | 31 | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-85 | 2;7 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | 29 | 76 | 5th percentile | 71-83 | 2;5 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Total Language | 154, summed standard scores | 75 | 5th percentile | 70-82 | 2;6 |

Confidence intervals above use the 90% level. Age equivalents are descriptive test values and do not represent the child’s overall developmental age. The family should interpret the table together with the language history, functional observations, and limitations described below.

COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

On Auditory Comprehension, the child identified familiar objects and understood several routine action words. He followed simple directions most consistently when the object was visible and the activity was familiar. He had more difficulty with directions that combined an action and a location or required choosing between similar pictures.

In an informal probe, he followed 8/10 familiar single-step directions independently. He followed 3 of 5 related two-step directions with mod cues. When the clinician reduced the wording and demonstrated the sequence, performance improved to 4 of 5. These informal results describe supported participation and are separate from standardized scoring.

The child sometimes looked toward his mother before answering. That behavior appeared to seek reassurance rather than provide clear evidence of misunderstanding. Cuando la actividad era conocida, he responded with less hesitation. Novel picture scenes required more time and occasionally led to guessing.

EXPRESIÓN / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

On Expressive Communication, the child used words, gestures, and short combinations to request, label, protest, and comment. His spontaneous messages included "más agua", "my truck", "no cabe", and "mami, help". Code-switching occurred within meaningful exchanges and was not treated as an error by itself.

He named familiar objects more readily than he explained events. When a toy fell behind a chair, he pointed and said "allá". After a model, he produced "cayó atrás". He used "open", "abre", and "abre box" in different turns, depending on the adult and the immediate model.

The language sample showed emerging combinations but limited detail about who did what. The child often omitted a word when excited. One production, "yo carro", received the sample code [EW] because an expected word was absent in that context. The sample was too brief for a reliable comparison with a language-sample reference database.

HABLA / SPEECH PRODUCTION

Speech was easier to understand when the listener knew the activity. In a structured set of familiar requests, the clinician understood 70% of attempts without caregiver clarification. That estimate reflects this sample only. It does not describe every setting or listener.

Observed patterns included replacement of /k/ with /t/, written here as /k/ becoming /t/, and an occasional [w] production in place of an English liquid. Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent. These observations were considered within the child’s bilingual sound systems and the limited sample. No conclusion rested on a single sound difference.

For the target "casa", the child produced "tasa". For "spoon", he produced "poon". For "agua", he produced "awa". He improved the initial consonant in "casa" with max cues, then maintained it briefly with mod cues. Independent carryover was not established.

The oral mechanism screening showed functional movement for the sampled speech tasks. The child did not complete every imitation request. Voice and fluency did not raise a concern during the visit, although the sample was limited. The clinician will continue monitoring speech as the child produces longer and more varied messages.

JUEGO, PARTICIPACIÓN Y APRENDIZAJE

The child shared enjoyment, checked an adult’s face, and brought objects to request assistance. He used pretend actions with a doll and accepted an adult’s expansion of the play sequence. When the clinician paused before operating a toy, he looked up and initiated a request.

He sustained a brief turn-taking routine with min cues. He needed mod cues to repair a misunderstood message. The most useful repair support was a choice between showing the object and trying another word. Repeated requests to say the same unclear word increased frustration.

The child responded well to a predictable sequence: observe, offer a short model, wait, and acknowledge any meaningful attempt. During teaching trials, he used a new action word in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. He later used that word once without a direct model. This responsiveness supports a treatment plan that includes caregiver coaching and repeated practice within meaningful activities.

IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

The evaluation supports a mixed receptive-expressive language concern affecting functional participation in both languages. Difficulties included understanding longer directions, combining words to explain events, and repairing communication breakdowns. The pattern extends beyond the expected use of two languages because similar needs appeared in familiar Spanish routines and in English-supported activities.

Speech sound differences also reduced clarity. Some observations may reflect developmental patterns or differences between Spanish and English. Other patterns require a larger connected-speech sample and monitoring across treatment. The clinician therefore recommends continued speech assessment rather than assigning every observed difference to a single cause.

The working language diagnosis is ICD-10 F80.2. Speech sound findings will be monitored under ICD-10 F80.0 pending fuller assessment. Evaluation billing is CPT 92523 with modifier GN. These codes accompany this fictional clinical record and do not replace the descriptive findings.

The child’s strengths include social interest, useful gestures, pretend play, responsiveness to teaching, and caregivers who recognize his communication attempts. His needs are most visible when directions become longer, the listener lacks context, or frustration limits his available words. Intervention should build from those strengths.

RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN EN CASA Y EN EL SALÓN

1. Begin speech-language intervention focused on functional understanding, useful word combinations, communication repair, and speech clarity. A proposed schedule is a weekly visit with caregiver participation. Confirm the final schedule with the family and coordinator.

2. Keep Spanish and English available. Each caregiver should use the language that allows warm, natural interaction. Model a short phrase in the language of the current exchange. Accept a meaningful response in either language.

3. Use caregiver coaching informed by Hanen principles. During dressing, snacks, and play, follow the child’s focus, model one useful message, and pause. Practice should fit existing routines rather than create a separate homework period.

4. Coordinate with the classroom staff. Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen can pair spoken directions with a simple visual sequence, then reduce support as the child becomes familiar with the routine. Document whether he responds independently or after assistance.

5. Offer communication repair choices. An adult can say, “Show me or tell me another way.” If the child points, acknowledge the message before adding a spoken model. Avoid requiring repeated attempts while he is crying or pulling away.

6. Trial speech activities using Cycles only after gathering a fuller sound sample and choosing patterns that affect intelligibility across languages. PROMPT is not part of the current plan. PECS is not prescribed at this stage; simple visual choices may still support participation.

7. Complete the pending hearing evaluation. The family and Dr. Samuel Rivas should review the result before attributing inconsistent listening entirely to language difficulty. Share relevant findings with the therapy team.

8. Coordinate with Maya Corderdo on transitions and regulation supports. Consult Daniel Figueroa if playground access continues to limit peer participation. Keep communication practice embedded in activities the child can comfortably join.

PROPUESTAS DE METAS / COORDINATION NOTES

For transition planning, proposed IFSP outcome 1 addresses communicating needs during family routines. Proposed IFSP outcome 2 addresses understanding and participating in shared activities. These are draft outcome references for coordinator review; they are not presented as an active signed plan.

A proposed communication goal is using a meaningful combination or an effective repair strategy in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. A proposed comprehension goal is following a familiar related sequence in 80% of opportunities with min cues. Record the language used and the support provided.

Review progress on December 15, 2026. The review should include caregiver examples, classroom observations, and repeated functional probes. Use the family’s priorities to decide whether the plan improves daily communication.

Thank you for sharing the routines that matter most to your family. Con tiempo, modelos claros, y oportunidades reales, the treatment team can help the child communicate more successfully during everyday activities.

BACKGROUND / ANTECEDENTES

Nico attends Little Learners Daycare on weekdays. His classroom teacher, Ms. Celia Robles, described him as affectionate, observant, and eager to participate in songs with gestures. The parents requested coordination so that adults use similar communication supports across settings.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY / NACIMIENTO Y SALUD

[X] Late preterm  [ ] Full term  [ ] Birth history unavailable
[X] Hearing screening completed  [ ] Current hearing concerns

The parent reported delivery at 36 weeks, 2 days of gestation at Willow Harbor Birth Hospital. Birth weight was 5 pounds, 8 ounces. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The child stayed in the newborn unit for feeding observation and temperature support. The parent did not report prolonged ventilation, seizures, or a diagnosed neurological condition.

Early feeding involved breast milk and formula. The family described a slow transition to textured foods. At approximately 18 months, he accepted soft foods more readily than mixed textures. He currently eats several familiar foods and drinks from an open cup with occasional spills. The parent denied current choking, persistent coughing during meals, or unexplained weight loss.

Dr. Amalia Varela follows routine pediatric care. Occupational therapist Lucinda Reyes addresses dressing, sensory regulation, and mealtime participation. Physical therapist Evan Soltero previously supported balance and stair use. The parent reported that physical therapy ended after functional goals were met.

A hearing screening at Cedarmist Children’s Hospital on May 12, 2026 documented a pass in both ears. The available report did not include a complete diagnostic audiology assessment. The family reported occasional ear infections during toddlerhood, with no current ear pain. No daily prescription medication was reported.

Sleep varies with the family’s work schedule. Bedtime usually begins near 8:30 p.m.. The parent reported that tiredness can reduce patience during communication breakdowns. No developmental regression was reported. Medical information in this section reflects the supplied fictional records and caregiver history; it was not independently examined during this visit.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY / FAMILIA E IDIOMAS

[X] Spanish at home  [X] English at daycare  [X] Mixed language routines

Nicolás lives with both parents and his sister, Alma Elenares, age 7 years. His maternal grandmother, Beatriz Lujano, provides care several afternoons each week. A family babysitter, Teresa Valdés, helps when the parents’ shifts overlap. The family’s dog, Chispa, often joins floor play.

Mom works nights at Moonbridge Packaging Works as a packaging line technician. Her shift begins at 10:00 p.m.. Dad works at Cedar Lantern Grocery as a stock clerk. His shift usually ends at 3:30 p.m.. These schedules affect which caregiver attends appointments and practices home activities.

Spanish has been present since birth. Regular English exposure increased when daycare began at 22 months. The mother estimated current weekly exposure at approximately 60% Spanish and 40% English. These estimates describe opportunities to hear language, not measured proficiency. Both parents use Spanish for comfort, family stories, and most home directions.

His sister frequently switches languages during play. The grandmother primarily uses Spanish. The babysitter uses Spanish with some English activity words. The family attends Iglesia Camino de Luz, where pastor Esteban Loria leads family gatherings. They also visit Cedarmist Family Reading Circle, a library program coordinated by Mina Carrow.

The mother stated, “No queremos quitarle el español. Queremos que pueda contar lo que necesita en los dos idiomas.” The clinician supported continued use of the family’s languages. Code-switching was treated as part of bilingual communication. Concern centered on limited message length, comprehension, and speech clarity across languages, rather than language mixing itself.

BEHAVIOR AND PARTICIPATION / OBSERVACIONES

[X] Alert  [X] Socially engaged  [X] Needed movement breaks
[ ] Persistent refusal  [ ] Evaluation stopped early

Nico entered holding his mother’s hand, then approached the toy shelf after a brief demonstration. He shared smiles, brought objects to adults, and checked their reactions during a pretend surprise. He accepted the interpreter’s presence but directed most communication toward his mother and the clinician.

Interpreter Rafael Mendieta supported the caregiver interview and clarified regional vocabulary. The bilingual clinician conducted language testing directly. The interpreter did not translate standardized test items during scored administration. This distinction matters because item translation can change what a standardized score represents.

During play, the child used pointing, giving, facial expression, and short spoken phrases. Examples included “mira carro”, “I want más”, and “no cabe”. When the dog appeared in a family photograph, he said, “Chispa come acá.” The name-containing utterance was recorded as a functional communication example.

He maintained a shared activity most successfully when the adult followed his interest and used brief turns. With unfamiliar materials, he sometimes repeated the last word of a question. Repetition did not consistently show comprehension. The clinician checked understanding through actions, choices, and changes in the task.

Transitions improved with a visual cue and a short warning. He moved from blocks to picture activities with min cues. Ending a preferred vehicle activity required mod cues. A snack and movement break restored participation. No single behavior prevented completion, although fatigue likely reduced performance near the end.

The oral mechanism screen showed facial symmetry and functional lip closure during the observed tasks. Tongue movement was visible during imitation and eating. This brief screen did not identify an obvious structural concern. Voice quality and resonance were unremarkable in the sample. No consistent stuttering-like behavior was observed.

ASSESSMENT METHODS / MÉTODOS

The clinician administered Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish using its bilingual procedures. The report refers to this measure as PLS-5 Spanish. The child’s chronological age was 4;2. Scores describe performance during this session and require interpretation alongside exposure, functional observations, and caregiver information.

The clinician also administered Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition, abbreviated GFTA-3, for descriptive English speech sampling. Its normative comparison was not used to establish a bilingual speech diagnosis. Spanish word probes, connected speech, and response to teaching supplied additional evidence.

Earlier records contained Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition results and observations organized with Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale. Those records were completed when the child was 26 months. They provide historical context and do not represent current testing.

Selected items from Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition supported an informal vocabulary discussion. Because administration included teaching and Spanish follow-up, no standard score or percentile was calculated. The task helped identify useful teaching targets rather than rank vocabulary against a normative group.

RESULTADOS / SCORE SUMMARY

| Measure or subtest | Score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 82 | 12th percentile | 76–90 | 3;3 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | Standard score 74 | 4th percentile | 68–83 | 2;10 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Total Language | Standard score 77 | 6th percentile | 71–85 | 3;0 |
| Historical Bayley-4 Language | Composite score 79 | 8th percentile | 73–87 | Not reported |
| Historical Bayley-4 Receptive Communication | Scaled score 6 | Not reported | Not reported | 20 months |
| Historical Bayley-4 Expressive Communication | Scaled score 7 | Not reported | Not reported | 21 months |
| Historical Rossetti Language Comprehension | Descriptive skills only | Not applicable | Not applicable | Skills within 18–24 months |
| Historical Rossetti Language Expression | Descriptive skills only | Not applicable | Not applicable | Skills within 15–21 months |
| GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words | Raw score 46 | Not interpreted | Not interpreted | Not interpreted |
| Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition | Nonstandard administration | Not calculated | Not calculated | Not calculated |

Confidence intervals above are reported at the 90% level. Age equivalents are descriptive test outputs. They do not mean that the child functions like a younger child in every area. Historical scores were transcribed from the supplied records and should not be compared directly with current scores as a measure of treatment gain.

RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE / COMPRENSIÓN

Nicolás identified familiar objects and actions more consistently than relational concepts. He followed routine directions such as “put it in” and “dame el carro” when materials were visible. Accuracy decreased when directions included several details or required remembering information without visual support.

He completed 8/10 familiar single-step directions independently. For directions involving location and an object attribute, he completed 3 of 5 with mod cues. He identified basic actions in 7/10 picture trials. Responses to questions about an unfamiliar story were less consistent.

Understanding improved after the clinician modeled the task and reduced sentence length. He responded to “¿Dónde está?” more reliably than questions requiring an explanation. Difficulty appeared in both languages, although vocabulary familiarity affected individual items. The pattern supports a language concern beyond English exposure alone.

EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE / EXPRESIÓN

The sample contained spontaneous requests, protests, labels, and brief comments. Longer messages usually followed an adult model. Examples included “car go fast”, “se cayó aquí”, and “más bubbles please”. Spanish and English words sometimes appeared in the same sentence without disrupting the message.

He requested an action in 6/10 natural opportunities independently and in 9/10 with min cues. He rarely supplied enough information to explain a past event. During a picture sequence, he named objects but needed support to connect actions and identify who did them.

A descriptive transcript used SALT conventions. The clinician marked an extra word with [EW] when the transcription context supported that interpretation. These codes describe language samples; they are not diagnoses. The sample was too brief and context-dependent for a broad quantitative bilingual comparison.

During supported learning, the clinician modeled “quiero el grande” and “I need help”. The child adopted a longer request in 4/6 subsequent opportunities with mod cues. This response suggests that modeling, repetition, and meaningful routines can support learning. It does not remove the observed functional difficulties.

SPEECH SOUND PRODUCTION / HABLA

Speech was clearer in familiar routines than in longer, spontaneous messages. The clinician observed fronting of /k/, represented here as /k/, toward [t in some English words. Spanish productions also showed inconsistent omission of unstressed syllables. English consonant clusters were frequently reduced.

Recorded examples included “tat” for “cat”, “poon” for “spoon”, and “pelota” with variable syllable completeness. The Spanish tap /ɾ/ was inconsistent. These observations require continued sampling because developmental expectations and language structure differ across Spanish and English.

A familiar caregiver understood an estimated 80% of the play sample. The clinician understood approximately 60% without contextual clarification. These are session estimates, not standardized scores. The child produced /k/ in isolation in 4/5 attempts with max cues, but carryover to words remained limited.

IMPRESSIONS / IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Findings support mixed receptive-expressive language difficulties that affect participation across home and daycare. The strongest evidence includes limited message length in both languages, difficulty with novel directions, caregiver concerns, classroom reports, and current assessment results. Bilingual exposure and code-switching do not explain the full pattern.

Speech sound difficulties also reduce intelligibility. The observed patterns include errors shared across language samples and patterns that require language-specific interpretation. Continued assessment should distinguish developmental variation from persistent difficulty. The present sample supports intervention while that distinction becomes clearer.

Clinical coding: ICD-10 F80.2 for mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and ICD-10 F80.0 for speech sound disorder. These codes summarize the fictional clinical impressions. No diagnosis of childhood apraxia of speech was established from this evaluation.

Strengths include social interest, shared enjoyment, gesture use, family involvement, and improved responses after teaching. Prognosis for functional progress is favorable with consistent access, caregiver coaching, and coordinated practice. Progress may vary with sleep, attendance, task demands, and opportunities to communicate.

RECOMMENDATIONS / PLAN Y RECOMENDACIONES

[X] Speech-language therapy recommended
[X] Caregiver coaching  [X] Daycare coordination
[X] Maintain Spanish and English  [X] Review hearing as needed

1. Begin speech-language treatment twice weekly, with one visit including caregiver participation when scheduling permits. Combine direct practice with everyday routines. Coordinate appointment options with the family’s work shifts and transportation needs.

2. Continue participation in Little Learners Program. Use shared communication supports with Little Learners Daycare. With caregiver consent, send a concise strategy sheet to Ms. Celia Robles and Jordan Peller. No outside communication occurred during this evaluation.

3. Use responsive interaction strategies informed by Hanen. Follow the child’s focus, pause, and expand his message by one useful element. If he says “carro”, model “carro rojo”. Accept Spanish, English, gestures, and combinations that communicate his intent.

4. Trial visual choices during dressing, snack, and play. Consider selected PECS procedures only after assessing the child’s communication needs and caregiver preferences. A visual support should help him communicate without making speech a condition for receiving help.

5. Address speech patterns through meaningful words and brief practice. Consider Cycles when repeated sampling supports a pattern-based plan. PROMPT was not administered during this visit. Any motor-based method requires an appropriate assessment and clinician training.

6. For goal 1, support following a novel direction containing two meaningful details in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Practice in both languages using familiar objects before increasing task demands.

7. For goal 2, support a functional phrase of at least three words in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Include requests, comments, and help-seeking. Accept mixed-language phrases when the message is clear.

8. For goal 3, support a communication repair in 80% of observed breakdowns with mod cues. Repairs may include repeating, pointing, showing, or adding a word. Adults should acknowledge the message before requesting another attempt.

9. For goal 4, establish selected speech targets with 70% accuracy in practiced words and mod cues. Initial targets may include /k/ and complete syllable shapes. Select vocabulary with the family and confirm relevance in each language.

10. Coordinate sensory and positioning supports with OT Lucinda Reyes. Consult PT Evan Soltero only if new movement concerns affect participation. Refer back to Dr. Amalia Varela for medical concerns or a change in hearing status.

11. Review progress on November 18, 2026. Compare functional samples, caregiver reports, and classroom participation. Repeat standardized assessment only when clinically useful. Adjust goals when skills generalize or barriers change.

CIERRE / FAMILY REVIEW

Mariela Elenares identified snack requests and asking for help as the first home priorities. Tomás Elenares preferred a short written practice plan in Spanish with English examples. Both caregivers demonstrated expansion and wait time during play. Their return demonstration supported understanding of the proposed strategies.

The clinician reviewed findings in Spanish and English. The family received time to clarify terms and discuss scheduling. Therapy consent and outside information-sharing consent remain separate administrative steps. The report recommends services; it does not document that all recommended services have started.

DOCUMENT STATUS

This report is entirely fictional and was created for offline de-identification testing. All people, organizations, locations, identifiers, and clinical findings are invented. It describes no actual child and does not establish eligibility, authorize treatment, or document a real service.

MOTIVO DE REFERENCIA / REASON FOR REFERRAL

Nico Esteban Valera was referred because his family and preschool staff described difficulty understanding longer directions, combining words, and making speech understood. His mother, Elena Marisol Valera, stated, "En casa sabe mucho, pero cuando quiere explicar algo, se queda buscando las palabras." His father, Tomas Adrian Valera, requested practical strategies that both parents could use during meals and play.

Ms. Dalia Merrow, the classroom teacher, reported that Nico participates in familiar routines but often watches another child before beginning an unfamiliar activity. Classroom assistant Mr. Owen Bellcrest described stronger participation when directions include gestures and pictures. Staff requested help distinguishing language learning needs from difficulty caused by an unfamiliar classroom language.

The referral came from pediatrician Dr. Leila Fenwick at Willowbend Children's Hospital. Former service coordinator Carmen Alder supplied historical records from Heronfield Children's Developmental Services Agency. The evaluation considered communication across languages, settings, and partners. English performance alone was not used to decide whether a language disorder was present.

ANTECEDENTES / BACKGROUND

Nico attended Little Orchard Playhouse before entering his current preschool. His mother reported that the daycare used mostly English, with occasional Spanish greetings. At Lantern Finch Early Learning School, instruction occurs primarily in English. Staff use a picture schedule, songs, movement activities, and small group play.

Attendance has been consistent except for brief absences associated with common respiratory illnesses. The family denied a recent loss of skills. Transitions can be difficult when an activity ends unexpectedly. He usually settles when an adult names the next activity and offers a clear choice.

Teacher observations described cooperative play with classmate Mila Thorne and parallel play beside Evan Reedwell. During pretend cooking, Nico handed food pieces to Mila and waited for a response. During outdoor play, friend Arlo Cress frequently interpreted his gestures for other children.

The family identified communication during disagreements as the main concern. When misunderstood, Nico may point repeatedly, pull an adult toward an object, or leave the interaction. His mother said, "No es que no quiera hablar; cuando nadie entiende, ya no intenta." The family wants him to explain needs without losing his natural use of Spanish.

HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO Y SALUD

Nico was born on August 9, 2022, at Willowbend Children's Hospital, following a reported gestational age of 38 weeks, 4 days. Birth weight was 7 lb 2 oz. Available fictional birth records listed Apgar scores of 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. His mother reported an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and routine discharge.

Feeding history included early breastfeeding followed by mixed feeding. The family reported no persistent coughing with liquids, prolonged meals, or current food restriction. Sleep is generally regular. No seizure history, major injury, or known neurological diagnosis was reported.

Two episodes of middle ear infection were reported. Audiologist Peter Halden completed a hearing evaluation on September 18, 2026, at Willowbend Children's Hospital. The supplied record described hearing adequate for speech access. Today's screening observations did not replace that assessment.

First meaningful words reportedly emerged near 18 months, with regular word combinations near 30 months. The family recalled slower vocabulary growth in both languages. Early intervention began at 26 months. Historical IFSP documentation dated November 14, 2024, listed Outcome 2 for functional requesting. Transition planning occurred on May 21, 2025.

FAMILIA, TRABAJO Y LENGUAS

Nico lives with both parents and his sister, Luz Valera, age 7 years. Spanish is the main home language. His sister uses English during some games and reads bilingual books with him. The family also receives help from grandmother Ines Corvera and aunt Paz Corvera.

The family's dog, Mango, appears often in conversation and pretend play. During the parent interview, Nico pointed toward a photograph and said, "Mango come aqui." Because that production contains a name, the phrase is recorded without a KEEP span around the complete utterance.

Mom works nights at Silver Fern Cleaning Service as a cleaning technician, described at home as servicio de limpieza Silver Fern Cleaning Service. Her earlier jobs included stocking shelves at Lantern Basket Store, tienda Lantern Basket Store, and kitchen preparation at Juniper Table Restaurant, restaurante Juniper Table Restaurant.

Dad currently works at Cedar Span Construction Company as a framing helper, compania de construccion Cedar Span Construction Company. He previously packed produce at Meadow Ribbon Farm, granja Meadow Ribbon Farm, and operated packaging equipment at Willow Thread Plant, planta Willow Thread Plant. These changing schedules affect who supervises evening routines.

Babysitter Rita Solven uses Spanish. Family friend Ada Wrenlow sometimes drives the family to appointments but does not provide regular care. The family receives nutrition support through Heronfield WIC Office and book activities through Willowbend Smart Start Partnership.

PROCEDIMIENTOS / ASSESSMENT CONDITIONS

Marina Celeste Arvelo conducted the evaluation directly in Spanish and English. No interpreter was required. Activities included caregiver interview, record review, structured testing, play observation, a bilingual language sample, speech sampling, and brief teaching trials. Language choice followed the child's response and the purpose of each activity.

Nico entered comfortably with his mother. He explored the toys, accepted a visual schedule, and returned to the table after movement breaks. He showed interest in vehicles, animals, and pretend meals. Engagement decreased during tasks requiring several verbal details without visual support.

The PLS-5 Spanish was administered using its bilingual procedures. Scores below reflect the fictional administration described here. English-only tasks from the GFTA-3 were used descriptively because an English normative comparison would not adequately represent this child's language experience.

A connected speech sample was transcribed using selected SALT conventions. Codes included [EW] for an extra word and [OM] for an omitted word. These codes described sample features; they did not independently establish a diagnosis.

Dynamic assessment examined whether brief models improved performance. He learned new object labels more readily when the clinician paired speech with actions. He benefited from min cues for familiar requests and mod cues for novel descriptions. Attention, language exposure, and task familiarity were considered when interpreting results.

RESULTADOS / SCORE TABLE

| Measure | Score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 78 | 7th percentile | 73-83 | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | Standard score 75 | 5th percentile | 70-82 | 2;10 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | Standard score 75 | 5th percentile | 71-81 | 2;11 |
| Developmental task band, descriptive only | No standard score assigned | Not applicable | Not applicable | 2;6–3;0 |
| Familiar single-step directions | 8/10 correct | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not assigned |
| Novel two-step directions | 3 of 5 correct | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not assigned |
| Unfamiliar-listener speech sample | 62% understood | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not assigned |

The confidence intervals use the 90% level. Age equivalents describe performance on a particular item set. They do not represent the child's overall developmental age or prescribe placement. The descriptive task band summarizes observed skills and is not an additional standardized result.

COMPRENSION / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

Nico identified familiar objects, common actions, and several body parts in Spanish and English. He understood routine requests embedded in play. For example, he followed the target direction "Put the car in the box" when the materials were visible and the action was familiar.

Understanding decreased when directions contained order, location, and an unfamiliar object together. With verbal presentation alone, he completed 3/8 complex directions. With gestures and a repeated model, performance increased to 6/8. This improvement supports the use of visual teaching while language skills develop.

He answered concrete what questions more consistently than why questions. Spanish presentation improved access to familiar concepts, but did not remove all difficulty. Similar errors appeared across languages when questions required a relationship between events.

During a book activity, he selected a picture for the target "The boy is sleeping". He needed mod cues to distinguish the targets "before" and "after". He sometimes responded to the most familiar noun rather than the complete sentence. This pattern matched caregiver examples from home and teacher examples from class.

EXPRESION / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

Spontaneous communication included single words, short combinations, gestures, and occasional longer practiced phrases. Nico used both languages within the same interaction. Code-switching served communication and was not counted as an error solely because the languages changed.

Examples included "quiero blue car", "ese no cabe", and "baby esta sleeping". These productions showed meaningful choices of vocabulary across languages. Difficulties involved limited sentence expansion, reduced grammatical detail, and trouble explaining events beyond the immediate situation.

During pretend play, he produced "dog eat", then expanded to "the dog is eating" after a model and min cues. In Spanish, he changed "nene cae" to "el nene se cayo" with mod cues. Carryover was inconsistent when the clinician introduced a different picture.

He named familiar items but used general words when he could not retrieve a specific label. He combined speech with pointing effectively. When asked to tell his mother about a completed activity, he listed objects instead of describing what happened. He produced a simple event sequence with max cues and picture support.

HABLA / SPEECH SOUND FINDINGS

The speech sample showed reduced clarity in both languages. Observed patterns included omission of final consonants in English, cluster reduction, and inconsistent substitution of /t/ for /k/. These patterns were examined within each language's sound system.

Recorded productions included "tat" for the target "cat", "poon" for "spoon", and "pato" for "plato". The clinician did not count predictable differences between Spanish and English pronunciation as disorder evidence without examining context.

Nico produced /k/ in isolation with mod cues, but accuracy decreased in words. He produced initial /m/, /p/, and /n/ consistently in sampled familiar words. Gliding to [w] occurred in some English words. Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent and was interpreted with age and language experience in mind.

Familiar listeners understood more speech than the unfamiliar clinician. His mother's estimate was 80% in familiar routines. The clinician understood 62% of the recorded conversational sample. These figures reflect different contexts and are not interchangeable standardized scores.

Voice quality and fluency appeared functional during this brief sample. Oral movements supported the observed speech tasks. No feeding assessment was completed.

IMPRESIONES CLINICAS

The fictional findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language difficulty affecting everyday communication across Spanish and English. Evidence includes parent report, classroom observations, bilingual testing, and difficulty learning or explaining language during supported tasks. Bilingual exposure itself does not explain the full pattern.

Speech sound differences also reduce clarity. Additional sampling across contexts would help refine a treatment diagnosis. The proposed language code is ICD-10 F80.2; a possible speech sound code, pending further assessment, is ICD-10 F80.0.

Strengths include social interest, pretend play, willingness to imitate, gesture use, and improved performance with visual support. The family consistently recognizes communicative attempts and provides meaningful language models. His learning response suggests that intervention can build on existing skills.

Eligibility decisions require the relevant team's procedures and cannot be made from this fictional report alone.

RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN DE APOYO

Recommend speech-language treatment twice weekly for twelve weeks, with progress reviewed on January 8, 2027. Sessions should address comprehension, sentence expansion, repair strategies, and speech clarity through meaningful play. Include caregiver coaching and classroom consultation.

Use Hanen strategies to support waiting, following the child's interests, and expanding messages. A focused Cycles approach may address selected sound patterns after additional sampling. Consider PROMPT only if further assessment identifies a suitable motor speech target and the treating clinician has appropriate training. PECS is not required by the present findings; visual choices can still support access.

Maintain Spanish at home. Adults should use the language in which they can offer the clearest and richest interaction. Model a useful expansion, then continue the activity without requiring repeated performance. For example, respond to "mas agua" with the target "quiero mas agua".

Ms. Dalia Merrow can pair classroom directions with pictures and check understanding through action. Avoid using yes responses as the only comprehension check. Offer a supported way to ask for help and allow time for a response.

PROPOSED GOALS / METAS

Goal 1: Follow unfamiliar two-step directions with 80% accuracy across consecutive sessions, given min cues.

Goal 2: Produce an expanded functional message in 8/10 opportunities during play, given min cues.

Goal 3: Repair an unclear message in 4 of 5 opportunities using speech, gesture, or a visual choice.

Goal 4: Produce selected speech targets with 75% accuracy in practiced words, given mod cues.

Caregiver review is scheduled for October 16, 2026, at 4:20 PM. The family requested examples that fit meals, bath routines, and shared books.

Motivo de consulta / Background

The family requested this assessment because Nicolás often knows what he wants but cannot explain it clearly. His mother, Lucía Beltrán Rivas, described frequent gestures, short requests, and frustration when adults ask follow-up questions. She stated, “En casa nos cuenta pedacitos, pero cuando algo pasó en la escuela, no encuentra cómo explicarlo.”

His father, Andrés Rivas Montiel, reported that familiar routines are easier than unexpected changes. During meals, the child can request a preferred item. When something spills or breaks, he may point and repeat a single word instead of explaining the problem. Both parents want communication goals that work during ordinary family activities.

The referral followed a preschool conference on September 24, 2026. Ms. Alina Cordero reported difficulty answering questions about stories, following unfamiliar directions, and negotiating shared materials. Classroom assistant Brenna Solís observed that visual demonstrations help him enter activities.

The family previously received services through the Agencia de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil del Distrito de Arroyo Claro, identified in earlier records as CDSA Arroyo Claro. Service coordination came from the Agencia Comunitaria de Recursos y Puentes para la Primera Infancia, abbreviated RPE. The service coordinator, Elena Prado, supplied a transition summary dated July 18, 2025.

The family’s main question was whether exposure to two languages caused the communication difficulty. Current findings support a language disorder affecting learning and use across languages. Spanish exposure provides important communication opportunities. It does not explain the observed weaknesses.

Historia del nacimiento y salud / Birth and medical history

According to the parent interview and the copied discharge summary, pregnancy included routine prenatal care and maternal nausea. No prenatal infection, substance exposure, or major pregnancy complication was reported. Delivery occurred at 38 weeks, 4 days at River Lantern Children’s Hospital.

Birth weight was 3,175 grams. Apgar scores were 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. The infant remained with his mother after delivery. The record did not describe intensive care, respiratory support, or feeding tube use.

The parents reported early feeding without choking or prolonged meals. He now eats family foods with varied textures. He occasionally refuses mixed dishes but accepts separate foods from the same meal. This assessment did not include an instrumental swallowing study. No current swallowing concern emerged during the interview or snack observation.

Motor milestones were reported within the family’s expected range. Independent walking began at 14 months. First meaningful words appeared around 20 months. Consistent word combinations began near 31 months. These ages reflect caregiver recall, not contemporaneous developmental testing.

The family reported several episodes of middle ear fluid during toddlerhood. Audiologist Irene Valdés completed testing on September 30, 2026 at River Lantern Children’s Hospital. The supplied summary described hearing adequate for speech access during that visit. Continued monitoring was advised if infections or listening concerns return.

There is no reported history of seizures, head injury, developmental regression, or chronic medication use. Dr. Gabriel Soria remains the primary medical contact. Sleep is generally consistent, although late naps sometimes delay bedtime. The child was alert during testing and did not appear ill.

Historia familiar e idiomas / Family and language history

Spanish is the main home language. Both parents also use English for work, shopping, and communication with preschool staff. They usually address Nicolás in Spanish. He answers in Spanish, English, or a combination, depending on the partner and activity.

Older sister Camila Rivas often uses English during pretend play. Younger brother Tomás Rivas hears mostly Spanish at home. Their grandmother, Rosa Montiel Paredes, provides afternoon care and uses Spanish consistently. An aunt, Diana Beltrán, helps with transportation and uses both languages.

The family previously lived near El Cedralito de la Niebla, Guatemala. The grandmother’s mailing address remains Calle del Naranjo 18, Barrio Las Luciérnagas, El Cedralito de la Niebla, Guatemala. These details came from the intake form and were used only to describe the family’s language environment.

The mother works at Lantern Creek Textile Cooperative. Her rotating schedule affects which adult attends appointments. The father works at Blue Heron Fixture Works. Both requested short practice activities that caregivers can repeat without special materials.

The family dog, Chispa, motivates requests and comments. During the interview, the child said, “Chispa come aquí,” while pointing toward a photograph. This utterance showed spontaneous communication with a meaningful topic, although the clinician could not determine whether the intended message was a command or a description.

The parents reported a cousin with late language development. They did not report a diagnosed family hearing disorder. No relative attended as an interpreter. The evaluator conducted the interview and assessment directly in Spanish and English.

Language exposure estimates were 65% Spanish and 35% English across a typical week. These estimates describe opportunity for exposure. They do not measure proficiency. The family was advised to use the language that allows the richest, most comfortable interaction.

Entorno educativo / Classroom participation

Nico attends Meadow Lantern Early Learning Center on weekdays. The classroom uses English for most group instruction. Staff incorporate Spanish greetings, songs, and familiar routine words. This setting gives regular English exposure but limited opportunities for extended Spanish conversation.

Ms. Alina Cordero described strong interest in blocks, vehicles, and pretend cooking. He watches other children closely before joining. When a play routine repeats, he participates with less adult support. New activities require more demonstration and extra processing time.

Classmate Maya Serrano often invites him to the kitchen center. Another classmate, Owen Mercer, shares vehicle play. Staff reported that communication breakdowns occur when peers change the plan or request a specific role. He may hold an item silently, repeat a request, or leave the activity.

During a classroom observation on October 7, 2026, the child approached Maya and said, “Maya cook conmigo.” The peer responded and handed him a cup. This interaction showed useful code-switching and a clear social purpose.

At cleanup, he followed familiar directions after watching classmates. When the teacher changed the order, he needed mod cues and a visual demonstration. His response improved when the adult presented one action, paused, and then added the next action.

The planned transition conference with Juniper Hollow Elementary School is scheduled for November 4, 2026 at 1:30 PM. The current report can inform that discussion. School eligibility and service delivery require the school team’s own review of educational impact.

Procedimientos y condiciones / Assessment procedures

The evaluation combined caregiver interview, record review, structured testing, play observation, a bilingual language sample, and dynamic assessment. The clinician alternated languages when assessing functional understanding and learning. Standardized administration was preserved only where stated below.

The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) provided an English reference for receptive and expressive performance. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) sampled English speech production. Results were considered alongside Spanish productions and connected speech.

Earlier records included the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale, the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition (Bayley-4), and the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales, Second Edition (PDMS-2). Those instruments were not readministered during this visit.

The child initially stayed near his mother and spoke softly. After familiar play, he separated comfortably and completed activities at the table and on the floor. He benefited from movement breaks and clear transitions. Attention improved when tasks had a visible purpose.

English standardized scores have limited interpretive value for this bilingual profile. Spanish support, repeated instructions, and teaching trials were recorded separately from standardized items. Supported responses were not added to standardized totals. The report therefore distinguishes test performance from the child’s ability to learn with help.

Resultados / Score summary

| Instrument or subtest | Score type | Result | Percentile | Confidence interval or developmental range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension | Standard score | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-83 |
| PLS-5 Expressive Communication | Standard score | 75 | 5th percentile | 70–82 |
| PLS-5 Total Language | Standard score | 74 | 4th percentile | 69–81 |
| GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words | Standard score | 88 | 21st percentile | 83–95 |
| PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension | Age equivalent | 2;10 | Not applicable | Descriptive span 2;6–3;0 |
| PLS-5 Expressive Communication | Age equivalent | 2;8 | Not applicable | Descriptive span 2;4–2;11 |
| Historical Bayley-4 Receptive Communication | Scaled score | 6 | Not supplied | Assessed at 28 months |
| Historical Bayley-4 Expressive Communication | Scaled score | 5 | Not supplied | Assessed at 28 months |
| Historical PDMS-2 Fine Motor Quotient | Standard score | 96 | 39th percentile | Interval not supplied |

The confidence intervals above are 90% intervals for the current standard scores. Developmental spans are descriptive summaries of observed skill distribution. They are not confidence intervals. Age equivalents do not establish a single functional age or prescribe classroom placement.

Historical scores came from a report dated December 16, 2024. The earlier Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale described receptive skills distributed across 18–24 months and expressive skills across 15–21 months. That instrument’s criterion-based findings should not be treated as standard scores.

Comprensión / Receptive language

The child understood familiar action words and routine requests in both languages. In a supported Spanish task, he selected named objects in 8/10 opportunities, or 80%, with min cues. Accuracy decreased when the direction included an unfamiliar relationship or an additional action.

For related two-step directions, performance was 3 of 5 with mod cues. He often completed the last action heard. A gesture showing the order improved performance. This pattern suggests difficulty holding and organizing verbal information, especially when the message contains several parts.

He understood the target words “arriba” and “abajo” during movement play. Understanding of “detrás” and “entre” was inconsistent across objects and languages. The clinician varied materials to check whether responses reflected a learned routine.

Questions about visible actions were easier than questions requiring explanation. He answered “what happened?” by naming an object but often omitted the action. When asked “¿por qué?,” he sometimes repeated the final word instead of giving a reason.

A brief teaching trial paired spoken directions with pictures. After practice, accuracy increased from 4/10 to 8/10 with min cues. The improvement supports the use of visual support and repeated teaching. It does not erase the difficulty observed without support.

Expresión / Expressive language

Spontaneous speech included requests, labels, protests, and brief comments. Common productions included “más agua,” “I want carro,” and “no cabe”. These messages were effective when the listener could see the context.

The child used both languages within sentences. Code-switching itself was not counted as an error. For example, “the perro sleeping” communicated an agent and action. The relevant concern was limited sentence organization and difficulty adding information when the listener needed clarification.

In a picture sequence, he produced “boy fall” and then “agua aquí”. He identified important elements but did not independently explain their connection. With mod cues, he produced “el niño se cayó”. He did not retain the full sentence after the picture changed.

A sample analyzed with Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) included incomplete messages and revisions. The code [EW] identified selected English grammatical errors within English clauses. Spanish grammar and mixed-language clauses required separate clinical review. The code [SI] marked an unintelligible segment.

Narrative difficulty appeared in both languages. He needed max cues to introduce the setting, describe the problem, and explain the outcome. Sentence length increased during familiar pretend play, but longer utterances sometimes became less clear.

Habla, voz y fluidez / Speech production

Speech was more intelligible in familiar context than in a new conversation. The mother estimated that familiar listeners understood 85% of his speech. The clinician understood approximately 70% of connected speech without access to the intended message.

Observed patterns included occasional fronting of /k/ as [t] and variable cluster reduction. Specifically, /k/ was produced as [t] in several English words. The target “car” appeared as “tar”. He produced /k/ accurately during imitation with mod cues.

A gliding pattern included [w] for English /r/. Spanish /ɾ/ was variable in connected speech. These findings require language-specific interpretation. The clinician did not score an English pattern as evidence of a Spanish error without examining the Spanish context.

The historical Goldman-Fristoe shorthand in the referral referred to articulation testing, not a person involved in care. Likewise, Rossetti, Bayley, and Peabody in prior notes referred to assessment instruments.

Oral structures appeared adequate for observed speech tasks. Voice quality and loudness were functional after warm-up. No persistent stuttering pattern emerged during this sample. These observations describe this session and do not rule out concerns in other settings.

Comunicación social y aprendizaje / Social communication

The child shared enjoyment, shifted gaze between people and objects, and used gestures to direct attention. He brought a toy to the clinician and waited for a response. Social interest was a relative strength.

Communication repair was less consistent. When the clinician misunderstood a request, he repeated the same message without adding information. With mod cues, he pointed to the relevant object or selected a picture. This strategy helped the interaction continue.

During shared play, he completed 6/8 turn exchanges with min cues. He needed more support when the partner changed the topic. The task did not test peer participation under ordinary classroom noise or competing demands.

The clinician used mediated learning to model a short problem statement, wait, and invite a new attempt. He learned the target “help me open” during a container activity. After a break, he used “abre, please” independently. This was an appropriate bilingual request.

His learning response supports active intervention with meaningful repetition. It also supports measuring carryover across partners and settings. Performance with one adult during one visit should not be treated as proof of independent classroom use.

Impresiones clínicas / Clinical impressions

Findings support mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, ICD-10 F80.2. The central difficulties involve understanding complex messages, organizing sentences, explaining events, and repairing breakdowns. These difficulties affect home routines and preschool participation.

English test results alone cannot separate language difference from disorder. The diagnosis rests on converging information: concerns in Spanish and English, caregiver examples, classroom observations, limited narrative organization, and substantial support needs during functional tasks.

Speech sound differences also reduce intelligibility. Current evidence supports monitoring and targeted treatment within the communication plan. The available sample does not justify a separate motor speech diagnosis. Additional sampling may clarify which sound patterns persist across languages.

Strengths include social interest, meaningful gestures, engagement in pretend play, and improvement after teaching. The child communicates best when the topic is visible and the adult gives time to respond. These strengths provide practical starting points for intervention.

Metas funcionales / Proposed goals

The historical IFSP Outcome 2 addressed requesting help during family routines. IFSP Outcome 3 addressed participation in shared play. These outcomes provide continuity, but the preschool team should adopt current goals through its own planning process.

Proposed Goal 1: During a familiar activity, the child will request help or clarification in either language in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Acceptable targets include “ayúdame,” “help please,” or another clear message with the same purpose.

Proposed Goal 2: The child will follow related two-step directions in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. The clinician will vary objects, action order, and partners. Routine imitation alone will not count as independent understanding.

Proposed Goal 3: Given a shared event or picture sequence, the child will describe the actor, action, and outcome in 80% of opportunities with mod cues. Spanish, English, and meaningful mixed-language responses will be accepted.

Proposed Goal 4: The child will repair a misunderstood message by adding a word, gesture, or picture in 3 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Repeating the same unclear utterance will prompt additional teaching.

Proposed Goal 5: For selected functional words, the child will produce /k/ in 8/10 trials with mod cues. Targets will include “casa,” “cup,” and other words relevant to daily routines.

Recomendaciones / Recommendations

1. Begin individual speech-language treatment twice weekly for thirty minutes. Review participation, response to teaching, and family priorities after an initial treatment block. Use CPT 92507 with modifier GN when applicable to the documented service.

2. Use focused stimulation, expansions, and recasts during meaningful activities. The clinician should model language without requiring the child to repeat every sentence. Consider caregiver coaching through Hanen It Takes Two to Talk when the format fits the family.

3. Continue Spanish at home. Hablen como les salga natural. Adults should describe actions, pause for a response, and add one useful detail to the child’s message. Rich interaction matters more than assigning each language a rigid schedule.

4. Provide pictures for classroom routines and common problems. Teach the child how to point to a picture while attempting a message. A full PECS program is not recommended from this assessment alone.

5. Select speech targets after further bilingual sampling. A Cycles approach may be considered if consistent phonological patterns emerge. PROMPT is not indicated solely because a child has reduced intelligibility.

6. Coordinate with the preschool and receiving school. Share functional examples and cueing requirements. Ask staff to note whether skills occur independently, with min cues, or with mod cues. Use the same definitions across settings.

7. Continue hearing follow-up if new listening concerns occur. Review treatment progress on January 14, 2027. The family may contact the clinician sooner if communication skills regress or daily participation changes substantially.
