DOCUMENT STATUS: Fictional clinical report for offline de-identification testing  Record ID: PCP-260106-047
Report type: Bilingual pediatric speech-language evaluation  Setting: Outpatient clinic and caregiver interview
Child: Nicolás del Río-Vega  Preferred name: Nico  Pronouns: he/him
Date of birth: August 6, 2022  Age at evaluation: 4;2
Evaluation dates: October 6, 2026 and October 8, 2026  Report date: October 9, 2026
Session start: 9:15 a.m.  Session end: 10:35 a.m.
Parent: Elena de la Cruz  Parent: Adrián Vega-Santos
Address: 214 Marigold Lantern Lane  City: Cedrillo  State: North Carolina  ZIP: 27003
Parent telephone: 919-555-0146  Parent email: elena.delacruz@example.com
Medicaid member: 482716395K  Authorization: AUTH-261008-552
School: Cedar Kite Early Learning School  Teacher: Ms. Maribel Soto
Referring physician: Dr. Leandro Finch  Referral date: September 18, 2026
Evaluating clinician: Amalia Torres-Mendoza, MS, CCC-SLP  Languages used: Spanish and English
Employer: Puente Claro Pediatric Communication, PLLC  Office phone: 984-555-0162
Clinician email: amalia.torres@example.com  Website: https://puenteclaro.example.com
Procedure: CPT 92523  Proposed treatment: CPT 92507  Billing modifier: GN

MOTIVO DE CONSULTA / REASON FOR REFERRAL

Nicolás was referred because unfamiliar listeners have difficulty understanding his speech, and his sentences often omit important information. His parents requested assessment in both languages. They want him to explain what happened at school, join play, and ask for help without becoming upset.

Su mamá Elena de la Cruz reported, “En casa habla mucho, pero cuando quiere contar algo largo, se pierde.” His father, Adrián Vega-Santos, added, “He knows what he wants. Sometimes we guess too quickly because everyone is in a hurry.”

The family’s main concern is communication across daily routines. They do not seek to replace Spanish with English. They want both languages supported, con mucho respeto for the language used with relatives. This report combines caregiver information, classroom observations, direct assessment, and language samples. Findings describe current performance under the conditions documented below.

ANTECEDENTES / BACKGROUND

Nico attends Cedar Kite Early Learning School on weekday mornings. He previously attended Little Lantern Daycare. His current classroom uses English for most group instruction and Spanish during selected songs, greetings, and individual support.

Ms. Soto described him as curious, affectionate, and eager to help with classroom jobs. He participates readily when an activity has visible materials. During discussion without pictures, he may repeat part of a question or watch classmates before responding.

The teacher reported that he follows familiar routines but needs extra support when directions include several actions. He often approaches classmates Maya Bell and Tomás Reed during construction play. When a peer does not understand him, he sometimes repeats the same message louder instead of adding information.

Parents reported no previous speech-language therapy. A service coordinator, Irene Calder, at Pine Harbor Children’s Developmental Services Agency provided an earlier developmental screening. The family did not enroll in services then. The present referral followed increased communication demands at school.

HISTORIA DEL NACIMIENTO Y MÉDICA

Birth hospital: Willow Lantern Children’s Hospital  Birth date: August 6, 2022
Gestational age: 38 weeks, 4 days  Birth weight: 3,180 grams
Apgar scores: 8 and 9  Delivery: Vaginal, per caregiver report

The pregnancy and delivery history came from the parents. They reported routine prenatal care and no prolonged neonatal hospitalization. Feeding initially required help with positioning. The family described steady growth after discharge.

Nicolás reportedly experienced recurrent middle-ear infections during toddlerhood. Dr. Finch referred him to audiologist Celia Hart-Morales at Willow Lantern Children’s Hospital. The audiology summary dated September 23, 2026 documented hearing adequate for speech access at that visit. This report does not establish hearing status beyond that encounter.

Parents denied known neurologic injury, seizures, or developmental regression. They reported seasonal nasal congestion and occasional mouth breathing during sleep. No medication was given during either assessment session.

Early motor milestones were described as broadly expected. Caregivers recalled first meaningful words around 15 months and consistent word combinations around 30 months. These ages are estimates. There were no feeding concerns requiring assessment today. Parents described a varied diet, with reluctance toward unfamiliar mixed textures.

FAMILIA E HISTORIA LINGÜÍSTICA

Household members: Elena de la Cruz, Adrián Vega-Santos, Nicolás del Río-Vega, and sister Sol Vega-Santos
Sibling age: 2;9  Additional caregiver: Grandmother Rosa de la Cruz
Family pet: Luna  Home languages: Spanish and English

Spanish is the main language used by his mother and grandmother. His father uses both languages. His sister Sol hears both languages and often joins the same games. Grandmother Rosa provides care after school. Aunt Paz del Río visits regularly and reads picture books in Spanish.

His mother works at Maple Lantern Packaging. His father works at Blue Finch Equipment. Their schedules affect who completes evening routines, so language exposure varies by day. Caregivers estimated current exposure at 60% Spanish and 40% English. These estimates describe opportunity, not proficiency.

The family lives in Juniper Bend County. They reported regular contact with Spanish-speaking relatives and English-speaking neighbors. There is no reported family history of diagnosed developmental language disorder. His father recalled receiving school support for speech sounds, but records were unavailable.

Code-switching is common in family conversation. Expressions such as “vamos afuera after snack” are normal household language practices. Switching languages was not counted as an error. Assessment considered whether a difficulty appeared across languages and whether it persisted when unfamiliar vocabulary was explained.

OBSERVACIÓN CLÍNICA / PARTICIPATION

Nico entered the room holding a toy bus and greeted the clinician with eye contact and a smile. He explored materials, accepted transitions with a visual schedule, and shared objects to invite participation. His engagement improved when the examiner followed his play interests.

He used speech, pointing, facial expression, and gesture together. He checked whether the adult was watching before showing a surprising event. During pretend cooking, he offered food, assigned roles, and protested when the clinician intentionally used the wrong utensil.

Attention varied with task demands. He remained engaged during interactive play but needed movement breaks during picture-based testing. With min cues, he returned to the table after each break. No behavior prevented completion of the planned assessment.

When a message failed, he initially repeated it without changing the wording. With mod cues, he added a gesture or selected a more specific word. Frustration appeared during a difficult picture description, cuando no encontraba la palabra. The clinician acknowledged the message and allowed extra response time.

Oral structures appeared adequate for the observed speech tasks. Lip rounding, tongue movement, and jaw opening were functional during play imitation. This brief observation did not replace a comprehensive feeding or motor speech examination.

PROCEDIMIENTOS / ASSESSMENT CONDITIONS

The clinician administered PLS-5 Spanish using its dual-language procedures. English responses were considered where permitted. Scores were calculated from permitted responses only. Additional translated prompts and teaching trials occurred separately and were excluded from standardized scoring.

The evaluation also included caregiver interview, connected speech sampling, a structured speech sound probe, and a brief dynamic learning task. SALT conventions supported descriptive language-sample coding. These procedures helped interpret performance beyond a single standardized score.

Testing occurred across separate visits to reduce fatigue. The same bilingual clinician completed both visits. Parents remained available for clarification but did not supply answers during scored items. The examiner documented breaks, repetitions, and response language.

Standardized results require caution because bilingual experience varies across children. The scores provide one source of evidence. They do not measure intelligence, predict a fixed developmental outcome, or establish a disorder without supporting functional information.

RESULTADOS ESTANDARIZADOS

Instrument: PLS-5 Spanish  Scoring basis: Dual-language administration  Confidence level: 90%

| Test or subtest | Administration date | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auditory Comprehension | October 6, 2026 | 35 | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-85 | 3;0 |
| Expressive Communication | October 8, 2026 | 32 | 75 | 5th percentile | 70–83 | 2;9 |
| Total Language | October 8, 2026 | 67 | 75 | 5th percentile | 71-82 | 2;11 |

Age equivalents describe performance on these tasks. They are not developmental ages and should not determine placement or treatment goals. The confidence intervals show measurement uncertainty around the reported standard scores.

COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

On Auditory Comprehension, Nicolás identified familiar objects, common actions, and basic body parts. He understood routine directions with visible context. He followed simple location directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues.

Performance decreased when a direction required remembering several details. He completed unfamiliar directions containing linked actions in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. When the examiner reduced sentence length and added gestures, his responses became more consistent.

He showed emerging understanding of descriptive concepts. Comparisons involving size were easier than questions involving sequence or exclusion. During picture discussion, he sometimes selected an associated object instead of the object that matched the full question.

Errors appeared in both languages. Spanish support improved access to familiar vocabulary but did not consistently resolve difficulty with longer instructions. His responses suggested that vocabulary knowledge and sentence processing both affected comprehension. Classroom instructions should therefore include clear wording, visible support, and a check of understanding.

EXPRESIÓN / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

On Expressive Communication, he named familiar objects, combined words, and used language for requesting, commenting, and protesting. Longer responses often omitted grammatical elements or the relationship between ideas. This pattern appeared in Spanish and English samples.

He answered direct questions about visible events more successfully than questions about events outside the room. He could identify who was acting but often needed mod cues to explain why something happened. Specific action words improved after modeling.

During storytelling, he named characters and actions but did not independently establish a clear sequence. With pictures arranged in order, he described the beginning and ending. The middle event remained incomplete until the clinician used max cues.

Some English forms reflected expected cross-language influence. Those forms were not treated as disorder evidence by themselves. Concern centered on limited sentence expansion, weak event organization, and difficulty communicating essential information across both languages.

MUESTRA DE LENGUAJE / CHILD PRODUCTIONS

The sample included toy play, a wordless picture sequence, and conversation about home. Quoted productions below preserve the child’s wording. They include code-switching and speech approximations.

During animal play, he said, "Luna quiere my pan." He then moved the toy dog toward a plate. This message clearly expressed possession and intent, although the adult needed the play context to understand the object.

When asked who would ride the bus, he said, "Sol sit aquí conmigo." He placed a small figure beside himself. Later, he explained, "Luna corre y Sol no catch." These productions contained meaningful relationships across languages.

Other productions included "Yo want el grande", "He fall porque agua", and "No tiene shoe aquí". The clinician accepted the language switches and examined whether the intended relationship was clear. Missing information sometimes required follow-up questions.

During self-identification, he said, "Yo soy Nico." During discussion of school, he said, "Maya tiene blue uno." He named his teacher in the production, "Ms. Soto ayuda zipper."

The target word "sol" referred to the sun in a picture. The examiner clarified that the picture showed the sky, not his sister Sol. He then produced "tol". The shared word and family name required careful interpretation.

Sample coding included [EW] for an extraneous word and [EU] for an utterance-level error under the selected transcription conventions. These codes describe the sample. They do not independently establish severity or cause.

HABLA / SPEECH SOUND FINDINGS

Connected speech intelligibility was estimated at 65% for the unfamiliar clinician when context was available. Caregivers estimated 85% understanding at home. These estimates came from different listening conditions and are not directly interchangeable.

The structured probe showed inconsistent fronting of /k/ and /g/, cluster reduction, and variable production of Spanish /ɾ/. The target "casa" was produced as "tasa". The target "gato" was produced as "dato".

For the English target "rabbit", he used initial [w]. The clinician considered this pattern separately from errors affecting shared sounds. Dialect, language exposure, and developmental expectations must inform each target choice.

He imitated /k/ in isolation with mod cues and produced it in simple syllables in 4/6 trials. Accuracy declined during spontaneous words. No consistent vowel distortion, unusual prosody, or visible articulatory searching was observed in the sampled tasks.

PRUEBA DINÁMICA / RESPONSE TO TEACHING

The clinician taught a short story sequence using focused stimulation and recasting. Initial independent inclusion of essential story elements was 2/6. After teaching, inclusion increased to 4/6 with mod cues.

He retained familiar vocabulary after a movement break. He needed continued support to connect events and explain a character’s response. This pattern showed learning potential while confirming that brief exposure alone did not resolve the language difficulty.

The clinician also used Enhanced Milieu Teaching strategies during toy play. Waiting, arranging materials, and modeling a slightly longer message increased spontaneous requests. Parents observed the demonstration and practiced without requiring repeated imitation.

IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder. Proposed diagnostic codes are ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. The conclusion rests on converging functional concerns, direct observations, bilingual sampling, and assessment results.

Bilingualism does not explain the full pattern. Difficulties occurred across languages and remained when familiar vocabulary, visual support, and additional processing time were available. At the same time, language differences and code-switching must continue to be respected.

Strengths include social engagement, pretend play, communicative intent, family participation, and responsiveness to teaching. Speech errors reduce clarity, while language organization limits the detail of his messages. Both areas affect participation with unfamiliar adults and peers.

This evaluation did not assess literacy, cognition, or broader developmental functioning. Current findings do not support conclusions in those areas. Progress monitoring should examine communication during meaningful routines, not only accuracy during structured practice.

RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN DE APOYO

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy with caregiver participation. Use Enhanced Milieu Teaching, focused stimulation, and recasting to support comprehension and sentence expansion. Select meaningful routines that occur in both languages.

2. Address speech patterns through the Cycles approach when appropriate. Build accurate productions of shared sounds before increasing linguistic demands. Consider PROMPT only if further assessment identifies a suitable motor-based need.

3. Preserve Spanish at home. Parents should use the language that supports natural conversation. Read familiar books, describe daily events, and allow response time. Cuando él mezcle idiomas, respond to the meaning and provide a clear model.

4. Coordinate classroom support with Ms. Soto. Pair directions with pictures or gestures. Ask the child to show the next action instead of only answering whether he understands.

5. Monitor hearing with Dr. Finch if ear symptoms recur. Share this report with the family’s chosen providers after obtaining the required release.

PROPOSED GOALS / METAS

Goal 1: Follow directions containing linked actions with 80% accuracy across familiar routines, given min cues.

Goal 2: Describe an event using an actor, action, and relevant detail in 4 of 5 opportunities, given mod cues.

Goal 3: Produce /k/ and /g/ in selected functional words with 80% accuracy, given mod cues.

Goal 4: Repair an unclear message through added words, gesture, or demonstration in 3 of 4 opportunities, given min cues.

Review date: January 8, 2027  Family conference: October 14, 2026  Conference time: 4:30 p.m.

Parents participated in the closing discussion and described the recommendations in their own words. They selected snack preparation and bedtime reading as initial practice routines. Treatment goals remain proposed until the family and treating clinician complete the plan.

Signed: Amalia Torres-Mendoza, MS, CCC-SLP  Signature date: October 9, 2026
Employer: Puente Claro Pediatric Communication, PLLC  Clinical record: PCP-260106-047

**BILINGUAL PEDIATRIC SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION**  
**Evaluación bilingüe del habla y lenguaje**  
**Fictional clinical training record**

**Client:** Mateo Aranda  
**Preferred name:** Teo  
**Date of birth:** August 6, 2022  
**Evaluation date:** October 6, 2026  
**Chronological age:** 4;2  
**Report date:** October 11, 2026  
**Parent/guardian:** Lucía Aranda and Diego Aranda  
**Home address:** 184 Willow Lantern Lane, Piedraluna, North Carolina 27864  
**Telephone:** (919) 555-0147  
**Parent email:** lucia.aranda@example.com  
**School:** Piedraluna Early Learning School  
**Record number:** CBS-2026-10482  
**Medicaid member number:** 482761935A  
**Authorization number:** AUTH-261006-731  
**Examiner:** Emilia Valdés, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist  
**Practice:** Cedar Bridge Speech Services  
**Office:** 62 Juniper Court, Suite 204, Piedraluna, North Carolina 27864  
**Clinical contact:** evals@cedarbridgespeech.example.com  
**Website:** https://cedarbridgespeech.example.com  
**Evaluation interval:** 9:10 a.m.–11:05 a.m.  
**Billing:** CPT 92523; modifier GN

### 1. Reason for Referral / Motivo de consulta

#### 1.1 Presenting concerns

Mateo Aranda was referred for a bilingual evaluation because his family and classroom team reported difficulty understanding longer directions, combining ideas, and producing clear speech. His mother, Lucía Aranda, described a difference between familiar routines and new situations: “En casa sabemos lo que quiere, pero cuando cambia la pregunta, se pierde.” His father, Diego Aranda, reported that communication breakdowns sometimes lead to crying or leaving an activity.

The referral requested information about skills across Spanish and English. It also requested practical recommendations for home and school. The family wants Mateo to ask for help, explain basic needs, and participate with other children without depending on an adult to interpret each message.

#### 1.2 Evaluation questions

The evaluation examined whether observed difficulties reflected bilingual development, a language disorder, speech sound difficulties, or a combination. It also examined how visual support, repetition, and adult modeling affected performance.

This report integrates caregiver information, classroom observations, standardized testing, play samples, and supported teaching tasks. No single score determined the impressions. Spanish and English responses were considered in relation to exposure, familiarity, and communication demands.

### 2. Background and Records / Antecedentes

#### 2.1 Information sources

Sources included a caregiver interview, the school referral, a pediatric visit summary, an earlier IFSP, and direct assessment. The clinician reviewed the IFSP dated May 19, 2025 and the transition summary dated July 28, 2025.

Service coordinator Nora Beltrán from Alderbrook Children’s Developmental Services Agency supplied the transition summary with written family authorization. Her contact number is (919) 555-0162, and the case number is CDSA-AB-250419.

The earlier IFSP identified Outcome 2, requesting basic needs during daily routines, and Outcome 4, joining a shared play activity. These numbers identify service outcomes; they do not represent test scores.

#### 2.2 Prior services

The family reported that Mateo previously received home-based communication support. Sessions ended after transition from infant-toddler services. Records describe gains in pointing, requesting, and taking turns. They also describe continued difficulty producing flexible phrases.

No previous bilingual standardized evaluation was available. Earlier English screening results were not used as diagnostic scores because the records did not document sufficient information about administration or language exposure.

#### 2.3 Current educational setting

Mateo attends Piedraluna Early Learning School. His classroom teacher, Ms. Elena Brooks, provided written observations. Classroom assistant Mr. Javier Mena described better participation when directions include gestures.

The classroom uses English for most group instruction. Spanish appears during greetings, songs, and individual support. Staff reported that familiar visual routines help him enter activities, but transitions and open-ended questions remain difficult.

### 3. Birth and Medical History / Historia de nacimiento y salud

#### 3.1 Pregnancy and delivery

According to his mother, Mateo was born at Alderbrook Regional Women’s Hospital after a pregnancy complicated by maternal hypertension. Delivery occurred at 38 weeks, 2 days of gestation. Birth weight was 6 lb 9 oz.

The available discharge summary listed Apgar scores of 8 and 9. The family reported no prolonged respiratory support, feeding tube, or neonatal intensive care admission. These details were consistent with the summary reviewed for this evaluation.

#### 3.2 Developmental and medical course

Caregivers reported independent walking at 14 months and consistent meaningful words near 22 months. Flexible word combinations emerged later and remain inconsistent.

Pediatrician Dr. Mara Ellison at Piedraluna Children’s Health Clinic documented recurrent middle-ear infections. The latest recorded episode occurred on February 12, 2026. The family reported no current ear pain.

An audiology report dated September 18, 2026, signed by Luis Serrano, documented hearing adequate for speech access under the conditions tested. That finding supports interpretation of this assessment, although future hearing concerns should receive follow-up.

#### 3.3 Feeding, sleep, and regulation

The family reported a varied diet with reluctance toward unfamiliar textures. There were no reported choking episodes or swallowing concerns. Sleep was described as generally consistent.

During difficult communication exchanges, Mateo may turn away, repeat a request, or seek his mother’s hand. He returned to activities when an adult acknowledged the message and offered a clear next step. These observations describe participation during this visit and do not establish a separate behavioral diagnosis.

### 4. Family and Language History / Familia e idiomas

#### 4.1 Household and caregivers

Mateo lives with his parents and sister, Sol Aranda, whose age is 7;1. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Castañeda, provides care during some afternoons. His aunt, Inés Castañeda, helps with transportation.

Babysitter Alma Vivero provides occasional evening care. The family’s dog, Rocky, often participates in play routines. Caregivers described the dog as a useful topic for requests and simple comments.

His mother works at River Lantern Packaging, and his father works at Blue Orchard Equipment. Their schedules affect who attends appointments, but both requested copies of recommendations.

#### 4.2 Language exposure

Spanish is the main language used by adults at home. The caregiver estimated Spanish exposure at 70% and English exposure at 30%. These are family estimates, not measured totals.

English exposure increased after school entry. His sister, Sol, uses both languages during play. His grandmother, Rosa, speaks Spanish with him. His father, Diego, sometimes introduces English words from classroom materials while maintaining Spanish conversation.

The family reported that Mateo understands routine phrases in both languages. He uses more varied vocabulary in Spanish and several familiar English classroom expressions.

#### 4.3 Family priorities and community supports

The family attends play activities through Puente de Juego Family Support, a local nonprofit. Program facilitator Ms. Beatriz Loma organizes shared book reading and caregiver discussion.

The family also receives support through Alderbrook County WIC Office, Alderbrook County Department of Social Services, and Alderbrook Smart Start Partnership. Earlier records reference Lantern Valley Early Head Start.

These agencies provide distinct services. Their involvement does not establish any clinical diagnosis. The family’s priority remains clear: “Queremos que pueda decir lo que necesita, con sus propias palabras.”

### 5. Assessment Procedures and Participation

#### 5.1 Language access

The evaluation was conducted directly in Spanish and English by Emilia Valdés. No interpreter was required. Spanish was used first for unfamiliar tasks because caregiver history indicated stronger exposure in that language.

The clinician used the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish and its abbreviated name, PLS-5 Spanish, according to documented administration rules. English activities were used for descriptive comparison and classroom relevance.

#### 5.2 Additional procedures

Additional procedures included a caregiver interview, an oral mechanism examination, a speech sample, a play-based language sample, and dynamic assessment. The clinician also collected a brief narrative from a picture sequence.

The Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts framework supported descriptive review of utterances. Transcription included the SALT code [EW] when an extra word occurred. Sample findings were interpreted cautiously because task length and language choice affected output.

#### 5.3 Participation

Mateo entered the room holding his mother’s hand. He explored toy vehicles and accepted the clinician’s involvement. He remained engaged longer when the adult followed his play theme.

Participation improved with a visual schedule, short directions, and planned movement breaks. He completed structured activities with min cues initially and required mod cues as demands increased. Fatigue appeared near the end of the session, so later observations received less interpretive weight.

### 6. Standardized Results / Resultados de pruebas

#### 6.1 Score interpretation

The following scores reflect performance during this administration. Confidence intervals describe measurement uncertainty. They do not define fixed limits on learning.

Age-equivalent values are descriptive and should not be treated as a child’s overall developmental age. The age-equivalent ranges below combine adjacent task estimates for planning. They are not publisher-provided confidence intervals.

| Measure | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Descriptive age-equivalent range |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| PLS-5 Spanish — Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th | 73-83 | 2;6–3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Expressive Communication | 82 | 12th | 77–87 | 2;9–3;3 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Total Language | 79 | 8th | 74-84 | 2;7–3;1 |

#### 6.2 Receptive findings

On Auditory Comprehension, strengths included recognition of familiar objects, common actions, and routine spatial directions supported by context. Difficulty increased when tasks required grammatical distinctions, unfamiliar relational terms, or retention of multiple details.

Mateo sometimes selected an associated picture instead of the picture matching the complete sentence. For example, he attended to an action word but missed who performed the action. Similar patterns appeared in supported play.

#### 6.3 Expressive findings

On Expressive Communication, strengths included naming familiar items and producing short combinations. Difficulty involved sentence expansion, answering questions without visual choices, and describing relationships between events.

His Total Language score was considered alongside evidence across both languages. The score alone cannot separate language difference from disorder. The broader pattern, including difficulty in familiar Spanish routines and reduced learning efficiency, supports concern beyond limited English exposure.

### 7. Functional Language / Lenguaje funcional

#### 7.1 Understanding spoken language

In play, Mateo followed familiar single-step directions in 8/10 opportunities without added gestures. He followed unfamiliar two-part directions in 3 of 8 opportunities. Performance increased to 6 of 8 with gestures and repetition.

For Spanish location words, he identified the intended position in 4/6 opportunities. For corresponding English words, he succeeded in 2/6. This difference was consistent with exposure history.

However, difficulty with longer directions appeared in both languages. He often completed the final action and omitted the first action. Reduced sentence length and a visual sequence improved accuracy.

#### 7.2 Expressive communication

Spontaneous productions included "más carro", "no cabe", "yo quiero ese", and "my turn". He also said "quiero blue carro", showing code-switching within a meaningful request.

Code-switching was accepted as part of bilingual communication. The clinical concern involved limited flexibility, omitted relationships, and difficulty explaining messages when context was unavailable.

When describing a picture, he produced "niño agua". After a model, he produced "niño toma agua" with mod cues. He did not independently reuse that sentence pattern with a different action.

#### 7.3 Communication repair and social use

Mateo initiated requests and shared enjoyment through gaze, gestures, and words. When misunderstood, he usually repeated the same phrase. He added new information in 2 of 7 observed breakdowns.

A family-related production was recorded as “Rocky run.” Another was “Sol ven.” These utterances contained named referents.

He participated in reciprocal play exchanges in 7/10 opportunities with adult support. He showed interest in shared activity, but language demands sometimes interrupted sustained interaction.

### 8. Speech Production and Oral Mechanism

#### 8.1 Oral mechanism observations

Visible oral structures appeared adequate for speech tasks completed during the visit. Lip rounding, tongue movement, and jaw opening were functional during imitation. No consistent signs of structural restriction were observed.

The examination was brief and noninstrumental. It did not assess swallowing physiology. Voice quality and resonance were unremarkable in conversational speech. Fluency was not a primary concern during this sample.

#### 8.2 Speech sound findings

Speech samples showed reduced accuracy for velar sounds /k/ and /g/, variable production of Spanish tap /ɾ/, and occasional omission of unstressed syllables. Some English patterns were consistent with cross-language influence.

For the target casa, Mateo produced "tasa". For gato, he produced "dato". For carro, he produced "calo". The clinician considered sound context and language before interpreting these errors.

The picture target sol referred to the sun. His sister’s name, Sol, was a separate referent. During naming, he produced "tol" for the sun picture. This distinction was maintained in transcription.

#### 8.3 Intelligibility and stimulability

The clinician understood approximately 68% of words in an unfamiliar-context sample and 84% when play context was available. These estimates reflect one listener and this setting.

Mateo produced /k/ accurately in 5/10 imitation trials with mod cues. Accuracy for /g/ was 3/10 with max cues. He sometimes substituted [w] during English approximations.

Speech clarity improved when the adult reduced speaking rate, emphasized the target, and allowed another attempt. Findings support intervention, while continued sampling should distinguish persistent errors from emerging bilingual patterns.

### 9. Dynamic Assessment and Classroom Information

#### 9.1 Response to supported teaching

A short teaching sequence introduced unfamiliar action pictures. The clinician used focused stimulation, visual contrast, and repeated meaningful examples.

Before teaching, Mateo identified the intended action in 2/6 opportunities. After teaching, accuracy increased to 4/6 with mod cues. Delayed retrieval decreased to 2/6 after a different activity.

This pattern showed a response to support, junto con dificultad para mantener y generalizar lo aprendido. The finding contributes to clinical interpretation but is not diagnostic alone.

#### 9.2 Classroom participation

Ms. Brooks reported that Mateo joins predictable songs and imitates familiar motions. During group discussion, he often watches classmates before responding.

He seeks play with classmates Nico Salvatierra and Amaya Bell. Staff described successful exchanges around cars and blocks. Communication becomes harder when another child changes the plan.

Mr. Mena reported one exchange in which Mateo said “Nico mine” while holding a vehicle. Staff helped him clarify ownership and request a turn.

#### 9.3 Interpretation across settings

Home, school, and clinic descriptions showed a consistent reliance on context. Familiar adults often understood intended meanings before the full message was spoken.

Support should preserve this connection while helping him add information. The goal is functional communication that works with less familiar listeners, including peers and classroom staff.

### 10. Clinical Impressions / Impresiones clínicas

#### 10.1 Language

Findings are consistent with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder in a bilingual child. The impression reflects difficulty across languages, caregiver concerns in the stronger language, functional limitations, and supported learning observations.

The recommended language diagnosis is ICD-10-CM F80.2. Bilingual exposure does not explain the full pattern observed. English proficiency remains developing and should be described separately from disorder.

#### 10.2 Speech

Findings also support a speech sound disorder, with clinically relevant errors affecting intelligibility. The recommended speech diagnosis is ICD-10-CM F80.0.

Language-specific expectations must guide target selection. Spanish and English have different sound systems, and a difference between those systems should not automatically become a treatment target.

#### 10.3 Strengths and prognosis

Strengths include social interest, meaningful gestures, enjoyment of shared play, caregiver engagement, and a measurable response to visual support. Mateo also attempts both languages and accepts models during motivating activities.

Prognosis for improved functional communication is favorable with consistent intervention and coordinated support. The rate of progress cannot be predicted from this evaluation alone.

#### 10.4 Limits of the evaluation

The findings represent one clinic visit plus available records and reports. Classroom information was supplied by staff rather than obtained through direct observation.

The clinician recommends an additional naturalistic sample after treatment begins. That sample should examine generalization, message repair, and communication with unfamiliar listeners.

### 11. Recommendations / Recomendaciones

#### 11.1 Direct intervention

Begin speech-language treatment with a bilingual provider or a provider who can arrange appropriate language access. Use meaningful play and daily routines to address comprehension, flexible sentences, and speech clarity.

Recommended approaches include enhanced milieu teaching, focused stimulation, and recasts. Consider Cycles for suitable phonological targets after further analysis. PROMPT is not currently indicated by the available evidence.

Use visual communication supports when they improve participation. Formal PECS implementation is not required at this time. A Hanen caregiver program may provide useful support if available and appropriate to the family’s schedule.

#### 11.2 Home practice / En casa

Continue Spanish at home. Caregivers should use the language that supports their most natural, detailed interaction. Encourage English through enjoyable school-related routines without replacing Spanish conversation.

Model a short sentence, wait, and respond to the child’s meaning. For example, expand "carro rojo" to "quiero el carro rojo". Avoid requiring repeated correction during every exchange.

Use dialogic reading with familiar picture books. Offer choices, pause for responses, and connect pictures to daily experiences. Brief practice within routines is preferable to long drills.

#### 11.3 School supports

Provide short directions with visual cues. Confirm understanding through action instead of repeatedly asking whether he understands. Offer extra response time and predictable opportunities to speak.

Pair Mateo with supportive classmates during structured play. Staff should model requesting, turn-taking, and repair phrases. Useful targets include "ayúdame", "otra vez", and "I need help".

#### 11.4 Initial treatment goals

The proposed plan includes Goal 1: follow related two-part directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues.

Goal 2: produce flexible sentences that express an action and its participant in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

Goal 3: repair an unclear message by adding information in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues.

Goal 4: produce selected velar targets with 80% accuracy in meaningful practice with mod cues. Baselines and target difficulty should be confirmed during treatment.

### 12. Coordination, Follow-Up, and Authentication

#### 12.1 Service coordination

With current family authorization, share this report with the school team, pediatrician, and service coordinator Nora Beltrán. Her role is to support continuity and clarify available resources.

The clinician should confirm each agency’s current role before assigning follow-up tasks. Alderbrook Smart Start Partnership may assist with community resource information. School eligibility requires the school’s own review process.

#### 12.2 Review plan

The proposed plan-of-care review date is January 8, 2027. The proposed reassessment date is April 9, 2027. Adjust these dates if service access or clinical needs change.

Progress review should include caregiver priorities, classroom participation, language samples in both languages, and speech clarity beyond practiced words. Comparable measures should document improvement without treating changing language exposure as treatment failure.

#### 12.3 Family discussion

Results were discussed with Lucía Aranda in Spanish. She summarized the plan as “seguir hablando español, darle tiempo y ayudarle a completar la idea.” She requested a copy for Diego Aranda.

The clinician confirmed that the family can support communication through ordinary routines. Treatment should build on those routines and respect the family’s language choices.

Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist  
Cedar Bridge Speech Services

- Child: Elian Marín Soto, called Eli at home. Birth date: November 10, 2023. Current age: 34 months.
- IFSP record: IFSP-682194. Medicaid member number: 583920174Q. Family selected English documentation with Spanish explanations and bilingual intervention.

- Mother: Camila Soto. Father: Bruno Marín. Sister: Sol Marín Soto, age 7 years. Maternal grandmother: Teresa Soto. All participate in familiar routines.
- Home address: 4286 Lantern Finch Lane, Morrow Glen, NC 27584, in Hawthorn County.

- Service coordinator: Ms. Nadia Beltrán, Hawthorn Valley CDSA. Office address: 160 Cedar Lantern Drive, Morrow Glen, NC 27584.
- Coordinator telephone: 919-555-0173. Office information: https://hawthornvalleycdsa.example.org/families. Contact notes should state which language the family requests.
- Bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist: Isabel Ferrer, employed by Little Lantern Pediatric Communication. The clinician conducted this review in English and Spanish.
- Participants included both parents, grandmother, and the service coordinator. Ms. Isabel Ferrer interpreted routine discussion directly; no separate interpreter attended.

PREOCUPACIONES Y PRIORIDADES

- Mother stated, “Quiero entender lo que pide. Sometimes he points, then cries porque no sabemos si quiere agua o salir.”
- Father stated, “En español habla más conmigo, but at daycare he gets quiet. Queremos que pueda pedir ayuda without getting so frustrated.”
- Grandmother stated, “No quiero quitarle el español. Que tenga palabras para jugar, comer, y decir cuando algo le molesta.”
- Family priorities are requesting help, joining play, and participating in meals. The family wants strategies that fit ordinary routines without extra homework.
- Parents identified successful communication, rather than perfect pronunciation, as the immediate priority. They want both languages supported.

TRABAJO Y APOYOS FAMILIARES

- Mom works nights at Juniper Lantern Inn as a laundry attendant, from 10:30 p.m. until 6:00 a.m..
- Mother also works as a stock clerk at MVS, from 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on selected afternoons. She has two jobs.
- Father works as a bicycle mechanic at Copper Finch Cycles. His schedule allows him to lead breakfast and daycare drop-off.
- Grandmother provides afternoon care. A cousin, Mariela Soto, occasionally babysits. The family dog, Nube, often joins floor play.
- Family requests visits after the mother's rest period. Transportation is reliable, but changing work shifts can affect attendance.

RUTINAS DIARIAS / DAILY ROUTINES

- Breakfast begins around 7:15 a.m.. Child reaches toward food and brings an empty cup to an adult. Adults sometimes anticipate requests before a gesture or word occurs.
- During dressing, child chooses between shirts when adults hold both options. “Dame tiempo,” father said. “Si esperamos, intenta decir algo.”
- Daycare arrival occurs near 8:20 a.m.. Child watches classmates before approaching toys. Familiar songs help with the transition.
- At dinner, child stays longer when seated beside sister. Bath play includes cups, pouring, and repeated opportunities for requesting.
- Bedtime starts around 8:00 p.m.. Shared picture books work best when adults follow the child's page choices.

GUARDERÍA Y OTRAS AGENCIAS

- Child attends Willow Acorn Early Learning. Lead teacher Ms. Dalia Cruz reports stronger participation during movement songs than during large-group questions.
- Classmates Milo Ortega and Ana Vela regularly offer toy cars. Staff will support simple exchanges without requiring speech before access.
- The family receives nutrition support through Hawthorn Family WIC and activity materials from Bright Meadow Smart Start.
- Pediatrician Dr. Jonas Mercado practices at Cedar Lantern Children's Center. The family reports no current outside speech therapy.
- Coordinator will share agreed strategies with daycare after obtaining the family's release.

HISTORIA Y EVALUACIÓN

- Family reports birth at 39 weeks gestation, birth weight 3.24 kg, and Apgar scores of 8 and 9. These details were not independently verified.
- Evaluation occurred on September 21, 2026. PLS-5 Spanish findings included Auditory Comprehension standard score 78, percentile 7, and confidence interval 73-83.
- Expressive Communication standard score was 74, percentile 4, with confidence interval 69–79. Total Language standard score was 75, percentile 5.
- Reported age equivalents were 2;6–3;0 for comprehension tasks and 1;10–2;2 for expression tasks. These ranges describe test performance, not the child's overall developmental age.
- Scores were considered alongside bilingual observations and family report. English-only performance did not define overall communication ability.

COMUNICACIÓN ACTUAL

- Observed productions included "más", "agua", "go", and "no cabe". Child combined pointing with vocalization to request inaccessible materials.
- During play, child said “Nube come” and “Sol ven.” These utterances contained names and were recorded as meaningful social communication.
- Speech sampling showed variable production of /k/, substitution with [t], and emerging /ɾ/. Intelligibility improved with familiar context.
- A language sample contained an [EW] annotation for an omitted grammatical word. This observation will guide modeling, without requiring correction during every interaction.

OUTCOME 1: PEDIR AYUDA

- By January 11, 2027, child will request help during meals, dressing, and play using a gesture, word, or short combination in 4 of 5 opportunities across familiar adults.
- Adults will pause, offer a useful model, and respond immediately to intentional communication. Models include "ayuda", "help me", and "abre".
- Clinician will use Hanen strategies and coaching within routines. Initial support may include mod cues, with reduction toward min cues.
- Parents will describe successful requests during weekly check-ins. Baseline was 2/10 opportunities with spontaneous communication during the observed snack routine.

OUTCOME 2: JUGAR CON OTROS

- By March 8, 2027, child will complete reciprocal play exchanges in 3 of 5 opportunities during daycare and home play.
- Teacher will arrange paired car play, model "my turn", and accept a gesture as participation. Adults will avoid repeated testing questions.
- Sister may choose picture cards and model the ordinary noun "sol" while discussing sunny weather. Sister's name, Sol, has the same word form.
- Clinician will distinguish naming a person from labeling the sun when documenting language samples. Current participation reached 40% with max cues during unfamiliar peer play.

OUTCOME 3: PARTICIPAR EN COMIDAS

- By April 5, 2027, child will make a choice or indicate completion during family meals in 8/10 opportunities.
- Adults will present manageable choices and model "más arroz", "all done", or "terminé". Child may use either language.
- Family will keep familiar foods available while practicing communication. Mother said, “Que pedir sea fácil; la cena ya tiene suficiente trabajo.”
- Progress will reflect successful participation, including gestures. Clinician will document the adult's support and the routine in which each response occurred.

SERVICIOS, FECHAS Y SEGUIMIENTO

- Speech-language services will occur at home for 45 minutes weekly, from October 12, 2026 through April 5, 2027. Documentation will use CPT 92507, modifier GN, and ICD-10 F80.2.
- Service coordination will occur monthly and when the family requests support. A daycare consultation is planned for November 2, 2026.
- Next review: January 11, 2027. Parents agreed to the listed priorities and requested Spanish explanations of progress.
- Clinician signature: Isabel Ferrer. Coordinator signature: Nadia Beltrán. Signed on October 5, 2026.

Preocupaciones y prioridades / Family voice

The mother said, “Quiero entender lo que necesita antes de que llore. Sometimes I know, but sometimes estoy adivinando.”

The father said, “We want him to ask for help, en español o inglés. We do not want dinner to feel like an exam.”

The family prioritized requesting help, making choices, joining familiar play, and understanding brief directions. They asked the team to accept gestures and words in either language. They also requested practical ideas that fit meals, dressing, and pickup.

We discussed that bilingual exposure alone does not establish a language disorder. Interpretation will consider skills across languages, caregiver reports, observation, and the limits of standardized administration.

Rutinas diarias / Daily routines

Breakfast usually begins around 7:10 AM. The child chooses between two foods, points toward the refrigerator, and brings an empty cup to an adult. Adults often anticipate the request before a gesture or word develops. We will create brief, comfortable opportunities to communicate without withholding needed food.

Dressing follows breakfast. The child helps push an arm through a sleeve but becomes upset when adults give several directions together. The mother can pair one short direction with a gesture, then pause. Success means participation with support, not compliance under pressure.

At The Lantern Orchard, arrival is around 8:20 AM. Teacher Ms. Inés Rueda reports stronger participation with familiar songs and picture choices. Pickup occurs around 3:40 PM. Aunt Paz Herrera sometimes brings the child home. The family wants one shared picture card for requesting help, so adults use a consistent support across settings.

Resultados / Functional outcomes

Outcome 1: During meals and play, the child will communicate a choice or request using a gesture, picture, sign, or word in either language.

The family will offer two meaningful choices, show the objects, and wait briefly. Adults will respond to communication attempts, then model a short phrase. Suggested targets include “más”, “agua”, “help”, and “abre”. We will use responsive interaction informed by Hanen strategies. This does not indicate enrollment in a named course.

Baseline: independent requests occurred in 3 of 10 observed opportunities. With mod cues, participation increased to 8/10, or 80%. Progress will mean independent communication in 4 of 5 natural opportunities across meals and play, reported over consecutive family check-ins.

Outcome 2: During dressing, cleanup, and classroom transitions, the child will participate in a familiar one-step direction with an appropriate visual or gesture support.

Adults will simplify language, show the relevant object, and allow processing time. We will alternate Spanish and English naturally according to the speaker and routine. Targets include “dame”, “put in”, and “zapatos”. Adults should avoid repeated testing questions.

Baseline: participation occurred in 4/10 opportunities with min cues and 7/10 with mod cues. The team will look for 80% participation across two routines. We will record whether support helped, rather than score a distressed response as failure.

Outcome 3: During shared play, the child will sustain enjoyable exchanges with an adult or another child using actions, gestures, sounds, or words.

Strategies include following the child’s interest, copying an action, adding one small variation, and pausing for a response. The clinician will coach adults during blocks and pretend cooking. No forced repetition is planned.

Observed productions included “ma agua”, “up”, and “no tá”. The child also said, “Sol mira,” during the family observation. Emerging sounds included /m/, /p/, and [w]. We will monitor communication without setting an isolated articulation target for /k/ or /ɾ/ at this stage.

Baseline exchanges continued for 2 of 5 opportunities. The family’s desired change is sustained participation in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Session notes may use SALT conventions, including [EW], when analyzing a sample.

Provide weekly speech-language intervention for forty-five minutes in the home or classroom, with caregiver coaching embedded in routines. The usual appointment is Monday at 8:00 AM. The family may request a classroom visit when transition support is the main concern.

Clinical coding: 92507 for applicable treatment; 92523 for the completed evaluation; diagnosis F80.2; modifier GN when required by the payer. Codes describe documentation and billing categories. They do not replace the functional outcomes.

The coordinator will confirm service availability and provide the updated plan in the family’s preferred language. The clinician will document attendance, caregiver practice, communication examples, and supports used. Missed visits will prompt scheduling contact and discussion of barriers.

DOCUMENT INFORMATION / INFORMACIÓN DEL PLAN

- This fictional North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program IFSP review documents family routines, communication needs, agreed outcomes, and early intervention services. All names, organizations, locations, and identifiers are invented.
- Child: Nicolás Ríos Vega, called Nico at home. Date of birth: August 14, 2024. Age at review: 26 months. Home languages are Spanish and English.
- Review date: October 14, 2026. Initial IFSP date: April 14, 2026. Record number: ITP-0627419. Medicaid member number: 000482731Q.
- The family chose a home visit with Spanish discussion and an English summary. Parents reviewed the wording together and requested practical strategies that fit their work schedules.

FAMILY INFORMATION / NUESTRA FAMILIA

- Mother: Mariela Ríos. Father: Esteban Vega. Both parents share caregiving decisions. The family lives at 4827 Plover Gate Lane, Apartment 6, Cedarmere, North Carolina 27900, in Linden Shoal County.
- Sister Sol enjoys songs and picture books. Maternal aunt Dalia Ríos provides afternoon care. The household also includes a dog named Chispa, who often joins floor play.
- Mom works nights at Moonbridge Packaging as a quality checker. She also works weekend mornings at NFS. Her second workplace is identified only by its acronym.
- Dad repairs equipment at Tern Hollow Equipment Repair. Contact mother at (919) 555-0146 or mariela.rios@correo.example. Contact father at (984) 555-0172. Text before calling because shifts change.

SERVICE COORDINATION / COORDINACIÓN

- Service coordinator Ms. Elena Cruz works through Pine Lantern Children’s Developmental Services Agency, the family’s CDSA office. Office address: 216 Willow Arch Road, Cedarmere, North Carolina 27900.
- Coordinator contact: (252) 555-0138, elena.cruz@pinelantern.example. Family information website: https://pinelantern.example/familias. Parents prefer Spanish messages and an English copy when a form requires a signature.
- Reviewing clinician: Adriana Montes, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist employed by Little Lantern Pediatric Therapy. She conducted the visit in both languages and interpreted routine examples within her clinical role.
- The coordinator will confirm appointments, support referrals, and review family satisfaction. The clinician will document language samples and coach caregivers. Parents may request a meeting whenever priorities change.

FAMILY CONCERNS / LO QUE NOS PREOCUPA

- Mother shared, “Cuando no lo entendemos, se tira al piso. I want him to tell us what he needs before everybody gets upset.” Frustration occurs most often during snacks and dressing.
- Father stated, “Entiende más cuando hablamos despacio. At the playground he watches first, then follows. Queremos que pueda pedir ayuda without needing us to guess every time.”
- Mother added, “Con mis dos trabajos, no puedo hacer worksheets every night. Necesitamos ideas durante la comida, el baño y cuando salimos.” The team agreed to use familiar routines.
- Parents worry that daycare staff miss Spanish requests. They want shared examples across settings, without asking the family to stop Spanish. Both languages remain part of everyday interaction.

FAMILY PRIORITIES / LO MÁS IMPORTANTE

- The family’s first priority is successful requesting during meals, play, and transitions. Parents accept gestures, pictures, sounds, and words when the message is clear and the child remains engaged.
- Their next priority is understanding familiar directions during dressing and cleanup. Father said, “Primero que participe con nosotros; después podemos trabajar en palabras más claras.” Participation will guide strategy selection.
- The family wants enjoyable communication with sister Sol. Mother explained, “Ella quiere jugar, pero sometimes she answers for him.” Adults will model waiting without assigning the sibling responsibility for therapy.
- Parents also want consistent daycare responses. The clinician will share brief examples with permission. Family priorities will determine practice opportunities; caregivers can decline a strategy that does not fit.

DAILY ROUTINES / RUTINAS DIARIAS

- Breakfast usually starts at 7:15 a.m.. Father offers familiar foods while mother rests after work. Choices work best when both items are visible and the adult pauses before serving.
- Afternoon care begins around 2:30 p.m.. Aunt Dalia Ríos uses songs during handwashing. The child participates when gestures accompany the words, but becomes quiet when several people speak together.
- Bath time is near 7:00 p.m.. Pouring water supports turn taking. Parents report that short exchanges feel natural aquí, especially when adults follow the child’s interest instead of asking repeated questions.
- Bedtime begins around 8:15 p.m.. Sister Sol chooses a book, and father labels pictures. Weekend routines vary with mother’s shifts, so the plan includes flexible opportunities without a daily homework quota.

CHILDCARE AND COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION

- The child attends Pebble Nest Early Learning Center on weekdays. Lead teacher Ms. Camila Duarte reports strong interest in blocks, vehicles, and songs with predictable gestures.
- Classroom assistant Mr. Jonah Pike observes that peer Mila Torres often offers toys. Peer Owen Bell joins vehicle play. Adults will support exchanges without requiring spoken imitation.
- Sister attends Juniper Arc Primary School. School pickup sometimes overlaps with appointments. Community shuttle driver Arlo Finch knows the family’s usual stop, but receives no clinical information.
- Parents authorized a brief daycare communication summary. Staff may describe participation and helpful supports. They will contact the coordinator if routines change or the family requests a joint visit.

HEALTH AND DEVELOPMENT / SALUD Y DESARROLLO

- Parents report birth at Silver Heron Community Hospital at 38 weeks gestation, with birth weight 6 lb 14 oz. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9.
- Pediatrician Dr. Luciana Reed completed a well visit on September 18, 2026. Parents report no current feeding concerns. The team has not independently verified the birth history.
- Audiologist Micah Lane completed hearing screening on September 25, 2026. The available report describes responses within expected screening limits. Parents will report new concerns about hearing or ear discomfort.
- Existing documentation lists ICD-10 F80.2. Communication needs affect participation across routines. This review describes functional supports and does not establish a new medical diagnosis or replace ongoing pediatric care.

ASSESSMENT / EVALUACIÓN BILINGÜE

- On October 7, 2026, the clinician reviewed prior PLS-5 results: Auditory Comprehension standard score 78, percentile 7th, confidence interval 73-83; Expressive Communication standard score 75, percentile 5th, confidence interval 70-82.
- These scores came from the earlier English administration and require cautious interpretation. Spanish caregiver interviews, play observation, and language sampling provided additional information. Scores alone did not determine the service plan.
- During play, the child followed familiar directions in 6/10 opportunities with min cues. Requests occurred in 3 of 5 supported opportunities. Independent spoken requests represented approximately 40% of observed requests.
- Productions included "ma", "agua", and "go". Initial [ [KEEP|w] ] was transcribed as [w]; emerging sounds included /m/ and /b/. No speech sound drill was added to this review.

OUTCOME 1 / PEDIR LO QUE NECESITA

- During meals and play, the child will communicate a choice or request using a gesture, picture, sound, or word in 8/10 opportunities across familiar routines.
- Adults will use Enhanced Milieu Teaching and focused stimulation, offering choices and waiting. Models may include "más", "agua", "help", and "open", depending on the family’s language.
- Start with mod cues when needed, then reduce support as communication becomes easier. Adults will respond to the message before expanding it; food and essential items remain available.
- Parents and daycare staff will share brief examples at monthly check-ins. Success means more effective participation across settings, with fewer guesses by adults and no requirement to use one language exclusively.

OUTCOME 2 / PARTICIPAR EN LAS RUTINAS

- During dressing and cleanup, the child will follow a familiar direction with a gesture in 4 of 5 opportunities, with min cues, across home and daycare routines.
- Adults will pair short phrases with actions, using targets such as "shoes on", "pon aquí", and "give me". They will allow processing time before repeating the direction.
- Use routines-based intervention during actual activities. If the child becomes frustrated, simplify the step and reconnect. The family does not need to create a separate practice session.
- Caregivers will note which directions work in each language. The clinician will review examples and adjust support when a direction depends on unfamiliar vocabulary, environmental noise, or a rushed transition.

OUTCOME 3 / JUGAR Y COMPARTIR

- During sibling or peer play, the child will complete a reciprocal exchange in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues, using any clear communication form.
- Adults will apply Hanen interaction strategies during books, bubbles, and vehicle play. They will follow the child’s lead, pause, and model short language without requiring repetition.
- Sister Sol may join when she wants. During observation, the child said, “Sol ven.” The clinician treated this as a meaningful invitation and supported the shared play.
- Parents will report whether exchanges feel enjoyable and manageable. The team will adjust materials and adult support before increasing expectations. Progress includes staying engaged and communicating for another turn.

OTHER AGENCIES / APOYOS EN LA COMUNIDAD

- The family receives food support through Linden Shoal Family Nutrition Office. Staff contact Nora Salcedo helps coordinate appointments. Parents requested evening reminder messages whenever that option is available.
- Centro Comunitario de Acompañamiento Familiar y Recursos para la Primera Infancia (CCAFRPI) offers bilingual parent groups and transportation information. The family requested a referral, without sharing assessment scores.
- CCAFRPI will receive only the approved contact details. Linden Shoal Family Assistance Department remains a possible resource for childcare scheduling support; the family has not requested an application.
- The coordinator will confirm referral status at the next contact. Participation in community services is optional and does not change the family’s identified communication priorities or agreed early intervention schedule.

SERVICES, DATES, AND FOLLOW-UP

- Speech-language services: weekly home visits, beginning October 21, 2026 through April 20, 2027, delivered by Adriana Montes, MS, CCC-SLP, through Little Lantern Pediatric Therapy.
- Planned visit time: 4:30 p.m.. Visits include caregiver coaching and direct observation. Billing reference: CPT 92507, modifier GN. Authorization number: AUTH-261021-047.
- Service coordination continues monthly. Next family check-in: November 18, 2026. Formal review: April 14, 2027. The team will begin discussing transition preferences before the next review.
- Parents agreed to the listed priorities and requested Spanish explanations of future forms. Signature acknowledgment was recorded on October 14, 2026. The coordinator will provide copies in the family’s preferred formats.

Información familiar / People and supports

I completed this review with both parents at the family home. Spanish supported the discussion of family priorities; English supported coordination with daycare. The family received explanations in both languages and requested a bilingual summary.

Julián lives with his parents and his sister, Alma Salcedo, age 6 years. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Belén Cifuentes, provides afternoon care. His aunt, Nadia Cifuentes, helps with transportation when work shifts overlap. The family dog, Nube, often joins floor play.

The father works at Harbor Lantern Packaging. The mother works at Cedar Basket Market. Their schedules vary, so the family prefers reminders by text and written practice ideas that any caregiver can use. No employer contact is authorized.

The grandmother previously lived at Casa 14, Calle del Naranjal, Aldea Las Brisitas, Santa Lucera, Guatemala. The family uses video calls to maintain relationships there. During calls, relatives speak Spanish and wait for the child to respond with gestures, sounds, or words.

The family identifies shared meals, music, and helping one another as strengths. Both parents demonstrated patient waiting and noticed small communication attempts. “En nuestra casa hablamos los dos idiomas; queremos que él pueda participar con todos,” the mother explained.

Preocupaciones y prioridades / Family voice

The mother stated, “Yo sé muchas veces lo que quiere, pero cuando estoy cocinando no puedo adivinar todo. Quiero que me pida ayuda sin llorar.” The father added, “Cuando llego del trabajo, quiero entender qué hizo durante el día, aunque sea con una palabra y una seña.”

The parents prioritize requesting help, joining play, and communicating during meals. They do not want Spanish removed from home routines. “No queremos escoger un idioma y perder el otro,” the father said. We discussed accepting meaningful communication in either language and responding to the message.

The grandmother described transitions as difficult: “Si cambiamos de actividad muy rápido, se tira al piso. Si le enseño lo que sigue, entiende mejor.” The family wants a predictable way to move from play to meals and from home to daycare.

The sister wants shared play without taking every toy away to obtain a response. She stated, “Quiero que juegue conmigo y que me diga cuándo le toca.” Adults will supervise practice so that sibling play remains enjoyable.

The family also requested support with unfamiliar listeners. The mother said, “Conmigo habla más; con otras personas se queda mirando.” We agreed to build participation through familiar routines before increasing demands in larger groups.

Historia y evaluación / Clinical review

The pediatrician, Dr. Camila Renée Basto, referred the family after concerns about expressive communication. Parent report describes birth at 38 weeks gestation, birth weight 3.08 kg, and Apgar scores of 8 and 9. These details came from the family’s fictional intake record.

The family reported no recent loss of skills. Hearing follow-up remains scheduled for October 2, 2026 at Cedarbend Children’s Hearing Hospital. Current observations cannot establish hearing status. The coordinator will request the report after the family provides consent.

The bilingual evaluation used PLS-5 Spanish, caregiver interview, play observation, and a language sample. Recorded Auditory Comprehension standard score was 89, percentile 23, with a 90% confidence interval of 83–96. Recorded Expressive Communication standard score was 75, percentile 5, with a 90% confidence interval of 70–82.

The Total Language standard score was 80, percentile 9, with a 90% confidence interval of 74–87. The recorded Expressive Communication age equivalent was 1;6. Scores support the discussion but do not replace evidence from daily participation.

During this review, Juli followed familiar directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. He requested an item or action in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Spontaneous productions included "más", "agua", "up", and "no cabe".

He also said “Nube ven” while pointing toward the doorway. That utterance showed a meaningful attempt to direct another participant. Speech included [ [KEEP|w] ]-like movement in an English word; formal phonetic notation was [w]. Production of /k/ and /ɾ/ was inconsistent in this brief sample. No sound-specific outcome was added.

A sample coded with SALT included [EW] for an unexplained word attempt. Interpretation considered both languages, the activity, and adult familiarity. The working service diagnosis is F80.2. Treatment billing will use 92507 with modifier GN when applicable.

Rutinas diarias / Participation at home and daycare

Morning begins around 6:45 AM. The mother offers breakfast while the father prepares for work. Julián chooses between two familiar foods by reaching or pointing. When adults move quickly, he may cry before they notice his request. A short pause and visible choices helped during observation.

At dressing, he brings shoes to an adult but rarely requests assistance. The family will keep the needed item visible, acknowledge his attempt, and provide help promptly. Practice must not delay leaving home or turn a necessary task into repeated testing.

He attends Little Lantern Grove Daycare on weekdays. Lead teacher Ms. Beatriz Lema and classroom assistant Mr. Owen Pell report stronger participation during songs than during free play. Peer Mila Corven offers pretend food; peer Theo Arlen shares rolling toys.

During lunch, the child sometimes leaves the table when a container is difficult to open. Adults will pair an open-hand gesture with "help" or "ayuda", then respond to any clear attempt. Meals remain opportunities for eating and connection.

The afternoon routine includes grandmother care, outdoor movement, and a quiet book before dinner. At approximately 7:15 PM, the family begins bath and bedtime activities. Water play supports turn-taking, but ending the bath is difficult without advance notice.

Otras agencias / Community participation

The family receives nutrition support through Larkwater Family WIC Office. The coordinator will help align appointments so that service visits do not repeatedly interrupt meals or transportation arrangements.

The family attends a bilingual play circle at Cedarbend Smart Start Partnership. Facilitator Elena Paz Montoro provides songs, books, and open play. The mother values this group because caregivers can participate in Spanish without translating every interaction.

On Saturdays, the family visits Willow Lantern Community Library for its family story program. Program host Graham Solis welcomes movement and allows children to observe before joining. The family wants the child to stay for one short story and one song.

Occupational therapist Tessa Mirel Boone, OTR/L, addresses participation in dressing and meals. Physical therapist Adrian Lucero Finch, PT, DPT, reviews balance and access to playground activities. Interpreter Paula Inés Roldán supports visits conducted by providers who do not speak Spanish.

Resultados funcionales / Outcomes and strategies

Outcome 1: During meals and play, Julián will communicate requests for items, actions, or help using gestures, words, or combined forms.

The family selected a criterion of 4 of 5 natural opportunities across two familiar routines. Adults will document examples rather than create extra demands. Target words include "más", "abre", "help", and "otra vez".

We will use enhanced milieu teaching and caregiver coaching. Adults will follow his interest, pause briefly, offer an accessible model, and respond to the attempt. Start with mod cues and reduce support toward min cues as participation improves.

Outcome 2: During shared play, the child will initiate or continue an exchange with a caregiver, sibling, or peer.

The criterion is 3 of 5 observed opportunities during a familiar play activity. Strategies include rolling a ball, feeding toy animals, and taking turns with a simple vehicle ramp. Adults will accept a look, gesture, sound, or word as a turn.

Targets include "mi turno", "go", and "mira". The clinician will use Hanen strategies to help adults notice and extend communication. Adults will avoid requiring repetition before every turn. The sister may participate when she chooses, with adult support.

Outcome 3: During routine changes, the child will communicate readiness, a need for help, or a request for a brief pause.

The family selected 80% successful participation across recorded transitions. A successful transition includes access to communication and adult support; crying alone does not indicate failure. Adults will show the next activity, describe it briefly, and allow time to respond.

Targets include "terminé", "wait", and "vamos". Pictures will show familiar activities. They are visual supports within total communication, rather than a requirement to use PECS. Begin with max cues when needed and reduce assistance gradually.

Outcome 4: During books and community songs, the child will join a shared activity through looking, pointing, movement, sounds, or words.

The criterion is participation in 3 of 4 opportunities within one short activity. We will use dialogic reading with familiar pictures and predictable pauses. Targets include "otra página", "all done", and "aquí".

The family may leave or shorten a group activity when participation becomes difficult. Community practice will follow the child’s interest and regulation. Progress will reflect useful engagement, not quiet sitting.

Calendario de sesiones / Planned service schedule

| Service | Day | Start | Stop | Location |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bilingual speech-language therapy | Monday | 9:00 AM | 10:00 AM | Home: 482 Willow Lantern Lane, Apt 3B, Cedarbend, NC 27906 |
| Occupational therapy | Wednesday | 3:15 PM | 4:00 PM | Little Lantern Grove Daycare |
| Physical therapy consultation, monthly | Thursday | 10:30 AM | 11:00 AM | Little Lantern Grove Daycare |
| Service coordination, monthly | Friday | 12:15 PM | 12:45 PM | Parent telephone visit |
| Supported community observation, once | Saturday | 10:00 AM | 10:30 AM | Willow Lantern Community Library |

Speech-language and occupational therapy begin September 21, 2026 and September 23, 2026, respectively. Physical therapy consultation begins September 24, 2026. The community observation is planned for October 10, 2026, with family agreement.

Weekly speech visits last 60 minutes, including caregiver practice and planning. Occupational therapy visits last 45 minutes. The team will confirm monthly consultation dates individually. Travel problems or illness may require rescheduling within the authorized service period.

Coordinación, seguimiento y acuerdo

Dana Mercer will coordinate provider updates and obtain the hearing report. Paula Roldán will interpret the first occupational therapy visit if the family requests Spanish support. Providers will send brief summaries using the family’s preferred language and agreed contact method.

The parents will record one useful example from a routine when practical. No daily worksheet is required. The team will review participation, cueing needs, and family burden before adding strategies.

At the next review on December 11, 2026, the team will compare routine examples with the criteria for each outcome. The mother summarized her agreement: “Sí, esto nos sirve. Podemos practicar cuando estamos viviendo el día, sin hacer otra tarea grande.”

I reviewed the plan aloud in Spanish and English. Both parents reported that the outcomes reflect their priorities. They requested copies for home and daycare, with consent limited to the providers and classroom staff named in this document.

Rutinas, participación y evaluación

In play, Nicolás followed familiar directions in 8/10 opportunities, or 80%, with mod cues. He independently requested in 3 of 5 opportunities when desired materials were visible. His mother reported, “Yesterday he said ‘Chispa ven,’ and everyone stopped to listen.” The team recorded that example as a family report.

Other supports include Centro Comunitario de Acompañamiento al Desarrollo y Participación Familiar (CCADPF), which offers Spanish family groups and transportation planning. CCADPF contact worker Dalia Mena will provide a calendar after parental consent. Resultados y estrategias

Outcome 1: During meals and play, Nico will communicate a choice or request using a gesture, picture, sign, or word in 4 of 5 opportunities across two familiar routines.
